papers.abstract: Dexterity is, at its core, finger-level control, yet existing dexterous manipulation and human-object interaction (HOI) generation methods rarely let one specify how an interaction is performed: five-fingered hands are often reduced to grippers, or finger usage is copied from individual human demonstrations. We present FineDex, a framework that makes finger-level intent both expressible and executable. FineDex learns coordinated human body, hand, and object motions that follow fine-grained instructions on hand selection, individual fingers, and contacts with articulated objects. To bridge generation and execution, FineDex leverages generated interactions as actionable priors for an agent that discovers physically feasible contact strategies through practice in a physics-based digital twin. By adapting at test time without per-instance retraining, FineDex generalizes across fine-grained instructions and object configurations. Experiments demonstrate state-of-the-art HOI generation quality and fine-grained controllability, substantial improvements in dexterous manipulation success, and successful deployment on a real dexterous humanoid robot.
authors: Yujia Zeng, Yuxin Chen, Yuzhen Song, Runhan Huang, Chensheng Peng, Yiyang Shao, Koushil Sreenath, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Yilun Du
bullets: Addresses the lack of explicit control over hand choice, individual fingers, and contacts in existing HOI generation and manipulation methods.
Jointly generates coordinated human body, hand, and articulated-object motions conditioned on fine-grained interaction instructions.
Uses generated interactions as actionable priors for physics-based practice to discover feasible contact strategies.
Adapts at test time across instructions and object configurations without per-instance retraining.
Reports state-of-the-art HOI generation and controllability, improved manipulation success, and real humanoid-robot deployment.

papers.title: FineDex: Bridging Fine-Grained Human-Object Interaction Generation to Dexterous Humanoid Manipulation
papers.tldr: FineDex generates finger-level human–object interactions from detailed instructions and turns them into executable dexterous robot manipulation strategies.

papers.abstract: A first-person (ego) image reveals what a camera sees, but not who or what carries it. Given a synchronized third-person (exo) image, camera wearer identification asks who is ego: which candidate carries the ego camera? We extend this task beyond humans to robots, vehicles, animals, and drones, and broaden its spatial scope (where is ego) from selecting a provided candidate mask to wearer segmentation with absence prediction and mutual camera localization across ego-exo views. We introduce FindEgo-1M, comprising 1.16M real and simulated ego-exo pairs across 12 wearer types, 17 domains, and 111 test settings. Our approach exploits a geometric relation: the ego camera's projection into the exo image, i.e., the epipole, lies on or near its wearer. We introduce EgoRay-ZS, the first method to turn a frozen feed-forward 3D reconstruction model, VGGT-$\Omega$, into a training-free solution for wearer identification and segmentation. Its geometric readout ranks candidate masks or segmentation proposals by angular offset and distance to the ego camera, while the relative pose provides mutual camera directions. We then develop the full EgoRay model through pose-supervised training on FindEgo-1M and label-free test-time adaptation constrained by candidate masks. Without task-specific training, EgoRay-ZS achieves 78.0% identification accuracy on TF2023's original labels, versus 52.9% reported for the dataset-trained PEN. On FindEgo-1M, EgoRay achieves state-of-the-art chance-corrected accuracy of 87.1 and 77.7 on seen and unseen settings. On matched queries, EgoRay also outperforms GPT-6 Astra by 31.6 and 21.3 points on seen and unseen settings, respectively, while running $18\times$ faster. Data, code, and models will be released.
authors: Yifan Jin, Zheng Zhang, Tianwen Qian, Dong Wang, Bo Zhao, Yanwei Fu, Yuqian Fu
bullets: Extends camera-wearer identification from humans to robots, vehicles, animals, and drones, while adding wearer segmentation, absence prediction, and mutual camera localization.
Introduces FindEgo-1M, with 1.16M real and simulated ego–exo image pairs spanning 12 wearer types, 17 domains, and 111 test settings.
EgoRay-ZS uses the ego camera’s projected epipole and a frozen 3D reconstruction model for training-free candidate ranking and segmentation.
The fully developed EgoRay adds pose-supervised training and label-free test-time adaptation constrained by candidate masks.
EgoRay reaches 87.1% and 77.7% chance-corrected accuracy on seen and unseen settings, respectively, and is faster and more accurate than the reported baselines in the abstract.

papers.selection_reason: Ego-exo camera wearer identification and segmentation using feed-forward 3D reconstruction; relevant to egocentric video learning and 3D vision.
papers.title: Who Is Ego? Scaling Cross-View Camera Wearer Identification and Segmentation beyond Humans
papers.tldr: EgoRay uses cross-view geometry from 3D reconstruction to identify and segment the wearer of an ego camera—including nonhuman carriers—without requiring task-specific training.

papers.abstract: Human videos are abundant and cheap to obtain, whereas robot trajectories remain scarce and costly, making zero-shot skill transfer from a single human demonstration an appealing route to scalable robot learning. Existing methods, however, either retarget human-specific geometry or match only static visual goals, and thus stumble over the cross-embodiment dynamics mismatch and the ungrounded action execution. We present the Co-World Model (CoWM), a predictive framework jointly optimized from paired yet unsynchronized human and robot streams. To bridge the cross-embodiment dynamics gap, CoWM disentangles each observation into a shared object-relation state and embodiment-specific context. It aligns latent actions across embodiments using effect-swap and action-sensitivity objectives,such that actions are matched by their predicted effects on the manipulated objects rather than by embodimentdependent kinematics. For grounded execution, a phase-aware receding-horizon controller estimates demonstration progress, projects the inferred human action prior onto the robot action-support density, and translates the resulting latent dynamics into executable robot commands. Extensive experiments in simulation and on two physical robot platforms demonstrate the effectiveness of CoWM, its cross-platform generalizability, and the contribution of each component. See the demo video in the supporting information for details.
authors: Xuetao Li, Xuan Jiang, Chen Liu, Zhongrui Rao, Yu Ling, Hui Wang, Sheng Liu, Miao Li
bullets: Addresses scarce robot data and cross-embodiment dynamics mismatch in human-video-to-robot transfer.
Jointly learns from paired but unsynchronized human and robot streams.
Disentangles shared object-relation states from embodiment-specific context.
Aligns actions by their predicted effects on manipulated objects, rather than kinematic similarity.
Experiments in simulation and on two physical robot platforms show effectiveness, cross-platform generalizability, and contributions from its components.

figures.caption: Figure 2 Overview of the Co-World Model. Training (bottom): a frozen tracker with DINOv2 features factorizes paired yet unsynchronized human and robot streams into a shared object-relation state st with embodiment-private contexts ph,pr (Eq. (2)), while motion encoders map both streams into common latent actions uh,ur (Eq. (3)). The shared transition Ds (Eq. (13)) yields predicted object effects δ(s,u) (Eq. (1)), which the effect-swap loss (Eq. (15)) matches across embodiments while the action-sensitivity margin (Eq. (16)) separates different-effect actions. Test (top): given a single unseen human video, phase tracking (Eq. (33)) selects the human action prior Uh, a residual proposal corrects it with the robot state (Eq. (27)), and receding-horizon CEM planning (Eq. (39)) under the DP action-support density prden converts the shared latent evolution into executable commands, yielding zero-shot skill transfer.

Figure 1 Human-video-to-robot zero-shot transfer with the Co-World Model. Given a single unseen human demonstration (top film strip), the robot reasons in a co-constructed latent space where human and robot latent actions are bound to a shared latent world model by their predicted object effects, and grounds the induced plan into executable commands on its own embodiment (bottom film strip), acquiring the skill after watching the person once.

Figure 8 Real-robot rollouts on three representative tasks. (a) Placement: placing a cup onto a plate; (b) Transport: handing over a card; (c) Rearrangement: rearranging drinks into the color-matched plates. In each panel, the left block shows the human demonstration (top row) and the task executed by Platform B (bottom row), and the right block shows the task executed by Platform A.

Figure 4 Physical-robot zero-shot transfer. (a) Physical robot platforms used in the zero-shot transfer experiments. Left: Platform A, a humanoid robot whose 7-DoF arm ends in a dexterous hand. Right: Platform B, a table-mounted 6-DoF manipulator equipped with a dexterous hand. The frozen simulator-selected CoWM configuration is deployed on both platforms without per-platform tuning; test human videos are captured in situ and never paired with robot trajectories. (b) Qualitative zero-shot transfer on the physical platforms. Each column pairs the unseen human demonstration (top) with the corresponding robot execution (bottom) on three representative tabletop tasks, placing a cup onto a plate (Placement), handing over a card (Transport), and rearranging drinks into the color-matched plates (Rearrangement).

Figure 6 Cross-benchmark transfer and robot-data efficiency. (a) Results on the ManiSkill benchmark. Success rates on five ManiSkill task families under the LIBERO-selected configuration without per-benchmark tuning. (b) Robot-data efficiency with a fixed human stream. Bars give SR with 10–100% of the robot data, the curve the final object error, and the dashed line the matched world-model MPC on full data.

Figure 3 Hand tracking for the human stream. Left: joint-angle-only tracking adopted by prior methods. Middle: MANO-based hand mesh estimation. Right: our tracker combines the joint-angle estimates with the MANO mesh to produce the hand tracks ht consumed by CoWM.

Figure 5 Qualitative zero-shot transfer in simulation. Each numbered pair shows the unseen human demonstration (left) and the corresponding robot execution (right) at matched task phases on (a) the LIBERO benchmark and (b) the ManiSkill benchmark. Given one unseen human video, CoWM tracks the demonstrated object-relation evolution in the shared latent space and reproduces it with its own embodiment in both simulators (see the supplementary video for complete rollouts).

Figure 7 Visualization of world-model prediction in the DINOv2 feature space. Each of the two panels shows three held-out sequences (rows). Column ❶: the ground-truth observation (GT). Column ❷: the reconstruction decoded from the latent encoded directly from the observed goal frame (Goal-latent recon), which bounds what the decoder can recover. Column ❸: the reconstruction decoded from the latent rolled out by the shared dynamics Ds from an earlier state and the intervening latent actions (Pred-latent recon). The predicted latents preserve the object configuration and contact structure of the ground truth at a fidelity close to the goal-latent bound, so the rollout errors of the shared dynamics remain small in the task-relevant content rather than only in feature norm.

papers.selection_reason: Co-constructed shared latent dynamics for human-video-to-robot transfer.
papers.title: Co-World Model for Human-Video-to-Robot Transfer via Co-Constructed Shared Latent Dynamics
papers.tldr: CoWM enables zero-shot transfer of skills from a single human video to robots by learning shared object-centric dynamics and grounding them through phase-aware control.

papers.abstract: Physical hand interaction depends on configuration, contact, and force, yet nearly identical appearances can conceal different contact states and exerted forces. We therefore formulate physical hand state estimation from egocentric video and wrist surface electromyography (sEMG), combining visual geometry with neuromuscular evidence to jointly recover these coupled components. To support this task, we introduce EgoMyo, a benchmark spanning 5.75M video frames, 50 participants, 34 contact configurations, and repeated donnings, synchronizing these inputs with 3D hand pose and with contact and normal force registered onto the hand surface from bare-hand pressure. Controlled analysis reveals that vision resolves spatial structure while sEMG better estimates force magnitude, that sEMG's gains concentrate in regions where vision is least reliable, and that contact localization limits force accuracy. Guided by these findings, we propose MyoBridge, which makes the hand region the unit of vision-sEMG fusion, lets each region gate its own share of sEMG, and distributes regional force magnitudes only over predicted contact vertices at inference. On held-out trials, MyoBridge reduces pose and force error by 39.8% and 18.5% over the strongest baseline and achieves the lowest pose error on unseen sessions and subjects.
authors: Guanglong Sun, Kanglei Zhou, Ziteng Wang, Nana Wang, Hengkai Tan, Xiaolong Liu, Hang Su, Yi Zhong, Jun Zhu
bullets: Physical hand state estimation is challenging because similar visual appearances can hide different contact states and exerted forces.
EgoMyo synchronizes egocentric video and wrist sEMG with 3D hand pose, surface contact, and normal force measurements across diverse participants, configurations, and repeated donnings.
Analysis finds that vision captures spatial structure best, while sEMG better estimates force magnitude, especially where vision is unreliable.
MyoBridge performs region-level vision-sEMG fusion, with learned regional sEMG gating and force allocation restricted to predicted contact vertices.
On held-out trials, it reduces pose error by 39.8% and force error by 18.5% versus the strongest baseline; contact localization remains a limitation for force accuracy.

papers.selection_reason: Physical hand state estimation from egocentric video and sEMG; directly relevant to egocentric video learning and embodied interaction.
papers.title: EgoMyo: Physical Hand State Estimation from Egocentric Video and Wrist Electromyography
papers.tldr: EgoMyo introduces a multimodal benchmark and MyoBridge model that combine egocentric video with wrist sEMG to estimate hand pose, contact, and force, improving pose and force accuracy on held-out trials.

papers.abstract: Language-instructed manipulation requires robust closedloop policies, yet action-labeled robot trajectories are costly and limited in coverage. Human and robot videos provide complementary spatiotemporal priors for crossembodiment control. We propose X-World, which adapts pretrained video diffusion to variable views. A Q-Former compresses hidden states into tokens for a shared flowmatching expert that predicts action chunks. Datasetspecific projections map native states and actions. We adapt the backbone on large-scale robot and human videos, freeze it for action-only pretraining of the Q-Former and action expert, then post-train on the target platform. At inference, X-World responds at 20 Hz and overlaps updates with execution via asynchronous real-time chunking. X-World performs strongly on LIBERO and under zero-shot shifts on LIBERO-Plus. On hardware, it averages 81.7% success across six bimanual tasks on the side-mounted dual-arm UR5e, one of three real-robot configurations presented.
authors: Chun Gu, Xiaofei Wei, Yiming Chen, Juntong Zhang, Li Zhang
bullets: Addresses the cost and limited coverage of action-labeled robot trajectories.
Adapts pretrained video diffusion to variable views using a Q-Former and shared flow-matching action expert.
Uses dataset-specific projections to handle different states and actions, followed by target-platform post-training.
Reports strong performance on LIBERO and zero-shot shifts on LIBERO-Plus.
Achieves 81.7% average success across six bimanual tasks on a side-mounted dual-arm UR5e configuration.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of X-World. The video backbone is first adapted on robot and human videos with one to three camera views (left). A layer-aligned Q-Former then compresses its features into fixed-length tokens that condition the action DiT, while dataset-specific projections map native states and actions to and from the shared expert (right). Action pretraining learns this interface with the video backbone frozen; target-domain post-training updates all modules using video and action supervision.

papers.abstract: A growing body of recent work addresses the retargeting of human hand-object demonstrations to robotic hands. To train whole-robot policies, however, the retargeted motions must be kinematically feasible and physically executable, and be produced efficiently at scale. We present DexEngine, a simulation pipeline that turns human manipulation data into train-ready, physically executable arm-hand trajectories. DexEngine first places each clip's hand-object motion where the arms can reach it, finds an arm motion that follows the human hands, and then corrects the motion in physics simulation with residual reinforcement learning. From nine human hand-object datasets, we generate about 5,200 clips for each of four dexterous hands, augmented into 65,000 trajectories (116 h) and 325,000 episodes (578 h) in total. Even with arms attached, DexEngine tracks objects more accurately than prior floating-hand methods and runs over 10x faster than RL-based ones. Policies trained on our data far outperform those trained on the same clips without physics correction or with the arms attached after a floating-hand correction, showing that fine-tuning data need physics correction. Mid-training on our data further improves them at equal fine-tuning budget, in simulation and on a real robot.
authors: Wongyun Yu, Honggeun Kim, Donguk Lee, Minchan Kim, Kyoung Whan Choe, Minsu Cho
bullets: Addresses the need for kinematically feasible, physics-corrected arm-hand motions when retargeting human demonstrations.
Uses reachable scene placement, arm-motion tracking, and residual reinforcement learning in simulation to correct trajectories.
Processes nine datasets into roughly 5,200 clips per hand, expanded to 65,000 trajectories and 325,000 episodes.
Tracks objects more accurately than floating-hand methods while running over 10× faster than RL-based alternatives.
Physics-corrected data improves policy performance in simulation and on a real robot, including when used during mid-training.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video records what a person looks at, but often misses what their body does: the hands leave the frame, and arm motion goes unseen. An exocentric camera recovers this context, but it must be installed wherever the activity happens. Active acoustic sensing can recover it from the wearables themselves: a device's speaker emits inaudible chirps, and its microphone senses the motion of the hands, arms, and nearby objects from their echoes. Yet no public dataset pairs it with egocentric video. We present EgoCARBS, with two deliverables. The first is a multimodal dataset and benchmark: 15 participants cook unscripted meals in their own kitchens wearing camera glasses and an off-the-shelf smartwatch that both sense with active acoustics, synchronized with egocentric and exocentric video and the watch's audio and IMU, with 4,019 verb-noun action annotations in 11.4 hours. The second is a study of what the wearables add to egocentric video. On verb recognition, they add at least as much as an exocentric camera for participants seen in training, and even more for new participants, for whom the exocentric camera does not help. Active acoustics alone provides most of this gain, and helps most where the camera does not see the hands. Trimmed action recognition, detection, and anticipation remain open. We will release the data, our data collection and annotation tools, and pre-trained models.
authors: Saif Mahmud, Vineet Parikh, Bharath Hariharan, Cheng Zhang
bullets: Addresses the limitation that egocentric cameras often miss hand and arm movements during activities such as cooking.
Provides synchronized egocentric/exocentric video, smartwatch active acoustics, audio, and IMU data from 15 participants cooking in their own kitchens.
Includes 11.4 hours of recordings and 4,019 verb–noun action annotations, with benchmarks for action understanding.
Wearable sensing matches or exceeds the benefit of an exocentric camera for verb recognition, especially for unseen participants.
Active acoustics supplies most of the improvement and is most useful when the camera cannot see the hands; trimmed recognition, detection, and anticipation remain open.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon human-scene interaction requires coordinated spatial reasoning, physical feasibility, and the ability to recover from compounding execution errors. Text-driven motion models are largely scene-agnostic and lack closed-loop correction, while geometry-conditioned approaches depend on paired scene-motion training or explicit 3D preprocessing that limits generalization to novel layouts and open-vocabulary goals. We present InteractAgent, an agentic multimodal LLM system for long-horizon human-scene interaction that plans, executes, observes, and reflects in a closed loop, using a single MLLM as both planner and evaluator and a frozen MotionLLM as the executor. InteractAgent integrates Online Observation for step-wise recovery decisions (continue/redo/replan) and Memory-Augmented Reflection for multi-round plan refinement with adaptive stopping. On UniHSI, InteractAgent improves task success and reduces penetration compared with training-free baselines. Code: https://github.com/AIGeeksGroup/InteractAgent.
bullets: Addresses scene-agnostic text-driven motion generation and error accumulation in long-horizon interactions.
Uses one multimodal LLM as planner and evaluator, with a frozen MotionLLM executing motions.
Performs step-wise recovery via continue, redo, or replan decisions.
Refines plans across multiple rounds with memory-augmented reflection and adaptive stopping.
On UniHSI, improves task success and reduces penetration versus training-free baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of InteractAgent. Our framework couples a single multimodal LLM with a frozen MotionLLM executor. Two key components enable training-free, long-horizon interaction generation: (1) Online Observation provides step-wise visual feedback during execution, allowing the MLLM to correct local deviations; (2) Memory-Augmented Reflection aggregates planning–execution histories across rounds and refines future plans at the trajectory level. Together, these mechanisms form a dual-layer reflective loop that progressively improves motion quality and scene consistency.
Figure B.2: Online Observation example (steps 3–4 and final plan).
Figure 3. Trajectory visualization image used as a compact reflection signal for the MLLM.

Table 2. Comparison of SR and PC (Y/N decided by human) across different LLM types.

papers.title: InteractAgent: Agentic Human Motion Interaction with Memory-Augmented Reflection
papers.tldr: InteractAgent enables long-horizon human–scene interaction through closed-loop planning, execution, observation, and memory-based reflection.

papers.abstract: Real-world egocentric videos capture multi-step household procedures, but their recorded trajectories leave alternative actions and recovery from the learner's own mistakes largely unexplored. We introduce EgoVine, a post-training framework that turns a fixed demonstration set into interactive experience for long-horizon planning. EgoVine operates in executable symbolic environments compiled from real-world video annotations, where an agent must coordinate object manipulations under partial observation and account for delayed consequences. Restoring a decision state allows the learner to explore alternative actions and compare their eventual outcomes. Union jointly trains action generation and consequence prediction in one model, using the same executions to supervise candidate comparison and recovery. Verified repairs add recovery targets from failed attempts, while comparisons among sampled continuations guide policy updates. The updated planner then returns to the environments, with its own decisions and mistakes shaping the next round of experience. On a shared benchmark, EgoVine-1.5B achieves 81.8% success on Main planning tasks and 66.7% on longer task compositions, outperforming all evaluated Flash LLM baselines on both. EgoVine connects real demonstrations to an iterative learning process that trains compact planners on choices and futures beyond the recorded trajectories.
bullets: Converts annotated egocentric videos into executable symbolic environments with partial observation and delayed consequences.
Restores decision states to compare alternative actions and their eventual outcomes beyond recorded trajectories.
Jointly trains action generation and consequence prediction, while verified repairs provide recovery targets from failures.
Iteratively feeds the planner’s own decisions and mistakes back into subsequent experience.
EgoVine-1.5B reaches 81.8% success on main tasks and 66.7% on longer compositions, outperforming evaluated Flash LLM baselines.

papers.abstract: People can anticipate how an object moves and the effort an interaction may require by watching others. How can embodied agents acquire this understanding from video? Force measurements provide direct sensory supervision, but require specialized equipment and remain limited in quantity. We introduce VidForce, which estimates an interaction trajectory together with a force profile from a third-person RGB video; 2D contact clicks and textual object-action prompts are optional. Our approach makes limited instrumented measurements useful for interpreting human interactions through learned physical prototypes as a prior. The prototypes share learned force levels and temporal profiles across interactions of comparable effort, with visual and semantic cues determining their contribution to each observation. Geometric and vision-language features adapt this prior to the observed interaction, while a joint conditional flow refines an initial tracked trajectory together with the force profile. Paired human and instrumented-gripper recordings provide measured force references for supervising human video, and a separately trained torque model demonstrates that the formulation extends to other sensory quantities. We evaluate trajectory recovery and force estimation through baseline comparisons and controlled ablations on held-out interactions from the Hoi! dataset. On this evaluation subset, VidForce achieves 6.6 cm ATE, peak-force MAE and RMSE of 4.81 N and 5.92 N, respectively, and force-profile RMSE of 5.52 N. On real-world videos, VidForce infers motion and force reliably and consistently despite the variability in human execution. We further deploy VidForce on a Spot robot, where trajectories and force profiles estimated from human demonstrations drive real-world articulated-object manipulation, and report success rates across repeated trials. Project page: https://rafaymhddn.github.io/vidforce
authors: Rafay Mohiuddin, Jiaqi Chen, Marc Pollefeys, Hermann Blum
bullets: Addresses the scarcity and cost of force-measured interaction data for learning physical understanding from video.
Uses learned physical prototypes capturing shared force levels and temporal profiles across similarly effortful interactions.
Combines visual, semantic, geometric, and optional 2D contact cues, then jointly refines trajectories and force profiles with a conditional flow model.
Evaluated on held-out Hoi! interactions, achieving 6.6 cm trajectory ATE and force-profile RMSE of 5.52 N, with peak-force MAE/RMSE of 4.81/5.92 N.
Demonstrates transfer to torque prediction and deploys video-derived trajectories and forces for Spot robot manipulation; performance is evaluated across repeated trials.

papers.title: VidForce: Predicting Force-Aware Articulation by Observing Humans
papers.tldr: VidForce infers object articulation trajectories and interaction forces from third-person human RGB video, enabling force-aware robotic manipulation without requiring instrumented demonstrations for every interaction.

papers.abstract: Reasoning about human-object interaction from RGB cameras is important for gaming, VR environments, and robot learning. Yet 4D reconstruction from a monocular RGB camera is challenging, especially when articulated hands are involved. Prior full-body works neglect hands during reconstruction, causing them to penetrate into, or float from the object. We present HARI4D, a hand-articulation-aware method for reconstructing spatially and temporally consistent 4D human-object interaction from monocular RGB video. We introduce a history-aware object tracker that provides robust and stable tracking. Based on these tracks, we improve the interaction configuration through coarse-to-fine reasoning that follows the order of object manipulation: ReachNet first brings the full body and arms to the object during contact, and TouchNet then finalizes hand articulation according to temporal context and local object geometry. On ARCTIC, unseen in training, our method reduces the object error by 56% and improves hand contact F1 from 0.866 to 0.921 over prior art. Our method recovers accurate full body-object interaction with coherent hand articulations and applies to online videos. Our code and pretrained models will be released.
authors: Semin Kim, Xianghui Xie, Chuqiao Li, Jongyoo Kim, Gerard Pons-Moll
bullets: Targets hand penetration and floating artifacts in prior full-body reconstruction methods.
Uses a history-aware object tracker for robust, stable object motion estimation.
Applies coarse-to-fine interaction reasoning: ReachNet positions the body and arms, while TouchNet refines hand articulation using temporal context and object geometry.
On the unseen ARCTIC benchmark, reduces object error by 56% and raises hand-contact F1 from 0.866 to 0.921 over prior work.
Supports accurate full-body interaction reconstruction and online video processing.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Method Overview. Starting from foundation models, we initialize the human pose and metric-scale object mesh (Sec. 3.1). We then train a history conditioned object pose tracker to robustly track the object pose under dynamic movement occlusions (Sec. 3.2). We obtain plausible full body and hand articulations via coarse to fine interaction reasoning (Sec. 3.3), starting from ReachNet that brings the human and arms to the object when necessary, and then TouchNet which refines hand-object surface contacts.

Figure 3. Generalization to the ARCTIC dataset [12], unseen in training. CARI4D [73] does not model hand articulation and GraspHOI struggles to optimize wrist pose, leading to penetrations. Our method models interaction temporally and produces accurate full body interaction together with plausible hand contacts.

Figure 6. Architectures of ReachNet and TouchNet, with tensor shapes, where b is the batch size and t the number of frames. Each block applies temporal self-attention, spatial self-attention over the tokens of a frame, and a feed-forward layer.

Figure 4. Qualitative evaluation for BEHAVE dataset [3]. InterTrack [72] reconstructs object as a point cloud with hand penetration or missing contacts. Our method recovers accurate full body and object poses together with coherent hand-object surface interaction.

Figure 5. Ablation examples. Single head ReachNet (Tab. 3f) predicts inaccurate wrist positions due to a swing caused by collar rotation. Without contact labels the model (Tab. 3e) misses contact observed from the input image.

Figure 7. Failure cases, each shown as the input frame, our result from the input camera, and a close-up from another viewpoint with the object drawn semi-transparent. Left: on BEHAVE, the box hides the right hand over a long span, and the hand ends up inside the box as no information is available to infer the right hand. Right: in a video in the wild, the fingertips pass through the thin handle of a gas cylinder. Red marks the volume where the hand and the object intersect.

Table 1. Comparison on ARCTIC [12]. Contact is evaluated on hand vertices, and MJ2O on hand joints and fingertips. ∗ denotes 1 fps key frames only and † means cm/s2 for video frames at 1fps. Our method consistently outperforms baselines on all metrics.

Table 3. Ablation studies. We ablate our object tracking, ReachNet, and TouchNet design choices. Rows a–c pair each object tracker with the unrefined SAM 3D Body human, and rows d–g refine the human with the same object from c.

Table 2. Comparison on BEHAVE [3]. The “At contact” columns are measured when the ground-truth body is in contact with the object, contact scores are evaluated on whole body vertices, and MJ2O on the 22 body joints. Our method achieves more accurate human and object shapes, smoother motion, much less penetration and on par body contacts.

Table 5. Additional ablation on our object tracking designs on ARCTIC. “fine-tuned, no history” uses the refiner fine-tuned on our training data without the history branch. “w/o rescue, fill, slide” turns off the silhouette rescue and the contact-depth slide during tracking and the occlusion fill after it (Sec. 6.2).

Table 6. Weights of the ReachNet loss terms, listed by their group in Eq. (2), applied in every refinement iteration. Terms marked “both” are used on GRAB and BEHAVE, and terms marked “GRAB” on GRAB only, as these losses are not applicable to BEHAVE due to its limited annotation. The “body/hand vertices” terms place the body and hand, and the “centered” terms keep the shape and orientation errors from being outweighed when the hand is in the wrong place, where a large position error would otherwise dominate the plain vertex error.

papers.title: HARI4D: Hand-Articulation Aware 4D Reconstruction of Human-Object Interaction
papers.tldr: HARI4D reconstructs temporally consistent 4D human-object interactions from monocular RGB video by explicitly modeling hand articulation and contact.

papers.abstract: Recovering the continuous world-space motion of both hands from egocentric video is essential for applications such as human-to-robot policy transfer and augmented reality. Achieving this goes beyond reconstructing the hands from each individual frame, as the context that a frame needs is often spread over time, especially around occlusions or when a hand moves out of sight. Recent works have explored how to exploit temporal context, yet they mostly draw it from fixed-length windows. Such windows cannot guarantee that every frame has the context required to reconstruct the hands in world space with accurate poses and metric scale. To address this limitation, we introduce MemHand, a memory-enhanced framework for world-space hand motion reconstruction. MemHand maintains two complementary forms of memory. The Short-Term Event Memory keeps the context of the well-observed hand around each occlusion or out-of-sight event and supplies it to frames with weak or missing visual evidence. In addition, since the metric scale holds over the whole recording, the Long-Term Scale Memory retains the most reliable observations across the video as scale anchors within a bounded state. Across benchmarks featuring severe occlusions and frequent out-of-sight intervals, MemHand achieves state-of-the-art accuracy and generalizes well to unseen domains. Benefiting from the synergy of both memories, it cuts W-MPJPE by 57\% on ARCTIC and 70\% on HOT3D relative to StableHand, delivering continuous and metrically accurate world-space hand poses and trajectories. We will release our code and models at the project page: https://irmvlab.github.io/memhand.github.io
authors: Junyi Ma, Zhangshuo Qi, Erhang Zhang, Mingjie Li, Hesheng Wang
bullets: Targets failures caused by occlusions and hands moving out of view, where fixed temporal windows may lack sufficient context.
Uses Short-Term Event Memory to transfer well-observed hand context to frames with weak or missing visual evidence.
Uses Long-Term Scale Memory to preserve reliable metric-scale anchors throughout an entire recording.
Reports 57% and 70% W-MPJPE reductions versus StableHand on ARCTIC and HOT3D, respectively, with strong cross-domain generalization.
Code and models are planned for public release.

figures.caption: Fig. 2: System overview of MemHand. The Hand Localizer (a) decides which hands are in each frame and tracks hand keypoints (Sec. III-A). III-B). The Long-Term Scale Memory (c) keeps the most precise observations of the metric scale, from both metric depth and parallax of a static hand against head motion (Sec. III-C).

papers.abstract: Aligning inertial measurement unit (IMU) signals with text enables zero-shot activity recognition across wearable devices. A worn device's signal depends on its setup, the combination of body site and mounting. Leading IMU-language models make their encoders invariant to the mounting, which also discards the device's orientation relative to the body, such as the direction of gravity that separates sitting, standing and lying. We introduce SetCon, which replaces full invariance with selective invariance. It estimates each device's mounting on its known body site from a few unlabeled windows and conditions its encoder on this estimate. Because the mounting stays nearly fixed while the device is worn, the moving body serves as a calibration target. Both calibration and representation learning are supervised by 3D human motion, since one movement can be simulated under many known sensor setups. At test time, a class is represented by its name or by an anchor, which averages the text embeddings of the name and of activity descriptions and needs no labeled window. A language model built on the frozen encoder also answers how and in what order a movement is performed. Trained only on IMU simulated from the same Nymeria motion capture as AnyMo, SetCon reaches 56.6% mean zero-shot accuracy on 13 real datasets with class names and 65.3% with anchors, against 41.8% and 46.7% for AnyMo.
authors: Lennart Schiweck, Alaa Saleh, Crist\'obal Curio
bullets: Mounting affects IMU signals and provides orientation cues important for distinguishing activities such as sitting, standing, and lying.
The method estimates a device’s mounting from a few unlabeled windows and conditions the encoder on this setup.
3D human motion supervises both calibration and representation learning by simulating movements under varied sensor setups.
Class representations use either activity names or label-free anchors combining names with activity descriptions.
On 13 real datasets, SetCon achieves 56.6% mean zero-shot accuracy with class names and 65.3% with anchors, compared with AnyMo’s 41.8% and 46.7%.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of SetCon. The top row shows how the graph encoder, a spatio-temporal graph network over the body sites, reads a device. Every sample is rotated so that gravity points up and a calibrator estimates the setup reference Q̂ (orange) from unlabeled windows and the body site, so that the encoder also receives gravity in the segment frame. In the bottom row, stage 1 learns how a movement appears under a target setup and stage 2 aligns the encoder with captions under calibrator errors from an error bank. The weights stay fixed at test.

Figure 3. Embeddings of UCI-HAR. Each panel shows the first two principal components of one model’s embeddings of the scored windows, with the first seed in (c) and (d). Lying mixes with sitting in (b) and (c) but forms its own cluster in (d).

papers.title: SetCon: Setup-Conditioned IMU-Language Learning from 3D Human Motion

papers.abstract: Video foundation models have emerged as powerful generators of dynamic visual content, exhibiting remarkable capabilities in synthesizing complex actions and interactions. We argue that these models have also become excellent motion generators, with motion priors that are richer and more general than those learned by dedicated motion models. Their advantage extends beyond visual realism and is manifested in two important aspects: motion naturalness, including coherent body coordination, physical plausibility, and realistic interactions with objects and the environment; and motion scope, encompassing a much broader range of activities and semantic coherence, particularly uncommon, complex, and compound actions. To investigate this position, we introduce a common evaluation framework that compares video and dedicated motion models through three complementary settings: text-only motion generation, reconstruction of video-generated motion from sparse keyframes, and video-based enrichment of motion-model outputs. By converting all outputs into a shared 3D skeletal representation, we evaluate motion naturalness, semantic alignment, action coverage, physical motion characteristics, and fidelity to motion constraints. Our results suggest that video foundation models can generate more natural and semantically meaningful movements, particularly for complex and compound actions. Moreover, we investigate motion-conditioned generation through loose skeletal control, finding that dedicated motion models do not consistently improve video-generated motion, while video models can enrich skeletal animations using sparse motion guidance. Our findings suggest a shift in the role of specialized motion models, from generating complete animations to guiding and controlling the richer motion capabilities already embedded in video foundation models.
authors: Kian Izadpanah, Ali Mahdavi Amiri, Daniel Cohen-Or, Yiorgos Chrysanthou, Andreas Aristidou
bullets: They offer richer motion priors, producing more natural coordination, physical plausibility, and object-environment interactions.
Their motion scope covers a broader range of activities with stronger semantic coherence, particularly for uncommon or complex actions.
A unified framework compares both model types across text-to-motion, sparse-keyframe reconstruction, and video-based motion enrichment.
Outputs are converted to a shared 3D skeletal representation and evaluated for naturalness, semantic alignment, action coverage, physical characteristics, and constraint fidelity.
The findings reposition dedicated motion models primarily as guides or controllers for video models rather than standalone animation generators.

papers.abstract: Robot in-context learning (ICL) enables a policy to perform unseen tasks by following contextual demonstrations, without task-specific fine-tuning. This is increasingly valuable as large language models reasoning at low frequency can specify tasks through demonstrations and delegate high-frequency execution to such a policy. However, methods conditioned on human videos are bounded by scarce human-robot pairs, while those conditioned on robot demonstrations accept only one or two source types at limited scale. We present Any2Act, a foundation model for robot ICL. Our key insight is that a demonstration should be expressed in the camera layout and action space of the robot that performs it (the executor), not of whoever provided it (the demonstrator). This unified embodiment-grounded representation decouples learning to follow from admitting a new source. Any2Act learns to follow once, from robot-to-robot pairs that already take this form in 1.2M real trajectories spanning 10K tasks. Human videos, simulation, UMI, and other robots are then translated into this representation, and source-routed adapters trained on only a few hundred pairs each absorb the residual gap while the pretrained model stays frozen. For long horizons, a training-free tracker feeds only the demonstration window around the executor's progress, bounding the context and rolling back to redo failed steps. From a single demonstration, Any2Act achieves 57.5% success on unseen tasks without fine-tuning, exceeding VLAs fine-tuned on 50 demonstrations per task; other demonstrators retain 74-91% of the success achieved with the executor's own demonstrations.
authors: Ziang Ren, Zifan Wang, Zhuoyang Li, Benhao Qin, Haoyang Li, Qingtao Liu, Xuchuan Chen, Zekun Qi, He Wang, Yanchao Yang, Li Yi
bullets: Addresses limited scalability of robot ICL from scarce human–robot pairs and narrowly supported demonstration sources.
Represents every demonstration according to the executor’s camera layout and action space, decoupling task following from demonstration-source integration.
Pretrains on 1.2M real trajectories spanning 10K tasks, then uses source-routed adapters trained on a few hundred pairs per source while freezing the base model.
Uses a training-free progress tracker to provide bounded demonstration windows and roll back failed long-horizon steps.
Achieves 57.5% success from a single demonstration on unseen tasks; other sources retain 74–91% of executor-demonstration performance.

papers.abstract: Training humanoid vision-language-action (VLA) models relies heavily on costly real-robot teleoperation. Recent efforts convert egocentric human demonstrations into humanoid training data. However, most methods still require wearable motion trackers and leave important hand-object interaction cues implicit. Many also mix in real-robot teleoperation data for VLA post-training. These dependencies limit scalable data collection, while implicit interaction cues make precise contact harder to learn. To overcome these limitations, we propose EgoLoAF, the first paradigm to derive all training data for humanoid loco-manipulation directly from egocentric demonstrations without wearable motion trackers. We post-train the VLA on the converted data alone, without real-robot teleoperation demonstrations, and use explicit hand-object interaction cues to guide action generation. Specifically, to obtain humanoid action targets, we estimate torso motion from recorded camera poses and reconstruct both hand trajectories from video. From the same recording, we use each hand's current pose relative to the object to represent hand-object affordances. During post-training, we inject these affordances into the action expert through cross-attention while keeping the vision-language backbone frozen. Additionally, we release 128,400 egocentric demonstration episodes spanning 1,000 hours and 1,284 tasks, together with converted humanoid action trajectories and rendered robot-view observations. Across four real-world tasks, EgoLoAF nearly achieves teleoperation performance (73.1 vs. 74.4 in mean Task Progress Score), while achieving a mean 4.03 times improvement in data-collection efficiency.
authors: Yiming Zeng, Jiangyuxuan Dai, Yuheng Na, Tan Zhu Xuan, Zihan Lin, Xinfang Qi, Shijian Zhang, Chengqi Shi, Yihan Kuang, Zhide Zhong, Junjie He, Junfeng Li, Zimu Han, Naipeng Li, Haoang Li

Releases 128,400 episodes covering 1,000 hours and 1,284 tasks, including converted trajectories and rendered robot-view observations.
Across four real-world tasks, reaches a mean Task Progress Score of 73.1 versus 74.4 for teleoperation and improves data-collection efficiency by 4.03×.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon robot manipulation requires more than predicting the next action from the current observation. The policy must maintain a global procedural prior that specifies the expected progress of each subtask stage, while also tracking the realized progress produced by its interactions. To this end, we propose RoboDemo, a demonstration-augmented manipulation framework built on Dual-Cascaded Test-Time-Training. RoboDemo accepts either a task-relevant human demonstration video or a semantically compatible robot video retrieved from simulation corpus as reference, allowing us to evaluate its applicability with and without paired human demonstrations. Task semantics and physical motion information from the reference video are then transferred into persistent demonstration-intent memory. During deployment, we causally compress online observations, robot states, and executed actions into interaction-progress memory. To keep reference intent stable while interaction progress continually evolves, reference and execution video tokens independently update their respective fast-weight states. The action expert performs cascaded memory reads, first obtaining reference guidance and then refining it using realized progress, allowing the policy to adapt to execution deviations without overwriting the stored intent. RoboDemo achieves 90.7% success on Imitator Game and 73.3% success across three real-world household tasks. Real-world videos, code and hf-weights are available in our project website.

papers.abstract: While text-driven body motion generation has matured, pure-hand synthesis remains bottlenecked by data. Existing datasets often treat hands as rigid end-effectors, lack fine-grained captions, or are too limited in scale to support robust generalization. We introduce RoMo Hands, an in-the-wild, text-paired dataset of ~542K sequences (884 hours, 95.5M frames at 30 fps) which is an order of magnitude larger than prior work. To ensure high-quality supervision, a stringent dexterity filter discards low-articulation sequences, focusing the distribution on complex bimanual movement. Each clip is paired with five captions at increasing granularities from global semantic tags to atomic finger states, organized under a hierarchical taxonomy. To bridge the gap between body and hand architectures, we propose a novel 393-D bimanual representation that adapts redundant body-motion paradigms to the high-DoF kinematics of hands. Systematic benchmarking of diffusion, masked-token, and autoregressive generators reveals distinct trade-offs under these hand-specific adaptations, including a sharp divergence between semantic alignment and kinematic plausibility. Our dataset, representation, and benchmark establish a rigorous foundation for the next generation of dexterous motion synthesis. Project page: https://romodataset.github.io/romo-hands/.

papers.abstract: Large and diverse video sources, such as egocentric human video and heterogeneous robot recordings, carry rich dynamics but come either without actions or without a shared action space. Latent action models (LAMs) can recover these dynamics, but they train their inverse- and forward-dynamics models (IDM, FDM) from scratch, trading off pixel reconstruction against latent capacity and accuracy. Pretrained video world models natively generate high-fidelity dynamics, yet represent them densely, entangled across all layers. Viewing the world model as a LAM, we show that these dynamics can be extracted with minimal changes to the model. Native LAM operates one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both IDM and FDM, with learnable dynamics registers as the only causal bridge between the two, and trains on counterfactual temporal pairs that differ in motion alone, so that the registers distill a video's dynamics into a compact native latent action. We further propose a pretraining paradigm for vision-language-action (VLA) policies, Pretraining Actions from World models (PAWlicy), in which Native LAM serves as a dynamics teacher on large-scale video; unlike world action models, it never generates video. Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on the LARY benchmark in both action classification and control regression, and replay the same motion on new robots, in new scenes, and from human hands to robots, although no transfer objective is used in training. With a 3.8B model, PAWlicy reaches a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 trained with domain-randomized demonstrations, the highest among VLAs. On RoboDojo, it is competitive on every dimension we evaluate, and its Precision, evaluated by us, is on par with the leading leaderboard entries. On real robots, it improves over the pi_0.5 baseline on both tasks. Both stages use only public data and a publicly released world model.
authors: Qinyue Li, Weijie Qiao, Qingyi Tao, Zerui Gong, Zhe Yang, Quanzhou Li, Taolin Zhang, Jinglin He, Zhonghua Wu, Chen Change Loy
bullets: Addresses learning actions from diverse videos that lack actions or share no common action space.
Uses one pretrained video diffusion transformer as both inverse- and forward-dynamics models, connected by learnable dynamics registers.
Trains on counterfactual video pairs differing only in motion to distill compact latent actions without video generation.
Native latent actions outperform existing LAMs on LARY for action classification and control, and transfer motion across robots, scenes, and human-to-robot settings.
The PAWlicy pretraining paradigm achieves a 93.6% average success rate on RoboTwin 2.0 and improves over pi_0.5 on both evaluated real-robot tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1 World models as native latent action models. (a) Existing LAMs learn an IDM and an FDM from scratch. (b) A pretrained video world model is already an FDM. (c) Native LAM runs one world model in two modes, reading a latent action â from video and regenerating the future from â. (d) Latent actions share one space and replay the same motion from edited first frames in new setups. (e) PAWlicy pretrains a VLA on â without reconstructing pixels.

Figure 4 Native latent actions transfer. A latent â is read once from a source clip (blue) in the IDM mode of Native LAM and replayed in its FDM mode from a different first frame (orange), which is generated with GPT image generation from the source first frame; dotted frames are generated. The generated videos carry out the source motion with another embodiment, in another scene, from human to robot, and from simulation to a photorealistic scene, although no transfer objective is used in training.

Figure 2 Training Native LAM. (a) Each video x is paired with a retimed copy x′ = x ◦ ϕ of the same footage that shares the first frame but not the motion. (b) In IDM mode, dynamics registers read the clean video through a read-only attention mask and are projected to the latent action â; on AgiBot World and DROID, a kinematic head grounds â in end-effector motion. (c) In FDM mode, the same DiT regenerates the future from v0 and â alone, with â inserted into the token sequence through the adapter MLPin, taking over the conditioning role of text, trained with its original flow-matching loss; both clips of a pair share the noise and diffusion time, so only â can explain their difference.

Figure 3 PAWlicy. A frozen Native LAM labels each video window with one past and three future latent groups; t−1, t, . . . , t+3 index temporal groups, each containing four video frames. Sharing attention with the VLM, the latent action DiT reconstructs the past and predicts the future, and the action DiT conditions on it to generate actions. Video without actions still trains the latent pathway.

Figure 5 Interpolating latents interpolates the motion. Latents read from a still clip and a full-action clip are blended and replayed from the same first frame. The top and bottom rows are the two source clips; the dotted frames between them are generated. Each intermediate latent yields one coherent motion that travels part of the way, further as β grows; blending pixels instead superimposes static and moving arms (red box).

Figure 7 Counterfactual pairs prevent posterior collapse. A latent action is read in IDM mode from a source clip in which the left arm grasps the tissue (top) or from its still counterfactual, which holds the first frame (bottom), and the FDM regenerates the clip from the same start frame with shared prompt, noise, and seed. Circles mark the end pose of the arm. Trained for 2k steps without counterfactual pairs, the FDM reaches for the cup in both cases. This is posterior collapse: the FDM ignores the latent and hallucinates a reach for the cup from the first frame alone. With counterfactual pairs, the same 2k steps already keep the still latent still, although the moving latent still reaches for the cup. At 13k steps the generated end frames match the source in both cases.

papers.abstract: Proactive assistants that guide people through physical tasks must decide, every few seconds, whether a step is complete and whether a mistake has occurred. We find that two benchmarks for this task largely reward knowing when rather than seeing what: a timer that never looks at the video, raising an alarm at 25 s and confirming each step at 30 s, reaches a mistake F1 of 0.373 on Ego-MC-Bench, above every published result (at most 0.27). We formalize this as the video-blind frontier, the best trade-off between completion accuracy and mistake F1 that policies reach from the elapsed time, the instruction and training statistics alone: every published per-step result on Ego-MC-Bench lies inside it, and so do all twelve zero-shot models we run on QICD. To move beyond it, we introduce Evidence-Contrastive Training (ECT): fine-tune on the benchmark's own questions, and pair its positives with negatives from the same recording at the same elapsed time, so that elapsed time cannot separate the two sides of a pair. Trained on 209 QICD videos in about 15 GPU-hours, a 2B model with ECT crosses the frontier on both benchmarks in all four seeds; transferred to Ego-MC-Bench without adaptation, it confirms 59% of mistake-free steps in time, against 30% for a published model with the same backbone trained on about 25k synthetic counterfactuals and real recordings. Its decisions follow the video beyond what timing explains: at equal elapsed time it tells a finished step from an unfinished one in 90-92% of test pairs, where the instruction's typical duration reaches 65%, rescaling the time stamps between the frames leaves it essentially unchanged, and swapping in another recording, of the same recipe where one exists, cuts its completion accuracy by two thirds. The code and model weights will be publicly released.
bullets: Existing benchmarks can be largely solved by timing alone: a video-blind timer surpasses published mistake-detection results on Ego-MC-Bench, while published per-step systems and tested zero-shot models remain within the timing-based frontier.
Evidence-Contrastive Training pairs examples from the same recording at the same elapsed time, preventing models from using time as a shortcut.
A 2B model trained with ECT crossed the video-blind frontier on both benchmarks across all four seeds, using 209 QICD videos and about 15 GPU-hours.
Without adaptation, the model confirmed 59% of mistake-free steps on Ego-MC-Bench, compared with 30% for a published comparable-backbone model.

Its decisions reflect video content: it distinguished finished from unfinished steps in 90–92% of equal-time pairs, while time-based instruction statistics reached 65%; performance degraded substantially when recordings were swapped.

papers.title: Speak When You See It: Proactive Task Assistants Should Wait for Evidence, Not the Clock

papers.abstract: Learning robot manipulation from egocentric human videos requires accurate metric 3D hand motion. Recent methods leverage pretrained video diffusion model (VDM) priors to recover occluded hands directly from full-frame videos, but their appearance-based depth regression generalizes poorly to unseen cameras. In this work, we propose ViDiHand2, a geometry-driven framework that reformulates VDM-based hand depth estimation from direct regression into fine-grained geometric constraint solving. Specifically, we introduce Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting and Clip-Level Ray Fitting, which recover metric depth by enforcing geometric consistency between pixel-aligned 2D joints and the metric structure of MANO hands, while leveraging temporal observations across the clip. Since the lifting relies on these 2D joints, to improve robustness under occlusion and image truncation, we further develop Confidence-Gated Fusion to adaptively combine geometrically lifted joints with MANO predictions according to localization confidence. Finally, we enhance the VDM backbone to better capture spatial-temporal representations and produce the per-frame 2D joint and MANO predictions that both steps rely on. Extensive experiments on seven public datasets demonstrate that ViDiHand2 consistently outperforms 18 baselines, reducing in-the-wild absolute joint error by 42% and detection failures by 8.82x compared with the best baseline on each metric, while running at 57 FPS. The code is available at https://github.com/NTUYWANG103/ViDiHand.
authors: Yuxi Wang, Yufei Liu, Chengkai Jin, Qingyue Chen, Wenqi Ouyang, Tianyi Wei, Kerui Ren, Siyuan Huang, Zhiqi Shen, Hongsheng Li, Xingang Pan
bullets: Addresses poor cross-camera generalization of appearance-based hand depth regression in VDM-based methods.
Uses Fine-Grained Geometric Lifting and Clip-Level Ray Fitting to enforce consistency between 2D joints and metric MANO hand geometry across video clips.
Introduces Confidence-Gated Fusion to combine geometrically lifted joints with MANO predictions under occlusion and truncation.
Enhances the video diffusion backbone to predict per-frame 2D joints and MANO parameters with improved spatial-temporal representations.
On seven public datasets, outperforms 18 baselines, reducing in-the-wild absolute joint error by 42% and detection failures by 8.82×, while running at 57 FPS.

papers.title: ViDiHand2: Unifying Video Diffusion Priors and Hand Geometry for 3D Hand Motion Reconstruction in the Wild

papers.abstract: Demonstrations show how a task can be completed, but differences in embodiment, appearance, and execution speed make it difficult to identify the guidance relevant to the robot's current progress. We introduce JEPA-ICL, a vision-language-action framework that couples predictive planning with demonstration learning. The policy learns to plan by predicting ordered future states in JEPA feature space up to subtask completion, capturing what remains to be accomplished. These plans guide action generation and locate relevant stages in demonstrations, whose JEPA-supervised content features provide progress-aligned context. Learning from this context, in turn, updates the shared policy that produces the plans and actions. This coupling connects anticipating the robot's own execution with reusing demonstrated experience. On the Imitator Game, JEPA-ICL achieves 80.0% seen-task success under C15 pretraining, outperforming Zero-WAM by 12.0 percentage points. Without contextual demonstrations, JEPA-ICL outperforms the VLA-JEPA variant without human-video pretraining, improving success rates from 96.1% to 97.6% on LIBERO and from 62.9% to 73.2% on LIBERO-Plus. With demonstration-based training and contextual guidance at inference, LIBERO-Plus success further increases from 73.2% to 75.2%.
authors: Tingjun Dai, Jianxiang He, Mingfei Han, Qihao Yu, Longtao Jiang, Changlin Li, Minghao Jin, Zhihui Li, Xiaojun Chang

Achieves 80.0% seen-task success on Imitator Game under C15 pretraining, 12 percentage points above Zero-WAM.
Improves LIBERO-Plus success from 73.2% to 75.2% when demonstration-based training and contextual guidance are used at inference.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations provide a rich source of bimanual dexterous skills, yet transferring them to robot hands remains challenging. Existing methods primarily optimize object trajectory tracking, often overlooking how human hands interact with the object. Even with accurate tracking, robots may contact incorrect object parts or slide their fingers, resulting in unstable manipulation. We present DexDuet, a framework that learns contact-preserving bimanual dexterity from a single human demonstration. DexDuet employs two interaction rewards to preserve human hand-object configurations and contacts. To enable coordinated manipulation, we factorize the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies that condition on each other's states. We further propose assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum that adjusts object assistance and training starts across demonstration segments to overcome difficult manipulation phases. Across four benchmarks spanning three simulators and five robot embodiments, DexDuet improves object-tracking ADD-AUC by 11 to 41 points over the corresponding baselines while consistently achieving better contact preservation. Notably, among 122 paired runs with comparable object-tracking accuracy, DexDuet preserves the human's contacts better in 117 cases. Code and videos are available at https://rcl-robotics.github.io/Dexduet.io/
authors: Haoran Zhang, Haokai Ding, Han Zhou, Zuxing Lu, Heng Zhang, Xingxing Zuo
bullets: Addresses failures of object-only trajectory tracking, such as incorrect contacts and finger sliding.
Uses interaction rewards to preserve demonstrated hand-object configurations and contacts.
Factorizes the bimanual policy into two weight-sharing per-hand policies conditioned on each other’s states.
Introduces assisted reference-state initialization (A-RSI), an adaptive curriculum for difficult manipulation phases.
Across four benchmarks, three simulators, and five robot embodiments, it improves tracking and contact preservation over baselines; contact preservation is better in 117 of 122 comparable runs.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of DexDuet. (a) A human demonstration provides the object trajectory, which gives the policy πθ the next object pose, and the hand motion, which is retargeted to a reference motion that the robot hands imitate. Inside πθ , two per-hand policies share one network, and each maps its own observation o and the partner observation z to an action a. (b) Two interaction rewards compare each robot hand with the human hand relative to the object. The hand graph reward compares the palm and finger directions and the fingertip gaps, and the hand-object contact reward compares the distance and the closest point of each hand region to the object. (c) A-RSI gives each segment b of the demonstration its own assistance level hb, which it lowers (green) or raises (red), never above a ceiling h̄(u) that decreases over the updates u. Episodes start from states that the policy has reached, and their start segment is drawn from p(b), which favors the segments with a high failure rate fb.

papers.abstract: Coordinating locomotion and dexterous manipulation is fundamental to humanoid robots operating in human environments. A key challenge is learning motion priors from diverse data and using them effectively for coordinated robot control. We present CHAMP, a unified framework for humanoid loco-manipulation that combines whole-body motion pretraining with adaptive feature extraction. CHAMP pretrains a vision-language model to predict future body and hand motion from approximately 2,298 hours of heterogeneous human and robot data. A shared motion representation enables unified whole-body motion learning across embodiments from datasets with body annotations, hand annotations, or both. To ground these motion priors in robot control, we introduce a Coordination-oriented Action Expert (CAE) and train it on replay data generated using the target controller. Through sparse routing, CAE adaptively selects, transforms, and fuses features from multiple layers of the pretrained model to jointly generate body and hand actions. In experiments, CHAMP achieves overall success rates of 84.8% on seven simulated tasks and 91.4% on seven real-world tasks with a Unitree G1, outperforming the evaluated baselines in both settings. In particular, CHAMP achieves 70.0% success on the long-horizon popcorn-serving task, compared with 40.0% for the best-performing baseline.

papers.abstract: Wrist cameras provide an action-centric view that is directly relevant to robot manipulation. However, collecting human wrist-camera videos at scale is challenging due to cumbersome setups that can interfere with natural hand movements. In contrast, head-mounted human egocentric videos are much easier to scale. We introduce Ego2Wrist, which synthesizes synchronized wrist-camera views from human egocentric videos and task descriptions. Trained on approximately 940 hours of paired head- and wrist-camera recordings, Ego2Wrist jointly generates three views. To evaluate generated wrist views without ground truth, we propose hand-centric cross-view consistency (HCC), which measures consistency between generated wrist views and corresponding hand regions in the input head view. HCC ranks model checkpoints comparably to ground-truth-based LPIPS, and human evaluators prefer HCC-selected generations in 77% of responses. Evaluated on four datasets, Ego2Wrist outperforms fine-tuned WorldWander, reducing LPIPS by 28% and receiving human preference in 76% of responses. More importantly, HCC facilitates recursive self-improvement on in-the-wild egocentric videos by selecting generated wrist views for further training. Generation quality progressively improves over three rounds. These results demonstrate a scalable approach to generating real-world wrist-view human manipulation videos for robot policy training.

papers.abstract: We introduce Egocentric Human Motion Bridging, a task that generates a coherent 3D human motion sequence from two endpoint egocentric images. Unlike conventional motion in-betweening, which requires structured 3D endpoint poses, this setting uses raw first-person observations available from wearable devices in VR/AR and robotics. It presents challenges due to viewpoint variations, partial body visibility, and temporal ambiguity under cross-modal endpoint constraints. To address these challenges, we propose Ego-HMB, a unified diffusion-based framework that learns endpoint pose estimation and temporally consistent motion infilling within a single model through two training stages. First, Egocentric-to-Canonical Pretraining uses a hierarchical curriculum with progressively increasing temporal spans to strengthen endpoint pose priors. Second, Motion Bridge Diffusion Training incorporates endpoint and physics awareness, diffusing from neighboring poses to promote temporal continuity while preserving global endpoint constraints. Extensive experiments compare our approach with one-stage methods that directly generate motion from two egocentric images and two-stage pipelines that combine endpoint pose estimation with motion interpolation. Ego-HMB consistently outperforms these baselines in endpoint accuracy and motion generation quality. Code is available at https://github.com/gaogehan/Ego-HMB.

Targets wearable-device applications in VR/AR and robotics despite viewpoint variation, partial visibility, and temporal ambiguity.

papers.abstract: Human videos promise a scalable way to reduce expensive robot data collection, but the embodiment gap limits the resulting policies to coarse behaviors, and they fail at precise tasks such as insertion. Existing methods co-train or finetune a single policy on both data sources, treating each source as equally useful in every state: the policy either absorbs the embodiment error at precision-critical steps or spends scarce robot data relearning free-space motion. We observe that the value of each source depends on the state: human data is useful where precision requirements are low, while robot data is disproportionately valuable near precision-critical states. We therefore propose \textbf{DUO Policy} (Dual-Actor Policy), which decouples a manipulation skill into a hand policy, pretrained on human videos for global free-space motion, and a robot policy, trained on sparse in-hand data for local precise corrections, with a gate learned from human interventions switching between them. This design is robust to moderate embodiment error in human data and generalizes to scene layouts beyond the coverage of the robot data. On tasks such as K-cup coffee making, desk cleanup, and cluttered candy sorting, DUO Policy outperforms the baseline with the highest average success by 12.9 percentage points over four simulated tasks and by 51.7 points over three real-world tasks, and matches robot-only training with 2.75$\times$ less data-collection time. authors: Mingxi Jia, Patton Jiyang Yin, Haojie Huang, Ivy Xiao He, Xuanru Liu, Gefei Liu, Dian Wang, Stefanie Tellex

It improves average success over the strongest baseline by 12.9 points in simulation and 51.7 points in real-world tasks, while matching robot-only training with 2.75× less collection time.

papers.abstract: Action tokenizers let robot policies treat control as autoregressive next-token prediction. As these policies are trained on larger and more diverse datasets, they will need a universal tokenizer that can encode actions from many embodiments and data sources, including ones it has not seen. We study action tokenization at scale, training on 49k hours of action data from real-world robots, handheld grippers, simulation, and humans. We introduce Neural Action Tokenizer (NAT), a causal tokenizer whose decoder lets actions be executed as their tokens are generated. Across four simulation benchmarks, NAT outperforms FAST and prior neural action tokenizers when tokenizing unseen robot embodiments, and in vision-language-action models it outperforms FAST+ across four benchmarks and on a real robot when acting through its tokens. NAT tokens also close the performance gap to a flow-matching action head on some benchmarks while lowering the inference latency for first actions. Our experiments also find that robot data may not be necessary to learn an effective action space: a NAT trained only on human hand motion performs close to tokenizers trained on robot data.

papers.abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables foundation models to perform unseen tasks from context without parameter updates. In robotic manipulation, a human video provides the context that specifies how a task should be performed. However, scaling human-video ICL on world-action models (WAMs) faces two challenges: task-level human-robot pairs are not temporally aligned with robot actions, and standard action losses allow policies to rely on initial-scene or task-identity shortcuts rather than tracking the context. We present Entangle, an in-context world-action model that maps a single human video and current robot observations to future visual states and executable actions. To scale temporally aligned training data, we convert recorded robot videos into matched human contexts via video-to-video generation, supplemented by real paired recordings. For model training, we combine variable-length video windows with an intra-task contrastive objective that distinguishes the paired action trajectory from other executions of the same task, preventing task-identity shortcuts. Without task-specific fine-tuning, Entangle improves steadily as aligned training data scales, reaching an average score of 83.5/100 across six unseen tasks on an Astribot S1 robot, and achieves a 69.5% average success rate on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, outperforming Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points. Under Context-OOD, although trained only on scene-aligned pairs, Entangle transfers context-specified behaviors across rearranged layouts and substituted tools.

Achieves 83.5/100 across six unseen Astribot S1 tasks and 69.5% success on seven unseen RoboTwin tasks, surpassing Zero-WAM by 22.6 percentage points.
Transfers context-specified behaviors to rearranged layouts and substituted tools despite training only on scene-aligned pairs.

papers.abstract: Multimodal Egocentric Human Activity Recognition (Ego-HAR) leverages complementary cues from first-person vision (V) and inertial sensor data (S) to recognize daily activities, where video mainly captures appearance and object-related context while inertial signals capture motion cues that video may miss. However, existing pre-training methods typically supervise the fused representation with a single joint objective, which may underemphasize the complementarity between the two modalities and limit the model's ability to learn from distinct modality-oriented signals. To address this issue, we propose Multimodal Dual Representation Reconstruction (MDR2), a teacher-guided pre-training framework in which frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers each provide dense, modality-specific targets to a multimodal student trained on temporally sparse inputs. On the EvIs-Kitchen dataset, MDR2 improves noun/verb F1-macro over the supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at K=4 video key frames and by 1.21/1.82 points at K=32. These results show that MDR2 consistently achieves higher mean recognition performance across the evaluated video-observation settings under the unified backbone setting, with more pronounced gains under sparse inputs.
authors: Yuzhe Hao, Ikuro Sato, Rei Kawakami, Koichi Shinoda
bullets: Targets the limitation of single-objective pre-training, which can underuse differences between video and inertial modalities.
Uses frozen, label-informed video and inertial teachers to provide dense modality-specific targets.
Trains a multimodal student from temporally sparse inputs through dual representation reconstruction.
On EvIs-Kitchen, improves noun/verb F1-macro over supervised M-Baseline by 9.20/6.17 points at 4 frames and 1.21/1.82 points at 32 frames.
Reports larger gains under sparse video observation settings within the evaluated unified-backbone setup.
