papers.abstract: Linear manufacturing typically operates in highly structured settings with standardized objects, allowing robots to execute pre-programmed motions based on precise models. In contrast, circular manufacturing involves dynamic and less controlled environments, where product components can vary due to appearance and physical changes across different product generations. In this context, uncertainty arises from both the unknown or partially observed states of components (e.g., damaged surfaces, altered shapes) and the unstructured disassembly environment, often characterized by heavy clutter, occlusions, and limited sensing viewpoints. This demands a flexible and adaptable robotic grasping system that can cope with unexpected object changes. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an autonomous grasp learning framework designed for highly uncertain and variable conditions. The framework explicitly distinguishes between uncertainty due to noisy or incomplete sensory observations (aleatoric uncertainty) and uncertainty due to limited knowledge and distribution shift (epistemic uncertainty). Moreover, the framework employs an active perception strategy to reduce visual ambiguity: semantic and spatial scene understanding is achieved using vision language models (VLMs), while view planning enables the robot to adjust its viewpoint to improve observability. In addition, the approach leverages large-scale human demonstration data to learn interaction patterns, which are then transferred to robotic end-effectors, enabling robust manipulation in these variable settings. Quantitative validation, including the utility of active vision on disassembled components in practice, is expected to form an important part of future work.
authors: Yitian Shi, Rosa Wolf, Rania Rayyes
bullets: Targets uncertain disassembly environments with changing object appearances, damaged surfaces, clutter, occlusions, and limited viewpoints.
Separates aleatoric uncertainty from noisy or incomplete observations and epistemic uncertainty from limited knowledge or distribution shifts.
Uses active perception, including view planning, to reduce visual ambiguity and improve component observability.
Applies vision language models for semantic and spatial scene understanding.
Transfers interaction patterns learned from large-scale human demonstrations to robotic end-effectors; quantitative validation is identified as future work.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Overview of the proposed CIRCA-Grasp framework. In the digital asset pipeline, existing CAD models are used to generate analytic antipodal grasps and simulation-based training environments, which support pretraining of the probabilistic grasp learner vMF-Contact [4]. In the physical asset pipeline, large-scale human demonstrations are transferred through HOGraspFlow [10] to provide hand-object interaction priors, while real-world robot executions continuously generate grasp experiences for deployment and adaptation. During inference, VISO-Grasp [5] integrates the uncertainty-aware grasp model with active view planning to search for and grasp partially visible or occluded objects in clutter. All simulated and real interactions are stored in a grasp learning database, enabling continual improvement of the grasp policy across perception, planning, and execution.

Fig. 3. The connection between CIRCA-Grasp and the knowledge-based Intralogistics system from [14]. From the knowledge representation’s perspective, CIRCA-Grasp is the instantiation of the :GraspLearningSystem within the knowledge graph. (*Note: we use the same color scheme as [14], Fig. 7., to make them comparable)

Fig. 1. While linear production involves uniform objects with known geometries that are easily localized via pose matching (i.e., objects are typically “in distribution” (ID)), circular factories introduce significant distribution shifts. The high variance and unknown states of recycled materials require advanced, uncertainty-aware manipulation strategies to reliably grasp “out-of-distribution” (OOD) objects in cluttered environments.

papers.abstract: Visual perspective taking, the ability to infer what another person sees from their position, is fundamental to human collaboration. However, prior works reduced perspective taking to state estimation, geometric reconstruction, or discrete question answering, whereas existing cross-view video generation methods either inferred the target view from the input video alone or required an external camera that observes the target person. We introduce generative visual perspective taking: Given an ego person's egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and a collaborator's camera trajectory, the task is to generate the continuous egocentric video from the collaborator's perspective. This task is challenging given extreme viewpoint shifts, dynamic occlusions, and sparse visual overlap. We address these challenges with Ego2Ego -- a set of backbone-agnostic geometric modules that provide a pretrained video diffusion model with the 3D scene geometry shared by both interactants. Ego2Ego renders dense, temporally consistent scene coordinate maps into every view as a shared spatial reference, aligns cross-view tokens in 3D ray space through relative geometric attention, and recovers regions outside the ego person's current view from the ego person's visual memory. Experiments on the CoMind dataset across three video diffusion backbones show that Ego2Ego consistently improves visual quality, Level-2 scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion, outperforming state-of-the-art cross-view video generation baselines on every backbone. By generating the collaborator's egocentric video more accurately, Ego2Ego brings visual perspective taking to human-robot collaboration, where it can help infer what a human collaborator sees and does, and can turn single-person recordings into synchronised multi-perspective videos for robot learning.
authors: Chuhan Jiao, John Gideon, Anshul Gupta, Guy Rosman, Andreas Bulling
bullets: Addresses visual perspective taking beyond state estimation, reconstruction, and discrete question answering.
Uses backbone-agnostic geometric modules with scene coordinate maps, 3D ray-space token alignment, and visual-memory-based view completion.
Handles extreme viewpoint changes, dynamic occlusions, and sparse overlap between collaborators’ views.
Across three video diffusion backbones on CoMind, improves visual quality, scene layout accuracy, and collaborator motion over prior cross-view generation methods.
Enables applications in human–robot collaboration and synchronized multi-perspective video generation for robot learning.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of Ego2Ego. Given the ego person’s egocentric video, a scene point cloud, and both camera trajectories, Ego2Ego generates the collaborator’s egocentric video with a pretrained video diffusion transformer equipped with three geometry-grounded modules. All conditions are encoded by the frozen VAE and form a single token sequence with the noisy collaborator latent. (1) Since the same surface appears entirely different from the two viewpoints and hands occlude the scene, dense geometric rendering rasterises the point cloud into every view, colouring each pixel by its 3D coordinate in a shared frame, so that the same scene point carries the same colour across views and provides a shared spatial reference. (2) To relate tokens across substantially different viewpoints, relative geometric attention aligns the geometric components of keys and values to each query token’s ray-aligned frame. (3) To recover regions the ego person does not currently observe, the ego person’s visual memory supplies past ego-person frames together with their renderings.

papers.abstract: Latent action models let a robot policy learn from video by turning the change between two frames into a training target. In egocentric video, a cup can move across the image because a hand pushes it or because the wearer turns. Both changes help predict the next frame, but only the first describes manipulation. During training, EgoLAM supervises the action code with measured wrist motion and supplies camera motion separately to the forward model. Even when the wearer turns while pushing a cup, the training target still describes how the hand pushed it. The action encoder pools object slots around each hand, and wrist translation and rotation can be decoded from the code in a common reference frame. Extracting a code then requires only two RGB frames. Alongside LARYBench classification and regression, we measure how much wrist motion a frozen code retains and how strongly it responds to a synthetic view or lighting change. EgoLAM has the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight evaluated models. Across three LIBERO suites, policies pretrained on its codes and fine-tuned on expert demonstrations achieve 79.38% mean success, 28.73 points above expert behavior cloning and 9.76 points above the strongest other latent action model in each suite on average.
authors: Ziyi Ding, Yiwei Wang, Zhongxing Wei, Xianxin Lai, Yechi Liu, Xiaodi Huang, Jinghua Hou, Xiaoquan Sun, Haijier Chen, Zhe Liu, Yinan Chen, Junqiao Zhao, Xiao-Ping Zhang, Jiayu Chen
bullets: Problem: Egocentric frame changes mix hand manipulation with camera motion, making action targets ambiguous.
Method: Supervises latent action codes with measured wrist translation and rotation while providing camera motion separately to the forward model.
Design: Pools object representations around each hand and decodes wrist motion in a shared reference frame; inference uses only two RGB frames.
Evaluation: Tests hand-motion retention and robustness to synthetic viewpoint and lighting changes, alongside LARYBench tasks.
Results: Achieves the highest hand-motion decoding score among eight models and 79.38% mean LIBERO success, outperforming behavior cloning and other latent-action models on average.

papers.abstract: Surgical skill assessment, AR guidance, and robot learning from demonstration all benefit from 3D tracking of the surgeon's hands, yet no surgical dataset offers real egocentric articulated 3D hand pose. We introduce EgoSurgHands, a benchmark for real-captured egocentric hand pose estimation in open surgery training on synthetic pads. Captured with multi-sensor glasses, it contains 41,909 training hand-instance rows across 55 procedure recordings and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows across 13 held-out recordings, spanning 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees from first-year medical student to third-year resident. Each frame carries a multi-sensor stack: intrinsics, hand landmarks with per-hand confidence, timestamps, and eye gaze, plus SLAM extrinsics where SLAM succeeded. Evaluation labels combine sensor-fused pseudo-ground truth, human cross-review of every frame, surgeon adjudication of flagged cases, and an independent multi-view triangulated reference. Alongside the within-corpus, procedure-disjoint split, a leave-one-wearer-out protocol tested unseen trainees. Across eight methods evaluated zero-shot, from MANO-based reconstructors to the two-hand IntagHand and the keypoint-only MediaPipe Hands, egocentric pretraining was associated with stronger transfer on every held-out wearer. WildHands and JointTransformer had 18\% and 40\% lower PA-MPJPE, respectively, than the non-egocentric HaMeR. JointTransformer was the best performing model with an error of 14.95 mm. A substantial surgical domain gap remains, and the widely deployed MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1\% of evaluation rows. As a baseline, a 58K-parameter residual corrector (JRN) on frozen backbones reached 10.96-14.85 mm PA-MPJPE on held-out wearers for the two ego-pretrained backbones. We release the dataset and benchmark code at https://egosurghands.github.io
authors: Ankit Pal, Guillaume Kugener, Sofia Volpi, Joshua Schwartz, Alex Idarraga, Pranav Rajpurkar, Gabriel A. Brat
bullets: Provides 41,909 training hand instances and 9,476 human-validated evaluation rows from 68 procedure recordings, covering 13 tasks, 3 glove colors, and 4 trainees.
Includes multi-sensor imagery metadata, hand landmarks and confidence, timestamps, eye gaze, and SLAM extrinsics when available.
Uses procedure-disjoint and leave-one-wearer-out evaluation with sensor-fused, human-reviewed, surgeon-adjudicated, and multi-view reference labels.
Across eight zero-shot methods, JointTransformer performed best at 14.95 mm PA-MPJPE; ego-pretrained methods transferred better to held-out wearers.
MediaPipe Hands detected a hand in only 24.1% of evaluation rows, and a substantial surgical domain gap remains; the dataset and benchmark code are released publicly.

figures.caption: Figure 6: JRN architecture. The frozen backbone f (any of the eight evaluated methods) maps the input image I to a 21-joint prediction x ∈ R21×3 in camera frame. JRN is a 58,306-parameter two-headed MLP residual corrector. The pose head (blue, 32,831 params) consumes the root-relative pose x− x0 ∈ R63 and emits a 21× 3 root-relative residual δp. The translation head (orange, 25,475 params) consumes the root-relative pose concatenated with the raw wrist xyz, [x− x0, x0 ] ∈ R66, and emits a 3-D wrist correction δt broadcast to all 21 joints via 121. The corrected output is x̂ = x+ δp + δt · 121. Both heads are zero-initialized, so JRN equals the identity at t=0. The training loss panel reproduces the formal definition; targets are computed from the training partition only. Pose head and translation head are orthogonal on four of the five reported metrics (Appx. A.4): the pose head drives PA-MPJPE / MPJPE-RR / PA-P2D (translation-invariant under Procrustes), while the translation head drives Root err. MPJPE-abs depends on both heads; the full JRN trains them jointly.

Figure 4: Benchmark: zero-shot error with 95% PR-bootstrap CIs, and the effect of JRN. Ego-pretrained backbones (green) have the lowest zero-shot error among single-hand methods, 40% (JointTransformer) and 18% (WildHands) below the non-egocentric reference HaMeR. Left: PA-MPJPE (mm, vs Aria MPS). Right: PA-P2D (px); protocol as in Tab. 2. Circles: zero-shot, colored by model family, with CI bars; diamonds: +JRN. The green band spans the two ego-pretrained +JRN results, which reach the label resolution scale (§6.2) and are not ranked. †MediaPipe on the 24.1% of rows where it detects a hand.

Figure 2: EgoSurgHands data pipeline. (1) Capture: four wearers in three experience tiers perform 13 tasks in three glove colors with smart glasses. (2) MPS: each .vrs session is processed by Meta Machine Perception Services for SLAM trajectory, 3D hand landmarks, calibration, confidence, and eye gaze; audio is not released. (3) Pseudo-GT: landmarks are projected into the RGB frames, time-aligned, confidence-gated at ≥0.97, and inspected. (4) Validation: training rows use gated MPS labels (41,909 rows / 55 PRs); evaluation rows are further validated by multi-rater review, examiner review, and surgeon adjudication (9,476 rows / 13 held-out PRs).

Figure 3: JRN architecture. A frozen backbone predicts 21 camera-frame joints x; the pose head (blue) corrects the root-relative pose and the translation head (orange) the wrist position. Both are zero-initialized (identity at start); details in Appx. B.

papers.abstract: Motor decoding from electroencephalography (EEG) supports non-invasive brain-computer interfaces, yet existing methods either rely on costly cue-based trials and coarse categorical labels or use pretraining objectives that do not directly capture how movement unfolds, limiting their ability to learn transferable motor representations. To this end, we propose the Mind World Model (MWM), a framework that learns motor EEG representations from scalable naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations. MWM treats EEG observed up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model: a mind model encodes the EEG, and a world model uses it to predict the representation of a future frame, yielding a movement-grounded pretraining objective. We further introduce the Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT), which uses frame averaging to separate shared bilateral from side-specific lateral features, encoding hemispheric correspondence to reduce the burden of learning left-right relationships from data. MWM pretraining produces two models: a mind model for downstream motor decoding and a world model that can be adapted to prediction conditioned on real actions, opening a scalable and flexible path to collect egocentric data for embodied AI. Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, the mind model improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% relative to the strongest baseline in each task family. Compared with an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline, the world model achieves lower prediction error and benefits 3.3 times more from matched real actions within recordings and 4.7 times more on held-out subjects.
authors: Weikang Qiu, Zheng Huang, Tinglin Huang, Yujun Yan, Rex Ying
bullets: Addresses the limited transferability of EEG motor representations learned from cue-based trials, coarse labels, or movement-agnostic objectives.
Learns from naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations by treating current EEG as a latent action that predicts future visual representations.
Introduces a Lateralization-Aware Transformer to model shared bilateral and side-specific hemispheric features.
Across 9 classification and 7 regression tasks, improves task-averaged balanced accuracy by 5.9% and Pearson correlation by 16.2% over task-family baselines.
The world model has lower prediction error than an inverse-dynamics latent-action baseline and benefits more from matched real actions, including on held-out subjects.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Existing approaches (top) versus MWM (bottom) on the three challenges of motor EEG representation learning. (1) Cue-based trials are costly to scale, and categorical labels give one class to movements that unfold differently (Tangermann et al., 2012; Schirrmeister et al., 2017; Lawhern et al., 2018). (2) General-purpose EEG foundation models (FMs) pretrain with EEG-only objectives (Kostas et al., 2021; Jiang et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025a). MWM answers both with one mechanism: it treats the EEG recorded up to the current frame as the latent action of a world model that predicts the next visual state. It therefore learns from naturalistic EEG and egocentric video without action annotations, and its target is the visual consequence of behavior rather than the EEG itself. (3) Existing methods do not explicitly separate bilateral from lateral activity (Schirrmeister et al., 2017; Lawhern et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2025a); MWM does, and pairs each horizontal video mirror with an exchange of only the lateral component Hlat.

Figure 2: The Mind World Model. (a) A frozen encoder g maps the current frame to patch features that a residual predictor advances; the same frozen g builds the target from the next frame. (b) The mind model encodes the EEG window, which ends on the current frame; its LAT encoder is detailed in Figure 3. The EEG reaches the predictor only as AdaLN modulation, never as an input token: it occupies the slot a recorded action would.

Figure 3: The Lateralization-Aware Transformer (LAT) for EEG encoding. (a) Patch embedding, applied within each channel, (b) the learned gate G ∈ [0, 1]C×N×De and the electrode permutation Π ∈ {0, 1}C×C , which act on the embedded tokens before any Transformer block; the mirror acts on the decomposed pair and is an involution, (c) a criss-cross block, (d) a shared Transformer with invariant and equivariant readout heads; under the mirror, Hbi is unchanged and Hlat flips sign after aligning homologous channels, and (e) the paired EEG–video mirror. Only the learned lateral component is exchanged across hemispheres; the raw signal is never permuted.

Figure 4: Lateralization analysis. (a,b) Hand-motion correlations with 95% confidence intervals estimated by bootstrap resampling, using participants as the resampling unit. (c–e) Participantaveraged motor-imagery feature-energy contrasts, normalized by channel-wise mean energy; left– right contrasts share a color scale. Control features h(1) and h(2) are equal-sized halves of h.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video is the most scalable source of manipulation data for robot learning, but its difficulty lies in producing high-quality supervision. Existing large corpora lack metric 3D labels or rely on heterogeneous devices, motion-capture labs, or a headset's built-in real-time tracker, whose accuracy is not reported for the released data. We introduce RoboCap-10k: 10,000 curated hours of unscripted manipulation recorded during workers' paid shifts in 11 countries, spanning 18 task families, 200 task types, and 2,000 tasks. Every hour is captured on one device, the RoboCap, a 250 g hat with six synchronized global-shutter cameras and dual IMUs. Online calibration brings every device below 1 px of epipolar error, visual-inertial SLAM yields gravity-aligned 6-DoF head trajectories, and a multi-view hand tracker yields metric cm-precise hand poses. Each episode is annotated with task and sub-task language captions. Project page: https://robocap10k.com

papers.abstract: Egocentric videos offer a scalable source of human demonstrations for robot learning. However, recovering metric object geometry and motion from monocular video is hindered by scale-depth ambiguity and hand-induced occlusion, while image-derived contact and shape priors alone cannot uniquely determine metric scale. We introduce TacHOI, a training-free framework that integrates tactile contact with monocular vision for joint hand-object reconstruction and tracking, without requiring object templates or depth sensors. Starting from pretrained visual estimates, TacHOI uses tactile contact to constrain object depth relative to the estimated hand, while spatially separated contacts on a metrically calibrated hand provide a physical ruler for object extent. It incorporates these constraints into a joint optimization of hand poses, object trajectories, and anisotropic object scale alongside visual alignment. Across 100 ARCTIC and HO3D sequences with synthesized tactile observations, TacHOI achieves the lowest median ADD-S* among the evaluated baselines, reducing error from 15.6 to 3.6 cm on ARCTIC and achieving 2.8 cm on HO3D. Additional experiments on OpenTouch demonstrate its applicability to measured tactile observations.
authors: Jackson Codd, Haoyu Li, Xianyi Cheng
bullets: Addresses scale–depth ambiguity and hand occlusion in egocentric monocular videos.

papers.abstract: Reliable reasoning for long-horizon embodied tasks requires predictions grounded in the observed execution state. We present ACE-Brain-0.7, a 9B vision--language model that combines spatial grounding, task understanding, and progress estimation. To train the model, we curate 3.7 million question--answer pairs, drawing execution supervision from egocentric human videos, robot episodes, and simulation. These questions span different stages of an execution and connect task-level judgments with observed progress and outcomes. We then fine-tune Qwen3.5-9B on this collection together with additional task, spatial-grounding, and progress-estimation data. Across six public task-reasoning benchmarks, ACE-Brain-0.7 achieves an average score of 76.5, ahead of GPT-6 Astra at 72.7 and Claude Opus 5.5 at 73.5. Our model also leads the evaluated models in spatial grounding, averaging 75.90 across seven benchmarks and reaching 91.25 Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg. Controlled evaluations further indicate that our task-only model makes more effective use of visual history and more accurately distinguishes execution states. Together, these results show that ACE-Brain-0.7 effectively combines spatial perception with temporal understanding, delivering strong execution-grounded reasoning and comparing favorably with closed-source models.

Leads evaluated models in spatial grounding, averaging 75.90 across seven benchmarks and achieving 91.25 Acc@0.5 on RefCOCOg.

papers.abstract: First-person manipulation datasets treat the observation-action pair as the atomic unit and compress the generation and execution of an action into a policy network's weights, rendering the intent state behind the action unobservable. Human motor control research shows that intent mediates between observation and action and leaves observable traces along the intent pathway from decision to effect: gaze reaches the target before the hand, muscle load builds before contact, and cortical activity precedes the motor command. To record this pathway at scale, we present HumanCOIN, a first-person manipulation dataset built around human intent: 12,500 hours across 38 scene classes with three tiers of proxies. At the output end, the L1 attention tier (10,000 h) infers gaze from headband camera video, exposing the operator's next object of attention and reach before the hand moves. Midway, the L2 exertion tier (2,000 h) records surface EMG from armbands, making load expectations readable before execution is complete. At the origin, the L3 cognition tier (500 h) records scalp EEG, giving early readouts of task decisions and monitoring. Each tier inherits all proxies from the tiers below. The dataset further provides multi-view RGB images, depth maps and point clouds, 6-DoF head and wrist pose, and step-level action and object annotations. The controlled L3 setting additionally measures gaze, hand pose and finger kinematics directly. Clock and calibration data are released with the dataset so that any read rate can be re-aligned. The three tiers cover three stations, from visual orienting to cortical preparation, making the process behind visual-action pairs available for modeling at dataset scale. authors: Shihan Wu, You Liu, Chunyu He, Minghui Qin, Longhan Jiao, Jinbang Guo, Shaoxuan Xie, Kaixi Tian, Wenjie Chen, Jingrui Pang, Yuanhang Zhang, Yichi Zhang, Miao Liu, Tengfei Pan, Yance Jiao, Yunyan Zhang, Yihang Li, Yongjian Shen, Li Liu, Kai Zhu, Chen Fang, Jianxing Chen, Sihan Liu, Xiaofeng Wang, Jie Zhao, Jing Li, Yueqi Wang, Yichen Tang, Wei Li, Zhexuan Yang, Yue Cao, Ji Zhao, Kai Wang, Dongsheng Jiang, Yongwei Wang, Wei Mu, Jiangmiao Pang, Maoqing Yao, Wenchao Ding, Zheng Zhu, Zhongpu Xia, Dalong Du, Jianwei Niu, Dahui Gao, Zhiwei Yu, Bo Lei, Huan Yang, Yonghua Lin, Tiejun Huang, Zhongyuan Wang, Guocai Yao

papers.selection_reason: Large egocentric manipulation dataset with intent proxies, directly useful for learning from human videos.
papers.title: HumanCOIN: A 12,500-Hour Dataset for Human Intent in Egocentric Manipulation
papers.tldr: HumanCOIN is a 12,500-hour egocentric manipulation dataset designed to expose human intent through gaze, muscle activity, and EEG alongside actions.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video captioning requires fine-grained detail and accurate timing, yet current multimodal large language models (MLLMs) often miss brief actions, confuse their order, or misinterpret the wearer's motion. Existing caption formats also offer limited support for combining detailed narration with precise timing. We present EgoCaptioner, which pairs a video-level overview of the setting, participants, and the wearer's overall activity with timed steps whose narration adapts to varying perceptual demands and marks key moments at specific timestamps. We develop a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline that establishes event structure before expanding step descriptions, yielding 50,000 training examples from eight egocentric video sources. Complementary rewards assess factual accuracy and coverage, measure step-level temporal alignment, and penalize fragmented or redundant narration, guiding caption refinement through Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO). To improve the reliability of factual supervision, we supplement caption references with pose-derived motion facts when sensor data are available. Across five egocentric benchmarks, EgoCaptioner achieves leading performance among evaluated open-source models in caption quality, caption-conditioned question answering, and temporal alignment. It also surpasses Gemini 3.1 Pro on PhysCapBench and all evaluated proprietary baselines on Minerva-Ego under the caption-to-QA protocol. Ablations support the complementary roles of factual and temporal rewards and show that coarse-to-fine annotation provides more effective supervision than single-pass annotation.
authors: Yuqi Tang, Yang Shi, Yuran Wang, Tengfei Liu, Rundong Wang, Zongyang Qiu, Qixun Wang, Zhuoran Zhang, Xuanyu Zhu, Yifan Xu, Yiyan Ji, Shujie Li, Shixuan Liu, Haotian Wang, Yuanxing Zhang, Pengfei Wan, Chengwei Qin
bullets: Targets missed brief actions, incorrect action order, and confusion about the camera wearer’s motion.
Uses a coarse-to-fine annotation pipeline to create structured captions with video overviews, timed steps, adaptive narration, and key moments.
Trains caption refinement with GRPO using rewards for factual accuracy, coverage, temporal alignment, and non-redundancy; pose-derived motion facts strengthen supervision when available.
Built from 50,000 examples across eight egocentric video sources and evaluated on five benchmarks.

Reports leading performance among evaluated open-source models, with additional gains over specified proprietary baselines on PhysCapBench and Minerva-Ego; ablations support the reward design and coarse-to-fine annotation.

(b) The draft caption is reviewed against the full video and corrected. (c) Each validated caption can yield full-video, event-conditioned, and overview instructions. (d) Body and camera poses are converted into timed motion facts.

The content reward 𝑅fact is the F1 of judge-scored precision and recall over extracted facts, the time reward 𝑅time greedily matches predicted and reference steps by temporal IoU, and the style reward 𝑅style penalizes steps that judges flag as fragmented or redundant.

papers.selection_reason: Develops EgoCaptioner, a fine-grained egocentric video captioning system using MLLMs. This directly addresses the 'Learning from Human Videos' subtopic and advances multimodal large language models for temporal understanding.
papers.title: EgoCaptioner: Towards Comprehensive and Fine-Grained Egocentric Video Captioning
papers.tldr: EgoCaptioner improves egocentric video captioning by combining comprehensive overviews with fine-grained, temporally aligned action steps refined using factual and temporal rewards.

papers.abstract: Recognizing when a requested spatial condition holds in streaming video can require maintaining and updating spatial knowledge across changing viewpoints. We study this capability through proactive spatial reasoning, where a model receives a query in advance and determines whether and when to respond as the stream unfolds. We introduce ProSpace-Bench, comprising nine tasks across object, camera, and scene reasoning, and ProSpace-Train for supervised training. To support spatial decisions, we propose ProSpace-VLM, which injects explicit geometric encodings estimated causally from incoming frames into intermediate VLM layers, using the existing KV cache as spatial memory and spatial token selection for efficient streaming. Experiments reveal a substantial gap between VLMs and humans, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines. Analyses examine how ProSpace-VLM represents previously observed spatial information across changing viewpoints.
authors: Junyoung Hong, Minsu Kim, Jaehyun Kim, Jeonghwan Cho, Jiwoo Lee, Seon Joo Kim
bullets: Studies proactive spatial reasoning: answering whether and when a queried spatial condition becomes true as video unfolds.
Introduces ProSpace-Bench with nine object-, camera-, and scene-level reasoning tasks, plus ProSpace-Train for supervised learning.
Injects causal geometric encodings into intermediate VLM layers, uses the KV cache as spatial memory, and selects spatial tokens for efficient streaming.
Experiments show a substantial VLM–human gap, while ProSpace-VLM improves timely responses and correct abstention over fine-tuned baselines.
Analyzes how the model retains previously observed spatial information across viewpoint changes.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Task overview of ProSpace-Bench. Bounding boxes mark target objects in object-level tasks. The blue needle in Ego Rotation indicates the camera’s viewing direction; the star in Origin Return and the cylinder in Visual Homing mark the starting position.

Figure 3. Architecture of ProSpace-VLM. A causal geometry encoder estimates 3D point maps and camera poses from incoming frames. The resulting geometric encodings are injected into visual tokens. The model reads the cache through causal attention to assess the current spatial state and decide when to respond.

Figure 4. Analysis of attention visualization. Rows below the observed frames show the decision token’s attention over cached visual tokens, placed at their 3D positions. Boxes mark each model’s response frame.

On Place Revisit, it mistakes a different bathroom for the starting one. papers.selection_reason: Proposes ProSpace-VLM for proactive spatial reasoning in streaming video, combining VLMs with explicit geometric encodings for spatiotemporal understanding.
papers.title: Thinking in Streams: Proactive Spatial Reasoning with Vision-Language Models
papers.tldr: ProSpace-VLM enables vision-language models to make timely spatial decisions in streaming video by maintaining geometric memory across changing viewpoints.

papers.abstract: Recalling where and when an object was last seen and who saw it requires recognizing it across days and people. Existing long-video benchmarks focus on events, object categories, or relative locations, leaving instance-level spatial memory largely untested in multimodal models. To address this gap, we present EgoWitness, a benchmark for instance-level spatial memory and reasoning in egocentric video. Its 8,453 human-verified questions span approximately 324 hours of week-long and short-horizon recordings and test seven abilities, from recognizing an object or room to recalling who saw it and reasoning about room visits. Over one million reviewed masks of 34 registered landmarks and 21 movable-object labels are linked through room timelines. Among twelve direct vision-language models (VLMs), open-weight models reach at most 46.97% accuracy, and none exceeds 35% on identifying who saw an object last. We therefore propose EgoClue, a spatial-memory agent that retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial and temporal relations with five tools. Two-stage training with supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) raises its 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65% accuracy on 1,320 held-out questions. Evidence-trace synthesis matches the best direct VLM at 74.85% on week-long questions and achieves 80.56% in environments excluded from training.
authors: Zhengru Fang, Zehao Liu, Mingyu Tsoi, Yaoyu Zhu, Junlong Li, Fengmao Lv, Sijie Cheng, Yuanliang Sun, Fang Yang, Jun Zhang
bullets: Benchmarks recalling where and when specific objects were last seen, who saw them, and room-visit relationships.
Includes 8,453 human-verified questions across about 324 hours of recordings, with linked masks for landmarks and movable objects.
Direct VLMs achieve limited performance, with none exceeding 35% on identifying who last saw an object.
EgoClue retrieves candidate intervals, verifies instance identity, and computes spatial-temporal relations using five tools.
Two-stage SFT and GRPO training raises a 4B controller from 23.64% to 72.65%; evidence traces reach 80.56% in unseen environments.

papers.selection_reason: Introduces EgoWitness benchmark and agent for instance-level spatial memory and reasoning in egocentric video, directly relevant to embodied memory and egocentric learning.
papers.title: EgoWitness: Benchmarking Instance-Level Spatial Memory and Reasoning in Egocentric Video Streams
papers.tldr: EgoWitness reveals that current VLMs struggle with instance-level spatial memory in egocentric video, while the EgoClue agent substantially improves reasoning through retrieval, verification, and temporal-spatial tools.

papers.abstract: An assistant monitoring a person performing a procedure is most useful when it can detect mistakes while there is still time to recover. This requires judging actions against task instructions as the video unfolds, identifying the attempted step, locating it in time, and assessing its execution. Existing online detectors do not use the instruction text, while instruction-conditioned methods operate offline. In this paper, we study online, instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric videos. Using only observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions, our model identifies and localizes completed action attempts and classifies them as correct, modified, slip, corrections, or additions; omitted steps are determined after the video ends. We compare a modular pipeline, with separate step identification, temporal localization, and execution verification, to a joint model that predicts all outputs in a single step. To support supervised learning from mistakes, we repartition EgoPER to include erroneous videos in all splits. The approaches achieve similar step-segmentation F1@0.5 (93.6% and 92.1%), while the joint model achieves higher binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 (84.1% vs. 80.7%), with its largest gain on slips (56.4% vs. 37.5%). Component-level analysis suggests that error propagation between stages contributes to the modular approach's lower detection score. On test videos containing mistakes, both designs outperform released AEM and ESTANet checkpoints under our evaluation protocol.
authors: Amit Feldman, Ilan Shimshoni, Rotem Dror
bullets: Addresses the need to identify and assess procedural mistakes before recovery is no longer possible.
Uses observed video, task instructions, and prior predictions to recognize completed steps, localize them temporally, and classify execution errors.
Compares separate modular components with a joint model that predicts step identity, timing, and correctness together.
The joint model improves binary mistake-detection F1@0.5 from 80.7% to 84.1%, with the largest gain for slips.
The dataset split is revised to include erroneous videos across all splits; omitted steps are identified only after the video ends.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Overview of the two approaches. At each call, the system receives the current window V [τ, t] (sampled at 1 fps), the task description d, the instruction list I , and its prediction history. (a) The modular approach chains a Step Identifier, which selects an instruction s ∈ I or EXTRA; a Temporal Localizer, which predicts the attempt’s boundaries [a, b]; and an Execution Verifier, which classifies the cropped attempt V [τ+a, τ+b] as CORRECT, MODIFICATION, SLIP, or CORRECTION, using its previous execution labels as context. Extra actions are labeled ADDITION without verification. (b) The joint approach predicts all fields in a single structured response, conditioned on up to 12 previous predictions. In both, a NOT COMPLETED output (dashed) keeps the window start τ and extends the window by ∆ = 5 s; an accepted record updates the history and starts the next window at the predicted end.

Figure 2. Mistake predictions on two test videos. Our approaches assign a class to each segment; AEM and ESTANet give a binary error decision (pink). The number in each row is the binary F1@0.5 on that video. grey marks that no action is detected.

Figure 3. Examples of detected mistakes. (a) The joint approach flags a slip: the tortilla is dropped on the floor instead of being placed on the cutting board. (b) The modular approach flags a modification: the oats are poured directly from the container instead of being measured with a tablespoon. Span: predicted start and end of the action; decided at: the video time at which the decision was made.
Figure 4. Step segmentation on two test videos. Each color is one step of the recipe; grey is background and black an off-script step. The number in each row is the segmental F1@0.5 on that video.

Table 9. Model-call durations in seconds on the full test split.

papers.selection_reason: Online instruction-conditioned mistake detection in egocentric procedural video; fits embodied video learning and video understanding.
papers.title: Online Mistake Detection in Instruction-Conditioned Procedural Video
papers.tldr: The paper introduces online, instruction-conditioned detection and localization of procedural mistakes from egocentric video, finding that a joint model detects errors better than a modular pipeline.

papers.abstract: Training Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and World-Action Models (WAMs) is computationally expensive, while their heterogeneous architectures and fragmented training stacks make system optimizations difficult to reuse across models. To address these challenges, we present LoongForge-Embodied, a native-PyTorch framework that unifies and accelerates the training of heterogeneous embodied models. At its core, LoongForge-Embodied introduces a common abstraction layer that decouples model-specific implementations from shared training infrastructure, enabling cross-model reuse without constraining individual architectures or execution requirements. Buildingon this unified infrastructure, the framework combines reusable acceleration mechanisms with model-specific and hardware-aware optimization strategies across computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8-based communication optimizations for DDP and FSDP. Beyond training acceleration, LoongForge-Embodied integrates a unified data infrastructure with a pipeline for synthesizing robot data from egocentric data, and an efficient evaluation framework that supports concurrency and optimized computation in simulator. Experiments across representative VLA and WAM models demonstrate 1.47x-4.38x end-to-end training throughput improvements over their corresponding open-source baselines, as well as 4.1x-23.2x faster evaluation under the same protocols.
bullets: Addresses the high computational cost and fragmented, model-specific training stacks of embodied models.
Uses a common abstraction layer to share infrastructure without restricting model architectures or execution requirements.
Combines reusable and hardware-aware optimizations spanning computation, execution, memory, data I/O, and distributed communication, including FP8 communication for DDP/FSDP.
Also provides unified data infrastructure, egocentric-to-robot data synthesis, and concurrent simulator evaluation.
Reports 1.47×–4.38× higher training throughput and 4.1×–23.2× faster evaluation than corresponding open-source baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: LoongForge-Embodied system architecture. The framework unifies heterogeneous VLA and WAM models under a single native-PyTorch training stack, combining an integrated data pipeline (Ego2Robot, unified data loaders, and composable transforms), an acceleration toolkit of shared optimizations with model-specific execution paths, distributed training with FP8 communication, and an integrated evaluation orchestrator. The right-hand panels preview representative results on training speedup, trainingloss consistency, and benchmark success rates (Section 8).

Figure 3: Training-aligned evaluation architecture. A unified entry point launches a benchmark client process and a model inference server process, which exchange only model inputs and predicted actions over WebSocket RPC. Numbered markers denote the four pipeline stages: observation adaptation (1), payload construction (2), and action decoding (4) run in the client, whereas action prediction through the shared training-side predict_action interface (3) runs in the server, which also hosts the model registry/factory and the action-chunk cache. The client loop returns from each environment step to observation adaptation until the episode terminates.

Figure 2: Unified data architecture of LoongForge-Embodied. Heterogeneous embodied datasets are integrated through a format abstraction layer that exposes a common sample contract. Model-specific data processing is supported through extensible registries for transformations, preprocessing, collation, and sampling, enabling diverse VLA and WAM models to share the same data infrastructure.

Figure 5: Training-loss alignment between the original reference implementations and LoongForgeEmbodied across eight embodied models. The solid blue and dashed orange curves denote the reference and LoongForge-Embodied, respectively. Each model retains its original loss metric and plotted trainingstep interval; FastWAM uses a logarithmic loss axis.

Figure 4: End-to-end training throughput speedup of LoongForge-Embodied over the corresponding opensource implementations across nine embodied foundation models. Higher is better. DreamZero is measured with the Wan2.2-TI2V-5B backbone and precomputed features on eight GPUs, excluding featurepreparation time.

Figure A17: Reported effects of optimizations specific to Cosmos 3, all measured on the larger-memory, lower-interconnect-bandwidth platform: (a) supported per-device batch size with torch.compile; (b) cross-platform throughput ratio with compilation enabled; (c) the same ratio under selective FSDP sharding; and (d) compute performance with FP8, normalized to a baseline of 1.0. The ratio in (c) is per-device training throughput on this platform divided by that on the higher-bandwidth reference platform at matched model and global batch size; a value above 1.0 means one device here replaces more than one reference device. The two panels come from separate measurements and do not share a baseline. These are metricspecific comparisons, not an aggregate end-to-end throughput improvement.
Figure 6: Ego2Robot cross-embodiment retargeting. (a) Original human egocentric video frame; (b)–(p) the same interaction retargeted to 15 different robot embodiments.

Figure 7: Cross-embodiment synthesis stages for the reference Ego2Robot implementation and our metric-guided variant. All eight panels show the same frame of the same human egocentric episode: the reference implementation in the top row, (a)–(d), ours in the bottom row, (e)–(h). Left to right: reconstructed hand keypoints, hand and forearm segmentation, the frame after human removal and background inpainting, and the retargeted robot rendered into the scene. The inpainted frame in (g) preserves table edges, floor structure, and object texture that are lost in (c), the visual difference behind the object-fidelity margin in Table 7. At this frame the reference gripper in (d) closes short of the target object, leaving a visible gap, while in (h) the fingers enclose it. papers.abstract: Understanding an egocentric environment requires reasoning about how surrounding entities affect the observer's actions. Existing evaluations of multimodal foundation models (MFMs) examine observer localization, motion trajectories, and action feasibility, but leave the discovery and interpretation of evolving observer-entity interactions insufficiently assessed. We introduce EgoPass-Bench, a benchmark for observer-relative interaction understanding in real-world egocentric video. EgoPass-Bench comprises 284 manually reviewed evaluation clips recorded using Ray-Ban Meta (Gen 2) smart glasses and 2,201 distinct questions across five tasks assessing motion perception, interaction judgments about specified entities, and relevant-entity discovery without target cues. Our evaluation of eight frame-based and six native-video configurations reveals a pronounced discrepancy between motion perception and interaction understanding. The strongest evaluated model, GPT-6 Astra, correctly recognizes object motion in 91.37% of 394 comparisons involving the same targets, but correctly identifies changes in passage constraints in only 66.50%. Across all 574 entity-discovery questions, it trails the two-person human baseline by $23.65 \pm 7.45$ percentage points (paired 95% CI), while exceeding the always-empty baseline (36.76%) by at least 18.9 percentage points. Further analysis reveals frequent inclusion of entities that neither pose a plausible physical conflict nor constrain passage, showing that accurate motion recognition does not ensure reliable relevant-entity discovery.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human recordings are far cheaper than dexterous robot demonstrations, promising stronger pretraining and direct skill learning without task-specific robot data. Yet humans and robots differ in morphology and kinematics, so human recordings lack the joint positions and actuator commands that supervise robot policies, providing only retargeted end-effector (EEF) actions. This raises two questions: how human data should supervise the policy, and how a dexterous robot should read out actions at deployment. We address both in SHAPE (Supervision from Human Action tokens with Parallel Executable streams), a vision-language-action (VLA) model whose backbone predicts discrete action tokens of EEF chunks as an auxiliary task, while a shared flow-matching expert outputs two executable streams, EEF and joint. On a bimanual robot with 22-DoF hands, a matched study shows that discrete supervision helps learn from human data, driving backbone gradients and shaping action-informative representations across domains. Under standard control pipelines at deployment, direct joint readout excels at fine-grained control with robot demonstrations, scoring 0.80 across six tasks against 0.63 for π0.5, whereas IK-based EEF readout excels at human-to-robot transfer. Pretrained with human data and discrete tokens, SHAPE learns new tasks from human demonstrations without task-specific robot data.
bullets: Human recordings provide useful visual and action information but lack robot joint positions and actuator commands.
A VLA backbone predicts discrete EEF action chunks, while a shared flow-matching expert produces executable EEF and joint streams.
Discrete supervision drives informative cross-domain representations and improves learning from human data.
Joint readout is effective for fine-grained control with robot demonstrations, while IK-based EEF readout better supports human-to-robot transfer.
The method can learn new tasks from human demonstrations without task-specific robot data.

papers.abstract: We introduce $Z$-sight, a unified robot foundation model that couples vision-language-action (VLA) and generative latent world modeling. Video-based world action models (WAMs) show the value of joint future-and-action generation for control, yet inherit the heavy cost of video generators. Recent latent-space policies avoid pixel generation, yet typically align intermediate features or rely on frozen target encoders, decoupling future prediction from the VLM's native feature space. $Z$-sight instead predicts the future directly in the visual token space in which its VLM perceives the present. Coupling a foresight expert and a continuous action expert with the VLM in a mixture-of-transformers, $Z$-sight jointly denoises future spatial tokens and actions at inference without pixel reconstruction or external encoders. Trained on human video and robot trajectories, $Z$-sight achieves 81.9% success on SIMPLE (+9.6 points over the strongest baseline) and 73.3% across six Unitree G1 tasks (+20.0 points) at 110 ms per chunk, while remaining competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

Predicts future spatial tokens directly in the VLM’s native visual-token space.

Also remains competitive on tabletop benchmarks.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in world models are opening new possibilities for fine-grained embodied tasks, with hand-object interaction offering a particularly demanding setting. Modeling these interactions involves capturing how hand actions change objects and how the resulting states persist over time. Yet systematic evaluation tailored to these hand-centric capabilities remains underdeveloped. To address this gap, we introduce HandWorldBench, a unified benchmark that systematically evaluates hand-centric world models across human hands, simulated dexterous hands, and real dexterous hands along six dimensions: visual quality, hand fidelity, appearance consistency, instruction following, physical consistency, and temporal coherence. To construct the benchmark, we develop a data curation pipeline that extracts hand-object interaction clips and screens them for quality, yielding 20,500 high-quality egocentric clips from over 600 hours of footage. We then manually select 500 clips covering seven task families for evaluation. Benchmarking eleven models under a unified protocol reveals that stronger hand-pose control does not consistently translate into coherent object-state evolution and persistence or robust cross-embodiment performance, with several specialized hand-control models underperforming general-purpose text/image-to-video generators on dexterous-hand tasks.

papers.abstract: Questions about long egocentric video often depend on one brief moment, such as the second a hand puts an object down. A vision-language model (VLM) that sees a few evenly spaced frames usually misses it. Training-free methods rank frames with a separate image-text model or ask the VLM to write a time. In a controlled test, the VLM itself locates the moment better when it chooses among labeled frames, and we read this choice from its output distribution. With the same candidates, this choice lands on the evidence more often than image-text scores or a written time span, and it compares all candidates in one decision. Based on this finding, we propose EgoJev, a training-free frame selector for wearable assistants. EgoJev reads where the evidence is from labeled thumbnails and looks again at the windows it points to. It places its few answer frames at the quantiles of the resulting distribution. One frozen VLM selects, answers and returns the evidence time, with no second model. A wearable device can encode its coarse thumbnails while it records. With Qwen3.5-4B and 8 answer frames, EgoJev raises QAEgo4D accuracy from 51.2% with uniform sampling to 62.0%, and it outperforms recent training-free frame selectors on QAEgo4D and MyEgo. A single-level version runs on a Mac and an iPhone.
bullets: Uniformly sampled frames often miss the short moments needed to answer egocentric-video questions.
The method reads the VLM’s output distribution when it chooses among labeled candidate frames, rather than asking for a written timestamp.
EgoJev revisits the selected temporal windows and places a small number of answer frames at distribution quantiles.
With Qwen3.5-4B and 8 answer frames, accuracy on QAEgo4D improves from 51.2% with uniform sampling to 62.0%.
The approach is training-free, runs with one frozen VLM, and has a single-level version for Mac and iPhone deployment.

papers.abstract: Games are a rich testbed for visual agents, demanding perception, long-horizon planning, and precise control. However, collecting human gameplay is costly, and learning from gameplay videos requires inferring missing actions. Existing datasets also cover a limited range of games, often without explicit tasks or verifiable outcomes. To address these gaps, we introduce Game2Player, a framework that co-develops game environments and players to collect diverse and verifiable gameplay experience at scale. In the Game2Player loop, a Builder agent adapts existing web games, exposes their internal state, and defines tasks with state-based progress measures and success checks. A Coding Player and a VLM Player then attempt the tasks and report problems to the Builder for repair, so that play serves as both environment validation and training data collection. With Game2Player, we build 568 verified web games with 3,436 tasks, collect 15.7K trajectories (307 hours of gameplay), and hold out 50 games as the benchmark PlayerBench. To evaluate the collected experience as training data, we train VLM agents with progress-weighted SFT, assigning greater weight to steps that advance task progress. Game2Player-9B improves progress from 14.3% to 31.2% on PlayerBench and from 30.0% to 53.1% on the external GameWorld benchmark. More broadly, our work suggests a path for visual agents to scale their gameplay experience by building, verifying, and learning from existing game worlds.

papers.abstract: Embodied models depend on real interaction data, yet collecting it on physical robots is slow and labor-intensive. Recent ego-to-robot pipelines retarget first-person view human videos to robot data via transferring hand and arm motion. They judge fidelity mainly by visual appearance. However, trajectories often fail in terms of physics: fingers hover beside objects, and grippers close on empty space. We argue that how the object moves and the contacts that drive the motion count. Thus, we present Ego2X, an object-centric framework that converts monocular egocentric video into physically executable robot data across dexterous hands and parallel grippers. Ego2X centers on CORE (Contact-centric Object-interaction REpresentation), which records each contact on the object by its surface anchor, as well as relative force, grasp mode, and interaction state. Throughout the pipeline, CORE corrects hand-object drift via object-relative constraints, steers inverse kinematics toward contacts the robot must realize, and preserves held objects during arm erasure and robot compositing. On HOT3D, contact-driven correction reduces in-contact hand depth error by 33.7%, while on EgoDex, contact-driven retargeting realizes 62.9% of annotated contacts, surpassing the official HuRo pipeline (27.9%). In RoboTwin 2.0, post-training X-VLA on Ego2X episodes alone, without simulator demonstrations, raises task success rate from 40.5% zero-shot to 67.0% across 200 paired scenes. We will publicly release our conversion pipeline and CORE-annotated dataset for dexterous hands and parallel grippers.

papers.abstract: Forecasting future hand movements from egocentric videos plays an important role in understanding human intentions and hand-object interactions. However, different manipulation intentions can lead to substantially different hand trajectories even when interacting with the same object. Existing methods have not sufficiently explored the intrinsic relationships between articulated hand movements and object semantics to capture such operation-dependent motion patterns. Therefore, we propose TOMAS, a topology-aware operation modeling and adaptive staging framework for egocentric hand forecasting. Specifically, we develop a topology-aware hand-object reasoning mechanism that associates hand skeletal structures and articulation dynamics with object semantics and spatial relationships to jointly infer potential interaction targets and latent manipulation operations. The resulting object-operation representations provide interaction conditions for future hand trajectory prediction, with supervision adapted to the annotations available in each dataset. Furthermore, we introduce an adaptive staging mechanism that organizes future hand movements into ordered latent stages with learnable temporal boundaries. Stage-specific geometric subgoals are then incorporated to guide trajectory refinement according to the underlying manipulation patterns. Experimental results on multiple publicly available benchmarks demonstrate that TOMAS achieves state-of-the-art performance in multi-dimensional and multi-target hand motion forecasting.

bullets: Addresses varied hand trajectories caused by different manipulation intentions with the same object.

Infers potential interaction targets and latent operations to condition future trajectory prediction.

Achieves state-of-the-art performance on multiple public benchmarks for multi-dimensional and multi-target forecasting.

papers.abstract: Robot manipulation videos provide a rich visual experience, yet recovering robot action and gripper-state annotations from RGB observations still remains challenging. Using the embodiment-agnostic tool-center-point (TCP) pose as the action space, we present TCP4D, a unified model in which a shared 4D scene representation both tracks observed TCP motion and generates future TCP trajectories. Given a monocular video and initial 2D TCP queries, the tracker directly recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3) and gripper states alongside scene geometry and camera parameters. The generator samples local features from the same 4D representation along the recovered TCP tracks, then combines them with robot observations and language instructions to predict future TCP states. Our new cross-embodiment augmentation pipeline converts existing RGB videos into demonstrations for alternative embodiments by retargeting the recovered motion and synthesizing the corresponding observations, without recorded source-robot states. Experiments show that the tracker achieves absolute trajectory errors of 7.60 and 16.07 mm on DROID and RoboLab and adapts to a new embodiment with only ten demonstrations. The generator achieves 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin and outperforms well-established policy models on two real-world tasks, while joint training on source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.
authors: Haosong Peng, Xiangyang Liu, Zhengshen Zhang, Yunfeng Fan, Tianyu Qi, Xin Xia, Yufeng Zhan, Wenchao Xu
bullets: Recovers metric TCP poses in SE(3), gripper states, scene geometry, and camera parameters from RGB videos with initial 2D TCP queries.

Reports 7.60 mm and 16.07 mm absolute trajectory errors on DROID and RoboLab, respectively, and 69.19% mean success on RoboTwin.
Joint training with source and augmented demonstrations improves target-robot success by 41.5% over augmented-only training.

papers.abstract: Egocentric 3D hand pose estimators still miss hands at the image border, misplace occluded hands and jitter. Such failures are usually fixed by hand-written inference refinements and by fine-tuning, two interdependent steps that are tuned separately. We present HandRSI, a recursive self-improvement framework for a hand pose system that consists of a video estimator and its executable inference harness. In each round, coding agents refine the harness, and a change is accepted only if it improves a composite of all ten benchmark metrics on held-out data without significantly regressing any of them. The accepted harness then guides the estimator through selective distillation, which supervises hand presence and temporal consistency on frames without ground truth, while ground truth supervises pose. Since the updated estimator may change which refinements remain useful, the harness is re-validated on it. Starting from the released ACE-Ego-Hand model, five rounds reduce MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC and roughly halve jitter. On HOT3D, HandRSI's MPJPE-p is 16% lower than that of ACE-Ego-Hand fine-tuned on the same ground truth. Under a unified protocol, it outperforms nine re-run published methods on all ten metrics of both benchmarks. Hypervolume selection on the accuracy-speed front yields Lite, Medium and Heavy systems running at 20.7 to 41.1 FPS. This report gives the full method, every stage of every round and the complete protocol. Code, evaluator, harnesses and weights are public.
authors: Zhekai Wang, Luqing Luo, Wenhao Yao, Junjie Lu, Huanan Zhu, Feifei Gao, Yuhua Jiang
bullets: Targets border misses, occlusion errors, and temporal jitter in egocentric 3D hand pose estimation.
Alternates coding-agent refinement of an executable inference harness with selective distillation into the video estimator.
Accepts refinements only when they improve all ten benchmark metrics without significant regression.
Reduces MPJPE-p by 35% on HOT3D and 11% on ARCTIC, while roughly halving jitter.
Provides Lite, Medium, and Heavy accuracy-speed variants; code, evaluators, harnesses, and weights are public.

papers.abstract: How much does hand motion tell us about what a first-person camera will see next? EgoHandWAM forecasts three-dimensional wrist and fingertip trajectories and a future visual feature from the current image and recent hand states. We train on 751,065 EgoDex windows using a frozen DINOv2 encoder. On held-out development sessions, the action-only model reduces two-second wrist endpoint error from 60.26 to 56.48~mm relative to a stationary forecast. It still underestimates long reaches. Adding future-feature supervision gives nearly identical trajectory accuracy. With the recorded hand history, the visual head reduces smooth L1 error by 1.32\% relative to copying the current feature. Shuffling histories across sessions erases this gain. In a separate four-task probe, adding recorded future displacements to observed context and future tracking-validity masks reduces visual-feature error by 3.93\%. Masks alone give little improvement. A trajectory predicted from the same observations adds little. On two simulated RoboTwin tasks, substituting aligned human examples for an auxiliary batch of robot examples gives no consistent increase in task success across three training seeds.
authors: Kailin Wang, Haoxiang Jie, Yaoyuan Yan, Zhiyou Heng, Zhaosong Li
bullets: EgoHandWAM predicts future wrist/fingertip trajectories and visual features from current images and recent hand states.
On held-out EgoDex sessions, action-only forecasting improves two-second wrist endpoint error over a stationary baseline, but underestimates long reaches.
Future-feature supervision leaves trajectory accuracy nearly unchanged.
Recorded hand history improves visual-feature prediction; shuffling histories removes the gain, indicating session-specific temporal information.
Observed future displacements and tracking-validity masks help in a four-task probe, while predicted trajectories and human examples do not consistently improve RoboTwin success.

papers.abstract: Robot policies trained by imitation generalize poorly outside the environments and objects seen in training. Published data-scaling studies find that generalization grows with the diversity of training environments and objects rather than with more demonstrations per environment. Robot data is costly to collect across many environments, whereas egocentric human video can be recorded in the wild at scale; existing egocentric video, however, mostly shows daily-life activity and contains little skilled work in real workplaces. We present HubEgo-100K, a dataset built for diversity. This version of the paper covers the first release, v1.0: 10,124 hours of 1080p egocentric video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial (IMU) data from one head-mounted phone camera. In v1.0, 12,227 contributors record their own unscripted work in 15,548 environments (each one contributor's own setting of one type, such as their kitchen or workshop) across 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types and 35 action families, with 83% of hours in workplace settings. The release comprises 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations, in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0. We measure diversity along each axis, show that inside v1.0, with episodes in random order, new contributors and words keep appearing, and relate the measurements to published evidence on six data properties tied to policy performance, including hand visibility and inertial sensing. We also document collection, curation, privacy measures and data format, and provide a datasheet. Later versions of this paper will add benchmarks and cover further releases toward 100,000 hours.
authors: Javad Amirian, Armin Kiani, Lo\"ic Schaeffer, Tim Sprecher, Mohamed Taha, Karthik Yadati
bullets: Addresses the limited environmental and object diversity of imitation-learning data and the scarcity of skilled work in existing egocentric video.
Contains 10,124 hours of 1080p head-mounted video with synchronized 100 Hz inertial data from 12,227 contributors.
Covers 15,548 environments, 11 setting types, 30 work categories, 56 task types, and 35 action families; 83% of footage is workplace-based.
Provides 72,754 episodes with machine-generated action and language annotations in LeRobot and MCAP formats under CC BY 4.0.
Measures dataset diversity and discusses collection, curation, privacy, data formats, and properties linked to policy performance; benchmarks are deferred to later releases.

papers.abstract: Collecting demonstrations for bimanual dexterous manipulation is costly, motivating the use of human videos as a source of robot training data. However, uncertainty in video-derived motion estimates and differences between human and robot embodiments make direct motion transfer challenging. In this work, we introduce PriDex, a framework that transforms human-video Priors into executable robot Dexterous manipulation demonstrations through reinforcement learning in simulation. PriDex preserves task-relevant interaction structure while allowing embodiment-specific behavior to be regenerated for the robot. Human-object interactions provide affordance cues for selecting task-relevant, robot-specific grasps from geometry-based candidates. For motion refinement, object trajectories provide a task-level reference, while relative bimanual wrist trajectories offer complementary guidance for coordinated motion. Since object-motion estimates can become unreliable under occlusion or visual ambiguity, PriDex uses object-motion confidence to adaptively balance these two priors, emphasizing object-level guidance when confidence is high and increasing the contribution of wrist-level guidance as confidence decreases. Reinforcement learning refines these video-derived priors under the robot's kinematic and physical constraints, and the resulting policies are rolled out to generate robot demonstrations for training a vision-based diffusion policy. We evaluate PriDex on four bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks, including pouring, sweeping into a dustpan, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate cleaning, assessing both simulation-based robot data generation and downstream visuomotor policy learning.
authors: Yanghong Liu, Yang Chen, Kailang Xu, Bang Du, Feiyang Yang, Jiawei Xia, Zhengtao Yao, Yubiao Zhang, Masayoshi Tomizuka, Ruihai Wu, Wei Zhan

Adaptively weights object- versus wrist-level guidance according to confidence in video-derived object motion, then refines behavior under robot constraints in simulation.
Evaluates simulation data generation and downstream vision-based diffusion-policy learning on pouring, sweeping, bottle-cap unscrewing, and plate-cleaning tasks.

The PPO policy then refines these priors in simulation: reliable object motion provides task-level guidance, while lower-confidence segments allow greater residual adaptation and increased wristmotion guidance. Successful full-episode rollouts under perturbed initial conditions are retained as robot demonstrations and distilled into a vision-based Diffusion Policy for real-robot deployment.

papers.abstract: Human manipulation data are widely used to train robots for human-like dexterity. However, low-cost, large-scale collection in the wild remains challenging. Existing methods remain limited in geometrically grounded metric-scale reconstruction, real-world generalization and inference speed. We present WinDEX, integrating (1) geometric-temporal optimization for metric 3D hand annotation from in-the-wild egocentric stereo videos, combined with visual-inertial SLAM for world-frame reconstruction; (2) WinDEX-Net, an end-to-end, fisheye-native network combining calibrated stereo, local detail and temporal context, with a data-model flywheel of model-assisted annotation and retraining; (3) distilled models for offline reconstruction and causal streaming, supporting reinforcement learning and teleoperation; and (4) low-cost CyberCap stereo-inertial capture, forming the WinDEX-Hand dataset with 1,000 hours of training annotations and held-out human-annotated in-the-wild 2D and independent optical motion-capture evaluation sets. Offline reconstruction runs at 43.61 FPS and causal streaming at 171 FPS. On held-out data, offline reconstruction achieves state-of-the-art accuracy: 14.5 pixels in-the-wild reprojection error and, with visual-inertial odometry, 37.29 mm world-frame joint error. We achieve 7.6 and 3.6 times the task success rates of reinforcement learning policies trained with WiLoR and HaWoR motion references, respectively, and demonstrate real-time arm-hand teleoperation. Project website: https://fruitrabbit.github.io/WinDEX/.
authors: Hongyu Ma, Hairong Qu, Shiqi Zhao, Yongsong Yang, Kai Shi, Jiahao Ai, Xin You, Peng Yin

Achieves 43.61 FPS offline and 171 FPS streaming; reports 14.5-pixel reprojection error and 37.29 mm world-frame joint error on held-out evaluations.

papers.abstract: Robot policy pretraining based on human videos is crucial for improving the policy's generalization ability. One main challenge for this task is the lack of explicit action-relevant representations in such unlabeled data. Recent works tend to estimate 3D hand motion trajectories from videos using 3D foundation models (3D FMs). However, they keep solely the sparse trajectories as supervision, ignoring the rich, fine-grained information produced during the trajectory extraction process. To address this issue, we propose LSA, a hierarchical robot policy pretraining framework that includes three phases: Lift, See, and Act. Specifically, the Lift phase elevates 2D video observations into dense 3D representations by adaptively aligning features in the policy's shallow layers with the intermediate representations extracted from multiple 3D FMs. Building upon these lifted representations, the See phase equips the policy with explicit geometric and interactive awareness through dual guidance. It introduces depth-map reconstruction to help the model comprehend 3D spatial layouts and utilizes hand region cues to explicitly supervise the encoder's attention toward task-relevant interaction hotspots. Empowered by the dense 3D representation learning and precise spatial guidance, our policy achieves robust and accurate robotic manipulation in the Act phase. Extensive experiments on diverse simulation and real-world tasks demonstrate that LSA significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches. The project page is available at: https://yiyuan00.github.io/Lift-See-Act.
authors: Yiyuan Ge, Changxing Ding, Ziyu Hao, Zijie Zheng, Xiangmin Xu
bullets: Addresses the lack of action-relevant supervision in unlabeled human videos for robot policy pretraining.
Lift aligns shallow policy features with intermediate representations from multiple 3D foundation models to create dense 3D representations.

Act uses these representations for robotic manipulation across diverse simulated and real-world tasks.
The abstract reports significant gains over current state-of-the-art methods, without specifying quantitative results.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Architecture overview of LSA. (a) In the data engine phase, we utilize two 3D FMs to extract depth maps and camera intrinsics, respectively. Combined with the extracted 2D wrist coordinates, we obtain 3D hand motion trajectories. Furthermore, we also extract dense geometric representations and depth maps. (b) In the pretraining phase, we first align the policy’s shallow-layer representations with the intermediate representations of the two 3D FMs pre-computed during the data engine phase. Then, we introduce depth-map reconstruction to equip the model with precise structural knowledge, and utilize hand heatmaps to guide the model’s attention toward interaction hotspots. Following this, we predict the 3D hand motion trajectories. (c) Finally, we freeze the pretrained LSA and combine it with a policy head to perform closed-loop robotic control.

papers.abstract: We present XMimic and XSoma, which learn humanoid motion tracking and locomotion on rough terrain in under a minute of training. Both follow SuperMimic, which learns a world model of the robot and optimizes the policy with analytic gradients through short rollouts imagined in this model. Existing implementations of this method do not make use of larger GPUs, as every training iteration is a long chain of small GPU operations that run one after another. XMimic and XSoma therefore shorten this chain and run the steps of every iteration at the same time on up to four GPUs. We compile the complete training loop with JAX, including the MuJoCo Warp simulator. For locomotion, XSoma leaves only the dynamics of the robot to the world model and computes everything else exactly, including the terrain height under the feet. It learns with a horizon of one second and without a critic. On four H100 GPUs, XMimic learns to track all 40 LAFAN1 clips with the Unitree G1 in 0.86 minutes, 3.7 times faster than BlinkMimic on one GPU. XSoma reaches the tracking target that Holosoma's tests set for FastSAC in 0.77 minutes, 12.3 times faster than FastSAC on one GPU, while needing only an eighth of its environment steps.
bullets: They build on SuperMimic, using a learned robot world model and analytic policy gradients through imagined short rollouts.
The training loop, including MuJoCo Warp simulation, is compiled with JAX and parallelized across up to four GPUs.
XMimic tracks all 40 LAFAN1 clips with a Unitree G1 in 0.86 minutes on four H100 GPUs.
XSoma learns rough-terrain locomotion with a one-second horizon, no critic, and exact computation of non-dynamics quantities such as foot terrain height.
The reported speedups are 3.7× over BlinkMimic and 12.3× over FastSAC, with XSoma using one-eighth as many environment steps as FastSAC.
