papers.abstract: Continuous and accurate estimation of human hand kinematics is important not only for intuitive human-machine interaction, but also for capturing fine-grained human manipulation demonstrations that can provide action supervision for embodied-intelligence datasets and dexterous robot learning. However, individual sensing modalities may be insufficient for reliable estimation under varying operating conditions. We present a finger-unencumbered multimodal framework for continuous regression of 20 hand joint angles from egocentric RGB images and 128-channel forearm high-density surface electromyography (HD-sEMG). The framework combines a Vision Transformer-based visual encoder, a Transformer-based EMG encoder, and a degree of freedom (DoF) query Transformer fusion decoder. To account for the varying informativeness of visual and EMG cues across joint DoFs and input conditions, the decoder assigns a separate learnable query to each DoF, enabling DoF-specific and context-adaptive fusion of the two modalities. The framework was evaluated on synchronized multimodal data from 10 participants. Averaged across participants, the proposed fusion model achieved a mean coefficient of determination ($R^2$) of $0.88$ and a mean absolute error (MAE) of $2.80^\circ$, compared with $0.82$ and $3.21^\circ$ for the vision-only model and $0.68$ and $5.13^\circ$ for the EMG-only model. It also outperformed the evaluated representative unimodal baselines and alternative fusion designs. DoF-wise analyses showed larger fusion gains for visually ambiguous joints and viewing conditions, while synthetic visual occlusion demonstrated greater robustness than vision-only estimation. These results highlight the complementary value of egocentric vision and forearm HD-sEMG for capturing fine-grained human hand kinematics, with potential applications in human demonstration acquisition and dexterous robot learning.
authors: Jiahang Liu, Wenbo Zhang, Junsong Wang, Zhenzhi Ying, Siqi Hou, Naohiko Sugita, Liming Shu
bullets: Addresses unreliable hand-kinematics estimation from any single modality under changing conditions.
Uses Vision and EMG Transformers with one learnable query per joint degree of freedom for context-adaptive multimodal fusion.
Evaluated on synchronized data from 10 participants, achieving mean R²=0.88 and MAE=2.80°.
Outperformed vision-only, EMG-only, and alternative fusion baselines; gains were strongest for visually ambiguous joints and conditions.
Synthetic occlusion tests indicated greater robustness than vision-only estimation, supporting demonstration capture and dexterous robot learning.

figures.caption: Fig. 1. Overview of the proposed multimodal fusion framework. The framework takes synchronized egocentric RGB images and forearm HD-sEMG signals as inputs. The vision branch extracts spatial hand-region tokens from cropped RGB patches using a ViT backbone, while the EMG branch converts windowed hand-crafted sEMG features into temporal EMG tokens using a Transformer encoder. After adding modality embeddings, tokens from both modalities are concatenated and fused by a query-based Transformer decoder, in which each hand DoF is represented by an independent learnable query and mapped to its corresponding joint angle through a shared multilayer perceptron (MLP) regression head for continuous estimation of 20 hand joint angles.

The red, blue, and yellow boxes indicate the egocentric RGB camera, motion-capture cameras, and the hand–forearm sensing setup, respectively. (B) Functional schematic of the wireless HD-sEMG acquisition unit. The unit comprises three main functional parts. The power-management unit (PMU) supplies power to the acquisition and processing circuits. The EMG signal-processing path receives the differential signals generated between the electrode-array channels and the wrist-mounted common reference electrode, and performs amplification, band-pass filtering, analog-to-digital conversion, and onboard signal processing. The microprocessor controls signal modulation and demodulation and communicates with the host computer through the radio-frequency wireless interface. (C) Placement of motion-capture markers and the HD-sEMG acquisition system. Reflective markers were attached to anatomical landmarks on the dorsal hand to record hand kinematics, with three palm markers defining the palm reference frame. Two 64-channel HD-sEMG electrode arrays were placed over the forearm flexor and extensor regions, respectively. Each array was connected to a wireless acquisition unit, and a wrist-mounted reference electrode provided the common reference for differential recording.

papers.abstract: Advancing from individual embodied intelligence to swarm embodied intelligence is a key step toward scalable, general-purpose embodied intelligence. Complex tasks often require multiple agents to divide responsibilities, coordinate handovers, and manipulate shared objects collaboratively. However, existing robot learning methods rely primarily on individual demonstrations, which provide limited supervision for modeling dependencies among agent actions, while collecting multi-robot demonstrations at scale remains difficult. Human egocentric demonstrations offer a scalable alternative, yet distributed observations from multiple participants cannot directly supervise decentralized policies. We introduce EgoSwarm, the first robot learning framework for learning decentralized multi-robot collaboration from human swarm demonstrations. EgoSwarm collects more than 50 hours of collaborative experience using a robot-free multi-person egocentric system. We introduce the Swarm Interaction Packet (SIP) and Swarm Interaction Token (SIT) to recover cross-agent interaction relations from distributed observations and transform this experience into local supervision consistent with deployment-time information constraints. We further propose SwarmVLA, which transfers knowledge of swarm behavior to decentralized policies conditioned on local observations, local history, and limited neighbor messages. SwarmVLA achieves a mean success rate of 72.2% across three categories of multi-robot collaborative tasks. Project page:https://xitong-c.github.io/EgoSwarm_Page/.
authors: Ziqiang Liu, Xitong Chen, Min Li, Yiqun Li, Zhuoping Yin
bullets: Addresses the lack of scalable multi-robot demonstrations and the difficulty of learning dependencies among agents’ actions.
Collects over 50 hours of collaborative experience with a robot-free, multi-person egocentric system.
Introduces Swarm Interaction Packets and Tokens to recover cross-agent relations and create deployment-consistent local supervision.
Proposes SwarmVLA, a decentralized policy conditioned on local observations, history, and limited neighbor messages.
Reports a mean success rate of 72.2% across three categories of multi-robot collaborative tasks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overview of EgoSwarm. EgoSwarm is the first robot learning framework for decentralized multi-robot collaboration from human swarm demonstrations. It reconstructs cross-agent interaction in the form of the Swarm Interaction Packet (SIP), encodes deployment-available interaction information into the Swarm Interaction Token (SIT), and learns locally executable collaboration policies through SwarmVLA.

Figure 3: EgoSwarm pipeline for decentralized multi-robot collaboration. (a) Multimodal egocentric recordings are temporally aligned and reconstructed into quality-annotated Swarm Interaction Packets (SIPs). (b) A causal CTDE teacher learns coordination representations and action flow fields from collective interaction supervision, which are distilled into the decentralized student policy. papers.abstract: Real-time whole-body imitation from monocular video requires both a robust universal tracker and high-quality real-time reconstruction. We present MoViC, a framework that uses live RGB video as a control signal for humanoid robots without wearable tracking devices. The framework combines monocular human motion reconstruction, robot retargeting, and a transformer-based behavior foundation model. The policy receives proprioceptive history, a single explicit next-step reference, and a compact frequency-domain motion representation that supplies temporal context without explicitly stacking future reference frames, which reduces the input dimension and network size. During deployment, our extrapolation method bridges the 10-Hz visual estimation with 50-Hz controller, enabling asynchronous visual processing and policy execution. Hardware experiments further demonstrate highly dynamic motion tracking and device-free teleoperation of bimanual and single-arm manipulation tasks from live monocular RGB input. Project page: https://movicproject.github.io/ .

papers.abstract: Imitation learning for visuomotor policies typically relies on teleoperated robot demonstrations, which are costly because every episode requires a trained operator controlling a physical robot in real time through teleoperation interfaces and wearable body-tracking hardware. Egocentric glasses capture human demonstrations without a robot or handheld grippers, yet they track only the head and in-view human hands, and directly copying human motion to a robot with different stature, arm reach and hand morphology fails to produce feasible contacts. \method{} converts egocentric glasses recordings into physically verified robot training trajectories. An agentic real-to-sim stage reconstructs collision and textured visual assets from the recorded RGB-D and head streams, completes unseen surfaces when needed, and predicts target contact bands on the manipulated objects. During motion adaptation, a grasp planner turns each contact band into a feasible robot wrist pose and finger closure, bilevel stance optimization plans collision-free standing postures that keep hand targets reachable, and a whole-body motion generator synthesizes lower-body locomotion and out-of-view arm motion. Two-stage motion correction then blends visibility transitions kinematically and trains a reinforcement-learning tracking policy in physics simulation under agent-designed semantic rewards, completing manipulation phases even when the object leaves the camera view. Rendering the reconstructed scene through the robot's onboard camera along the optimized rollout yields synchronized robot-view images, proprioception and verified action labels. Fine-tuned exclusively on this converted dataset, without real-robot demonstrations, GR00T N1.7 performed loco-manipulation tasks autonomously on a Unitree G1. Project page: https://robonana.github.io/ego2sim2humanoid/

Produces synchronized robot-view observations, proprioception, and verified action labels for policy training.
A GR00T N1.7 policy trained exclusively on the converted data autonomously performed loco-manipulation tasks on a Unitree G1.

figures.caption: Fig. 2. Architecture of E2S2H, illustrated on a bottle-lift recording. From egocentric video and tracked hand landmarks, agentic real-to-sim masks objects and builds a textured visual scene with simplified collision geometry. Each object pairs a visual mesh with a collision model marked by target contact regions. Along the human (orange) and adapted robot (green) camera paths, the robot poses trace adaptation and correction. During the approach with hands out of view (cyan), the whole-body motion generator drives locomotion and unseen arm motion, then begins blending arm targets prior to visibility. Once hands enter the camera view (blue), tracked human landmarks take over arm guidance. Placing the robot directly on the projected human head path (red) does not guarantee a collision-free stance. Stance adaptation is therefore required to keep clear of the table while holding targets within reach in a comfortable posture. Directly copying the human palm onto the robot hand likewise fails, causing finger penetration or missed contact in the grasp comparison above. The final pose (grey) combines bilevel stance adjustment with contact-band Dex3 grasp planning. Kinematic optimization and reinforcement learning in physics simulation refine this plan into a dynamically feasible rollout. E2S2H then renders the robot camera view from the reconstructed scene along the rollout path to produce synchronized training data.

papers.abstract: Multimodal large language models (LLMs) have enabled capable computer-use agents that perceive graphical user interfaces, reason over instructions, and execute actions. However, existing approaches to learning from video demonstrations typically convert videos into screenshot-based action trajectories, rather than directly leveraging their rich audio-visual information. We introduce VEX (Video as EXperience), a framework that uses audio-visual understanding to unify learning from external demonstrations and reflecting on an agent's own behavior. Following a watch-act-rewatch paradigm, the agent extracts procedural guidance from tutorial videos containing visual demonstrations and spoken explanations, executes tasks, and verifies its progress by rewatching its execution as video. We instantiate VEX with video-SALMONN-VEX, a 9B-scale audio-visual computer-use agent built on the video-SALMONN 2 architecture with a Qwen3.5-9B backbone. We further introduce Action-Grounded Guide Optimization (AGGO), a reinforcement learning method that optimizes video-derived guidance for downstream action prediction, and augment AgentNet, OSWorld, and CUA-Gym with over 24K real-world tutorial videos. Experiments on OSWorld and a complementary subset of CUA-Gym demonstrate consistent improvements, with video-SALMONN-VEX achieving a 22% relative increase in task success over its Qwen3.5 backbone on OSWorld. Moreover, its generated guidance improves Gemini-3.5-flash by 10% relatively on OSWorld. These results highlight the potential of audio-visual understanding as a unified interface for procedural learning and self-verification in computer-use agents.

papers.abstract: Training generalist GUI agents requires large volumes of interaction trajectories comprising screenshot sequences paired with grounded UI actions, yet collecting such data through human demonstration is expensive and difficult to scale. Although public software tutorial videos contain rich operational demonstrations, their continuous pixel streams lack discrete action boundaries, semantic intents, and precise spatial coordinates, making them difficult to use directly for model training. To address this, we present T2T (Tutorial-to-Trajectory), a fully automated pipeline for synthesizing GUI agent trajectories at scale. T2T spans desktop, web, and mobile platforms to convert unannotated video tutorials into structured, executable interaction trajectories. To guarantee trajectory quality, T2T combines active segment filtering, keyframe identification via localized UI change, shortcut-free observation frame selection, presence-aware grounding, and two-stage action-space normalization. These refined trajectories are then converted into multi-task training views spanning navigation, planning, forward dynamics, and grounding. We fine-tune Qwen3-VL-8B on a subset of the more than one million human-annotation-free training samples generated by this pipeline. Evaluations show that the model achieves consistent gains across multiple benchmarks covering desktop, web, and mobile environments, including OSWorld-G, ScreenSpot-Pro, AndroidControl, and AgentNetBench, indicating improved core capabilities in grounding, step-level instruction execution, and trajectory-level decision-making. Notably, all gains are achieved without any in-distribution training data from target domains. Learning exclusively from trajectories extracted from public videos via the T2T pipeline, the model exhibits cross-application and cross-task generalization capabilities.
authors: Qingsong Xie, Yanlin Fei, Nazhou Liu, Jiacheng Tang, Madalina Ciobanu, Navan Preet Singh, Qingqing Mao, Ritankar Das

Produces multi-task training views for navigation, planning, forward dynamics, and grounding.
Fine-tuning Qwen3-VL-8B on over one million generated samples yields gains across multiple desktop, web, and mobile benchmarks.
Reports cross-application and cross-task generalization without in-distribution training data from the target domains.

papers.abstract: In this paper, we investigate how human egocentric videos can benefit robot policy learning without action supervision. Building on a pretrained VLM, we propose Shared Prediction on Action and Representation (SPAR), an MoT architecture in which future visual state prediction can provide independent and complementary learning signals alongside action prediction. We find that representations learned from egocentric videos improve downstream performance on out-of-distribution robot tasks, with further gains as video data scales. We also study the effects of objective choices and data curation, providing insights into how to leverage action-free videos for scalable robot learning.

Builds on a pretrained VLM with a mixture-of-training architecture for shared action and representation prediction.
Uses future visual-state prediction as an independent, complementary signal to action prediction.
Egocentric-video representations improve downstream performance, with larger gains as video data scales.
Studies objective design and data curation for scalable use of action-free video.

papers.abstract: Learning semantically meaningful human movement representations from 3D pose sequences is essential for human behavior modeling. Existing self-supervised methods derive supervision from artificial assumptions, e.g., invariance to augmentation within a certain range or recoverability of masked regions at a certain temporal scale, introducing heuristic hyperparameters that make the learned semantics sensitive to their settings. We propose BAL, a self-supervised framework that instead exploits supervision intrinsic to human movement: the natural ordering structure of everyday behavior. BAL autoregressively predicts in a semantically abstract latent space, analogous to how humans anticipate others' actions rather than their precise joint configurations. Bidirectional autoregressive prediction, both forward and backward in time, fully leverages these ordering constraints while enabling representation extraction using both past and future context at inference. To suppress representation collapse, BAL decomposes each prediction target into a global component capturing sequence-level semantics and a local component capturing context-independent movement. We prove that the local targets retain nontrivial angular diversity unless the representations are completely collapsed, preserving a meaningful training signal. Experiments on large-scale datasets demonstrate that BAL's representations are highly effective for motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most evaluation metrics.
bullets: Addresses the heuristic assumptions and sensitive hyperparameters used by existing self-supervised movement-representation methods.
Predicts in latent space rather than reconstructing precise joint configurations, aligning with semantic anticipation of actions.
Uses forward and backward autoregressive prediction to exploit temporal ordering and combine past and future context at inference.
Separates prediction targets into global sequence semantics and local context-independent movement to prevent representation collapse.
Performs strongly on motion captioning, forecasting, and interpolation, outperforming baselines on most reported metrics.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations are becoming the main source of data for dexterous manipulation, and real-to-sim-to-real pipelines multiply each demonstration in simulation. These pipelines rebuild the interaction from vision, which recovers how the hand moves. Which fingers touch, when, and how hard remain unobserved, because a hand pose shows where each finger stops on the surface rather than how far it is driven to close. This gap is a force gap: on held-out recordings, a hand policy that imitates the observed pose grips with 0.31x the recorded force, and a policy trained on physics replays of vision-tracked poses grips with 1.55x. TouchTwin closes the gap with measured human touch. Each selected TouchScale recording, captured with head and wrist RGB-D cameras and an 880-taxel glove, is rebuilt in MuJoCo. Coding agents write the objects as physics-tested programs, and a per-subject tactile hand replays the interaction with the recorded touch setting the contact and the closing force of each finger. In simulation, a policy trained on touch-grounded replays grips at 0.99x the recorded force and succeeds in 20/20 trials on held-out recordings and 35/36 unseen perturbations; a contact predictor trained on them misses 13% of real contact frames, against 32% for vision-based replays. Each replay also seeds perturbed demonstrations with simulated contact and force labels, rendered as realistic video in new views and scenes.

papers.abstract: Embodied foundation models hinge on diverse robot interaction data, which are costly to collect. Egocentric human videos offer a complementary source of experience, and latent action models (LAMs) provide a popular means of leveraging these videos for policy supervision. Compared with world-action models (WAMs), LAMs can offer greater training efficiency and potentially lower inference costs by avoiding explicit pixel prediction during policy learning and execution. However, most existing LAMs learn latent actions solely through video reconstruction, which can cause their representations to cluster by visual appearance rather than by the underlying actions. As a result, they struggle to align human actions with their robot counterparts. To bridge the gap, we introduce SALA, which emphasizes establishing the semantic correspondence for latent actions. Without requiring paired data, we use the language descriptions of unpaired human and robot clips to estimate semantic similarities and supervise cross-embodiment correspondence. Specifically, we translate these similarities into soft neighborhood structures that guide human latent actions toward semantically related robot latents, while robot action reconstruction grounds the latent space in control. The resulting shared latent action space provides a unified supervision signal for training an embodied foundation model on both human and robot videos. Notably, latent action supervision enables scaling along two axes: (1) pre-training on increasing amounts of general human video consistently reduces robot action prediction error on downstream tasks, and (2) post-training on increasing amounts of task-specific human video substantially improves real-world robot task success rates.
bullets: Addresses the poor cross-embodiment alignment caused by learning latent actions primarily from video reconstruction.

Enables unified training on human and robot videos without requiring paired data.
Scaling general human video reduces downstream robot action prediction error, while task-specific human video improves real-world task success.

papers.abstract: Large foundation models such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Fable 5.1 have recently been shown to control robots directly from visual observations. They nevertheless remain brittle on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks in real-world environments. Further progress depends on two complementary resources: demonstrations of human behavior that supervise how tasks are performed, and interactive environments in which policies can be rolled out, evaluated, and improved in closed loop. Language models have advanced along well-characterized scaling laws; the corresponding question for physical AI is how capability scales with environments and behaviors, which first requires identifying which data to scale and how to produce and reuse such data continuously. To address this question, we introduce Ropedia Xperience 2, comprising 1,589 released metric-scale 3D scans and a collection of 4,230 egocentric recordings of 74 tasks (131 hours). We further show that each capture can be repurposed for robot learning: scenes are converted into physically interactive simulation environments, human motion is retargeted to whole-body robot trajectories, and additional robot behaviors are obtained through virtual teleoperation and automated long-horizon trajectory generation. We propose this joint capture of environments and behaviors as a gold standard for physical AI data collection, laying a data foundation for establishing scaling laws over environments and behaviors.

papers.abstract: Generalist manipulation policies can benefit from the complementary experience of humans, real robots, and simulated agents. However, differences in morphology, sensing, and control interfaces make it difficult to learn effectively from their combined demonstrations. We introduce EgoX, an egocentric cross-embodiment learning framework that organizes heterogeneous demonstrations through semantically corresponding observation and action modalities. EgoX pretrains a Modularized Cross-Embodiment Transformer with Embodiment Dreaming (MXT+) on this mixture and fine-tunes it on target-embodiment demonstrations. Within each embodiment, MXT+ assigns a dedicated tokenizer to each observation modality and a dedicated expert to each action modality, with a Transformer trunk shared across embodiments. A training-only embodiment-dreaming objective predicts latent representations of future visual and proprioceptive states, encouraging the shared trunk to model each embodiment's dynamics. Across 13 task-embodiment pairs spanning five tasks and six robot embodiments, including five physical robots and one simulated humanoid, cross-embodiment pretraining raises MXT+'s average normalized task progress from 0.63 to 0.80 over training from scratch. The gains are particularly pronounced under out-of-distribution conditions, where average task progress increases from 0.53 to 0.77. Ablations demonstrate the benefits of broader pretraining mixtures, modular interfaces, and embodiment dreaming, with dreaming producing more similar latent geometry across embodiments. papers.abstract: Physical AI aims to learn transferable physical knowledge from real-world experience to understand, predict, and act in the physical world. Internet videos and embodied demonstrations provide complementary observations of motion, interaction, and state evolution. A foundational data challenge is to measure and preserve this physical information as training supervision. In video-language pretraining, captions express observed processes in language, yet a semantically correct description can omit the interactions and transitions that define those processes. Rich physical experience in video does not automatically translate into sufficient language supervision. This gap calls for a yardstick to assess annotation quality, compare captioning strategies, and guide training-data refinement. Motivated by our data construction for world-model pretraining, we introduce PhysCapBench, to our knowledge the first unified physical-caption benchmark spanning all three domains: third-person scenes, egocentric manipulation, and handheld-gripper demonstrations. It provides human-verified annotations for 1,500 video sequences and evaluates accuracy and coverage through seven physical dimensions. We examine downstream utility through video reconstruction and manipulation-policy fine-tuning. Physical captions reduce reconstruction LPIPS by 8.6-9.5% on third-person videos and 26.9-30.9% on egocentric videos relative to metadata captions. Training-instruction enrichment improves both PhysCapBench scores and policy success, including a 7.5-percentage-point gain for pi0.5 on a RoboTwin 2.0 subtask. PhysCapBench makes the physical content of language supervision inspectable and comparable, providing a cross-domain basis for its evaluation and improvement.
authors: Haofeng Wang, Pengcheng Wen, Ruiqi Li, Yuhao Zhang, Tiange Zhang, Boren Zheng, Xuanyi Liu, Siyu Tao, Danni Yu, Gan Lin, Haocheng Tang, Tianzizhe Guo, Mingyuan Su, Boyuan Chen, Zhongyuan Wang

Provides a shared basis for inspecting, comparing, and refining physically grounded language supervision.

papers.abstract: We present VBot Exo2Ego Policy, a video generation model that turns third-person videos into first-person observations of a selected actor, offering a practical way to expand first-person operation data from abundant real-world footage. To support this goal, we introduce a lightweight data collection pipeline and mobile app that support first-person recording, third-person recording, and synchronized capture of both views. This setup combines accessible single-view collection with paired RGB and camera geometry for learning cross-view correspondence. Building on a pretrained video diffusion transformer, our model incorporates geometric guidance and auxiliary supervision from semantic masks and hand keypoints to facilitate optimization and improve the fidelity of hand-object interactions. Camera geometry is injected stochastically during training and gradually removed, allowing inference without target-camera calibration. To accommodate the diversity of Internet videos, we combine source-video perception and reasoning, optional actor references, and multi-shot adaptation to identify the intended actor and follow an operation across camera cuts. The collection system and generation model provide a foundation for expanding first-person operation data across tasks, scenes, and participants.

Targets improved fidelity for hand–object interactions and broader first-person data collection across tasks and scenes.

papers.abstract: Reusing a demonstrated gait can reduce the work of specifying the same motion for each biped. A video captures the timing of a step, but each robot must execute it with its own limbs and actuators. MotionSkill recovers a timed reference once from monocular video and adapts it to each target in simulation. It aligns root motion and body landmarks in a common frame and records which landmarks are available at each instant. At each source timestamp, the mapper preserves limb directions, uses the target segment lengths, and solves inverse kinematics under joint limits and closure constraints. In MuJoCo, we train a separate residual policy for each of ten bipeds on its mapped reference from one four-second walking clip. Each policy uses the measured robot state to correct joint commands during contact. From initial states held out during training, MotionSkill completed 98% of trials on the original video and 26% with the upper body occluded for one second.

Scope: evaluation is in simulation and depends on a single demonstrated walking clip.

papers.abstract: Reconstructing dynamic scenes and objects from monocular egocentric video is crucial for embodied AI, yet existing 4D Gaussian Splatting (4DGS) approaches struggle with everyday interactions involving topological changes, such as cutting, assembly, opening, or closing. Since 4DGS methods rely on deforming a fixed representation, events that split, merge, or reveal surfaces cause severe visual artifacts. To address this challenge, we introduce TopoEgo, the first benchmark dedicated to topological changes in egocentric video (covering fission, fusion, open, and close), alongside Topo-4DGS, a topology-aware reconstruction method. Topo4DGS jointly models part-level motion and time-varying surface support by assigning independent rigid transformations to interacting parts and dynamically activating or deactivating Gaussians as surfaces appear, disappear, or separate. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Topo-4DGS significantly outperforms state-of-the-art 4DGS approaches across topological changes, especially on post-event frames. Code and data will be made publicly available.
authors: Leonardo Vanni, Stefano Gasperini, Federico Tombari, Chiara Plizzari
bullets: Addresses failures of existing 4DGS methods on splitting, merging, opening, and closing interactions.

Outperforms existing 4DGS approaches across topological changes, particularly in post-event frames.
Code and data are planned for public release.

papers.abstract: Human videos offer scalable manipulation data, but the embodiment gap between human hands and robot manipulators limits their direct use. Existing video-editing methods replace hands with rendered robots, yet inaccurate interaction reconstruction and compositing can produce inconsistent grasps and implausible robot-object occlusions. We address these failures from two complementary physical aspects: interaction geometry and scene visibility. First, an interaction-aware contact reconstruction module combines hand-object segmentation with mesh-level contact prediction to recover dense 3D contacts, then converts them into temporally stabilized grasps for parallel-jaw grippers. Second, a depth-aware compositing module uses scene and robot depth to enforce physically consistent robot-object occlusions. The resulting videos preserve the interaction structure of human demonstrations in a robot-compatible form and are co-trained with robot demonstrations. Using identical human videos and robot data, we compare against robot-only training and the original Masquerade pipeline. Across four RoboTwin tasks and two Diffusion Policy visual encoders, our method achieves the highest average success rates, with especially strong gains under out-of-distribution scene variation. Real-world deployment further shows that the proposed co-training approach improves robustness to visual distractors when the task geometry is observable, while performance on depth-sensitive grasps remains limited by the single-camera setup.
bullets: Addresses the embodiment gap between human hands and robot manipulators in using human videos for robot learning.

Uses scene and robot depth to produce physically consistent robot-object occlusions during compositing.
Co-training with robot demonstrations achieves the best average success across four RoboTwin tasks and two visual encoders, with strong gains under out-of-distribution scene changes.
Real-world robustness improves with visual distractors when task geometry is observable; depth-sensitive grasps remain limited by the single-camera setup.

papers.abstract: We study how to generate diverse, physically executable robot demonstrations for dexterous vision-language-action (VLA) learning. Existing demonstration-generation methods typically rely on costly teleoperated examples. Meanwhile, human hand--object datasets provide a reusable source, but existing transfer methods mainly reproduce given interactions. Turning these interactions into VLA training data further requires coverage of different objects and manipulation locations, together with executable arm and finger actions, and visual observations. To achieve this, we present DexSeed, a framework for low-cost generation of dexterous robot data from human hand--object interactions. Our key idea is to expand human sequences while preserving their grasps and realizing the resulting motions under arm-tracking dynamics in physics simulation. Specifically, we organize source sequences by grasp mode with shared language descriptions. InteractionMesh-based retargeting and arm trajectory augmentation adapt these sequences to the robot hand, different object geometries, and pick-and-place locations while preserving local hand--object relationships. An RL finger-control policy produces executable rollouts, while the arm tracks precomputed trajectories. Rendered observations and recorded actions from successful rollouts are paired with grasp descriptions to fine-tune a VLA. Experiments show improved contact fidelity in retargeting and more reliable whole-arm execution than the evaluated baselines. Simulation evaluation and real-world deployment further demonstrate that a VLA fine-tuned solely on the generated demonstrations can execute language-specified grasps. papers.abstract: The complex interactive dependencies between human behavior and 3D scenes make accurately predicting human intent a major challenge for human motion prediction (HMP). While recent studies use human gaze to infer intent, gaze signals suffer from ambiguity, drift, and a reliance on eye-tracking hardware. Research in cognitive science indicates that egocentric views inherently encode potential interactions, while head motion serves as a crucial precursor in motion planning. Motivated by this, we propose EgoHMP, a novel framework that uses egocentric views and head motions as robust carriers of interaction intent. By translating this intent into an envisioning of future interactions, EgoHMP achieves precise HMP in 3D scenes. EgoHMP first employs a vision-motion alignment encoder to align the visual and motion feature spaces. Based on these aligned features, an egocentric intent predictor with a modality-aware modulation mechanism adaptively suppresses invalid interaction cues to predict an accurate interaction probability map. Furthermore, to enhance the stability and realism of the generated motions, we propose a contact-aware motion decoder. Specifically, inspired by the human cognitive process of planning trajectories prior to action execution, we first predict a global trajectory to serve as a self-prompt, effectively mitigating the optimization conflict in diffusion models. Subsequently, we introduce a multi-stage denoiser, which relieves motion artifacts by incorporating human contact modeling through a multi-stage optimization strategy. Finally, a GCN-based motion decoder is employed to synthesize physically plausible and semantically consistent motions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that EgoHMP achieves state-of-the-art performance.

bullets: Addresses ambiguity, drift, and hardware dependence in gaze-based intent inference.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human video (EHV) records close-range hand-object interaction (HOI) and the temporal structure of everyday activities, offering a potentially scalable source of experience for robot manipulation. Using this experience for robot control requires recovering useful supervision without recorded robot actions and accounting for differences in morphology, viewpoint, and action space. We define Ego2Robot learning as the process of learning or adapting robot manipulation policies from EHV, organized into four learning paradigms: explicit embodiment transfer, explicit action and task supervision, egocentric video representation pretraining, and latent action and dynamics modeling. The four paradigms differ in what they derive from human video: robot-format demonstrations, interpretable supervision, visual representations, or predictive models of actions and dynamics. For each paradigm, we trace what EHV information is extracted, how robot policies use it, and when the additional data is required. Besides, we review the benchmark datasets that cover EHV, robot demonstrations, and synthetic and simulated resources. This paper links EHV data's contribution to the task information preserved and the robot-specific grounding used during training or deployment. Finally, we identify challenges in physical feasibility, agent coordination, in-context adaptation, controlled evaluation, and predictive control.

papers.abstract: This paper tackles the task of hand-object contact transition detection in egocentric video, which aims to localize the two temporal boundaries of a contact episode: the moment a hand first establishes contact with an object (touch) and the moment contact is released (release). We propose a unified framework that jointly models the interacting hand and object to accurately localize both transition types. The proposed framework augments hand-centric spatiotemporal representations with object-aware features learned directly from the video and introduces a transition-aware event spotting formulation tailored to contact transitions, without relying on external object or hand-object interaction detectors during inference. To support this task, we present ContactTransition, a dataset comprising 4,021 egocentric videos with 8,498 touch and 8,077 release annotations, together with object-of-interest supervision. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed method consistently outperforms strong two-stage and end-to-end event-spotting baselines on both transition types. Finally, we show that detected contact transitions provide effective temporal anchors for downstream egocentric hand-object reasoning.

bullets: Localizes both boundaries of each contact episode: initial touch and final release.

Presents ContactTransition with 4,021 videos, 8,498 touch annotations, 8,077 release annotations, and object-of-interest supervision.

papers.abstract: AAA games offer a rich testbed for evaluating agent perception, reasoning, and control. However, evaluating whether agents can complete tasks in AAA games is challenging and often human-annotated because task outcomes are often difficult to verify automatically, let alone applying it for Reinforcement Learning (RL). We introduce GTAGym, an environment and framework for evaluation and RL on GTA V tasks. Its evaluation benchmark, GTAVBench, derived from GTA V main-story missions, contains 103 online tasks reconstructed across nine task families, alongside 47 image-based shooting and sniping tasks using GTA V imagery. A web server provides access to the online environment and evaluation interface, supporting parallel testing through screenshots and keyboard-mouse actions with automatic engine-state outcome checks. We evaluate six frontier LLMs on GTAVBench with textual task instructions and on its GTAVBench-AGI branch, where instructions appear only in the first screenshot and a harness automatically compresses interaction history. The best configuration achieves 70.9% overall accuracy in GTAVBench-AGI, yet aerial navigation, evasion and interception remain difficult. GTAGym also provides a scalable generator that samples task parameters within user-specified ranges and option sets under fixed templates, creating batches of 3D and image-based shooting environments for RL with automatic reward and termination signals. LoRA RL of Qwen3.8-27B on generated on-foot navigation tasks improves the in-domain performance and transfers to out-of-domain task categories, and native GTA V tasks from 15% to 23%.

papers.abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models have achieved promising performance for generalized robotic manipulation, yet their reliance on expensive real-robot data remains a fundamental bottleneck. A scalable alternative is to transfer knowledge from off-the-shelf human-centric videos. However, existing methods extract latent action representations that are entangled with scene-specific noise, diluting the transferred knowledge. Motivated by this limitation, we propose Action-Intent Transfer (AIT), a two-stage method that transfers knowledge through a clean action representation shared across humans and robots. In the first stage, AIT extracts explicit action intents and disentangles the implicit action intent from manipulation videos. In the second stage, AIT aligns the human and robot domains within this shared intent space and decodes the intent into executable robot actions. Extensive experiments in both simulation and real-world environments demonstrate that AIT transfers human knowledge more effectively and consistently outperforms prior baselines.
bullets: Addresses the need to reduce reliance on expensive real-robot training data.
Existing video-based transfer methods are hindered by action representations entangled with scene-specific noise.
AIT first extracts and disentangles explicit and implicit action intents from human manipulation videos.
It then aligns human and robot domains in a shared intent space and decodes intents into executable robot actions.
Experiments in simulation and real-world settings show more effective and consistent transfer than prior baselines.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Evolution of human-to-robot learning paradigms. (a) MoCap-based methods depend on specialized capture devices, so data remains costly to collect, and the large embodiment gap limits generalization. (b) Latent action learning is trained directly from abundant raw human videos, but the learned representations are contaminated by scene noise. (c) Our method also learns from easy-to-acquire raw videos, yet extracts a clean Action Intent shared across humans and robots, enabling noise-free knowledge transfer to the robot.

Figure 2: Action-Intent-Guided Latent Disentanglement stage. It comprises: 1) VLM-based and 2) Rule-based Generation, which synthesize instructions l and explicit intents lintent for human videos and robot data, respectively; and 3) Intent-Guided Disentanglement, which extracts the implicit intent Zic from these manipulation videos under intent guidance.

papers.abstract: Transferring visual representations pretrained on human videos to robot manipulation requires learning reliable correspondences between human and robot demonstrations. However, paired demonstrations can differ in execution rate and in the proportion of non-key frames that do not directly reflect task progress. Frames at the same relative timestamp may therefore represent different task stages, which can cause correspondence learning to fail. To address these issues, we propose Frame-Level Temporal Alignment (FLTA), a framework that uses two temporal priors to adapt visual encoders pretrained on human videos for robot manipulation. It learns shared task-progress representations without frame-level correspondence annotations, allowing frames at different relative temporal positions to match. A global progress prior combines normalized temporal positions with visual similarity to construct a soft correspondence target. A local temporal order prior penalizes backward transitions while allowing stays and varying forward rates to accommodate execution-rate differences. With ResNet-50 and ViT encoders, our method achieves relative improvements of 46.93% and 65.96%, respectively, over the best baselines in average simulation success rates and achieves higher task success rates on real-world manipulation tasks. These results also suggest that effective human-robot adaptation depends less on the number of parameters updated than on which parameters are selected. Our project page is available at https://rtx5090ultra.github.io/FLTA-Project-Page/.
bullets: Addresses mismatched execution rates and irrelevant non-key frames in human–robot demonstrations.
Learns shared task-progress representations without frame-level correspondence annotations.
Uses a global progress prior for soft correspondences and a local temporal-order prior that permits stays and variable forward rates.
Reports relative average simulation success improvements of 46.93% with ResNet-50 and 65.96% with ViT over the best baselines, plus higher real-world task success.
Suggests that selecting which encoder parameters to update may matter more than updating more parameters.

papers.abstract: Egocentric auto-labeling requires depth, camera pose, object, and human-pose estimates to agree across independently developed models. Differences in units, coordinate conventions, and scale can make individually plausible predictions geometrically inconsistent. We present \textbf{EgoLabel}, a zero-shot pipeline that combines off-the-shelf models without target-domain labeled training and provides explicit cross-modal registration and consistency diagnostics. The pipeline integrates MonST3R for geometry, LocateAnything with GMC-BoT-SORT and SAM~2 for objects, and V-HPOT for hands; FisheyeViT provides a separate whole-body compatibility demonstration. Our main hand evaluation uses H2O sensor depth. Across 20 sequences, per-hand depth anchoring reduces the mean of per-sequence median hand--depth residuals by $23\%$ relative to a single global scale, yielding a pooled median of $84.6\,\mathrm{mm}$ against a $20.5\,\mathrm{mm}$ ground-truth reference. Hand PA-MPJPE is $14.53\pm1.29\,\mathrm{mm}$, whereas absolute MPJPE is $119.1\pm31.3\,\mathrm{mm}$, revealing a substantial gap between aligned and metric accuracy. On three RGB-only sequences, camera ATE is $1.40\pm0.29\,\mathrm{cm}$ after $\mathrm{Sim}(3)$ alignment. We also identify a sliding-window implementation issue that allows sensor-initialized depth to change during optimization. Because hand anchoring and its residual share the same depth map, the residual measures internal consistency rather than independent accuracy. These results characterize both the utility and the current limits of the registration pipeline.
bullets: Addresses inconsistencies from differing units, coordinate conventions, and scales across independently developed models.
Combines MonST3R, LocateAnything, GMC-BoT-SORT, SAM 2, and V-HPOT, with FisheyeViT used for whole-body compatibility.
Per-hand depth anchoring reduces median hand–depth residuals by 23% versus a single global scale; pooled residual is 84.6 mm against a 20.5 mm reference.
Hand pose reaches 14.53 ± 1.29 mm PA-MPJPE but 119.1 ± 31.3 mm absolute MPJPE, showing a large aligned-versus-metric accuracy gap.
The hand–depth residual is only an internal-consistency measure because anchoring and evaluation use the same depth map; a sliding-window optimization issue is also identified.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Overall architecture of EgoLabel. Off-the-shelf models produce geometry (MonST3R), object annotations (LocateAnything + GMC-BoT-SORT + SAM 2), and hand poses (V-HPOT). Unit conversion, coordinate alignment, and per-hand depth anchoring connect these streams for joint inspection. Hand–depth residuals, object-trajectory smoothness, and control experiments assess their consistency. FisheyeViT is demonstrated on separate fisheye recordings, and structured manipulation captioning is a downstream application. Metric-scale limitations are detailed in Section 3.4.

Figure 4: Final end-to-end output of EgoLabel on H2O h1/0, as rendered in the Rerun viewer at four stages of the manipulation: (a) lifting the box to examine it, (b) peeling the top flaps, (c) removing the flaps, and (d) pulling the box sides. Each panel is one screenshot of the integrated viewer and simultaneously shows the object stream (LocateAnything detections, GMC-BoT-SORT track IDs, and SAM 2 masks, drawn as colored boxes on the overlay video), the 3D hand prediction (left/right V-HPOT skeletons and the camera+wrist trajectory in 3D), and the ASID task caption (bottom panel: hand usage, manipulated object, and action). Object, hand, and camera annotations are produced by independent zero-shot models; the ASID caption (bottom panel) is a GT-assisted downstream consumer (Section 3.5).

(a) Prediction only; (b)–(d) prediction overlaid with ground truth. The skeleton is mapped into the shared frame by the camera-to-world transform (Section 3.2.4); this is a compatibility demonstration on separate recordings, not a joint H2O result.

Figure 5: Cross-modal consistency of the V-HPOT hand stream against the depth map on H2O h1/0. (a) Distribution of the per-joint hand–depth residual; the solid line is the median. (b) Median residual for a single global scale, our per-hand anchoring, and the reprojected ground-truth hands. The figure shows a representative sequence; across the 20 sequences the per-sequence median ranges from 64.2 to 119.7mm, and the pooled medians are in Table 6. The residual is a consistency check (does the fused skeleton lie on the reconstructed surface?), not an independent accuracy metric.

Figure 6: Camera trajectory on H2O k1/0 for the sensor-depth-injection ablation (the RGB-only trajectory, which we take as the main camera result, is summarized in Table 5), in the first-frame camera frame. (a) Top view: ground-truth (gray) and MonST3R trajectory after 7-DoF Sim(3) alignment (blue). (b) Per-frame ATE (blue) with the mean as a dashed line. The injected run recovers the trajectory shape well, with the residual global-scale error left by the injection acting only as an initialization rather than a constraint (recomputed with the released estimator: Sim(3) ATE 1.76 cm, fitted scale 0.45, strict SE(3) 3.12 cm).

The independently estimated hand, object, and camera streams are drawn in one coordinate system for inspection.

(b) Per-frame PA-MPJPE over time (light) with a 15-frame smoothed curve and the sequence mean (dashed). The per-frame PA-MPJPE is broadly stable over the sequence. 20 sequences: 14.53±1.29 PA-MPJPE, 26.46±4.40 scale-aligned (mean±std).

Figure 2: Object tracking and segmentation on H2O h1/0 (frames 0, 225, 449). papers.abstract: We present a pipeline for transferring Awa Odori, a traditional Japanese festival dance, from monocular video to a commercial Unitree G1 EDU humanoid. The pipeline combines human mesh recovery, kinematic retargeting, reinforcement learning for motion tracking in simulation, and onboard deployment via ONNX. Training ran on a single RTX 5070 GPU. An eleven-version deployment ladder evaluated on hardware examines three interventions. We detect and repair silent corruption of deployment artifacts, model state-estimator drift during training, and edit the reference motion to support stable execution and a controlled ending. The final policies achieved three consecutive rope-free completions of a 43-second routine, a 46-second performance with automatic handoff, and a continuous 9.7-minute rope-free performance composed from the captured motion. In a live handover, a single remote request let the robot start from and return to the manufacturer's walking controller on stage, with a measured torque-free window of 45-140 ms. We report the training dynamics and hardware outcomes and discuss failure boundaries involving compliant flooring and occlusion in monocular capture.
bullets: Combines human mesh recovery, kinematic retargeting, simulated reinforcement-learning motion tracking, and ONNX onboard deployment.
An eleven-version hardware ladder addresses deployment-artifact corruption, state-estimator drift, and reference-motion edits for stable completion.
The robot completed the routine three consecutive times without a rope, performed a 46-second automatic-handoff demonstration, and sustained a 9.7-minute composed performance.
A live remote handoff returned control between the dance policy and the manufacturer's walking controller, with a measured torque-free window of 45–140 ms.
Failure boundaries include compliant flooring and occlusions in monocular video capture.
papers.selection_reason: Sim-to-real humanoid dance learning from monocular human video via RL and retargeting; directly fits embodied robot learning and human-video transfer.
papers.title: From Festival Video to the Stage: A Sim-to-Real Ladder for Long-Horizon Expressive Whole-Body Dance on a Commercial Humanoid
papers.tldr: A sim-to-real pipeline transfers a 43-second Awa Odori dance from monocular video to a Unitree G1 EDU, enabling repeated and extended hardware performances with automatic controller handoff.

papers.abstract: Learning whole-body musculoskeletal control from human motion is important for developing human-like robots, assistive devices, and rehabilitation systems. This task presents two main challenges, namely reference trajectories that are kinematically plausible but difficult to reproduce through muscle-driven dynamics, and a highly redundant 700-dimensional action space in which unstructured exploration can easily disrupt the target motion. In this paper, we propose a motion-to-policy pipeline that exploits muscle redundancy in two complementary stages. First, muscle-aware retargeting (MAR) performs bounded adaptation of kinematic trajectories subject to hard semantic, anatomical, and contact constraints. We motivate the constraint bounds by analyzing how reference-trajectory artifacts affect muscle-driven tracking. Second, null-space exploration (NSE) estimates a one-control-frame mapping from muscle excitations to generalized forces and injects bounded, anatomically structured perturbations along its null space into the actions of a value-guided flow policy. On a 24-clip motion-capture benchmark, MAR and NSE together solve every reference, reach the full horizon with half the samples of the baseline pipeline, and lower joint-center error by 44% without late collapse. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first end-to-end pipeline that transforms monocular video into a trained whole-body imitation policy controlling 700 muscles.
bullets: Addresses kinematically plausible references that are difficult to reproduce with muscle-driven dynamics and exploration in a 700-dimensional action space.
Muscle-aware retargeting adapts trajectories within semantic, anatomical, and contact constraints.
Null-space exploration adds bounded, anatomically structured perturbations that preserve generalized forces while guiding policy learning.
On 24 motion-capture clips, the combined method solved every reference, used half the baseline samples, and reduced joint-center error by 44%.
Scope: whole-body musculoskeletal control with 700 muscles; the abstract does not report broader settings beyond this benchmark.

papers.abstract: Creative tool use is a fundamental human capability and an important step toward general-purpose embodied intelligence. It requires agents to reason about object affordances, physical constraints, and manipulation strategies, especially when standard tools are unavailable. However, progress in this area is limited by the lack of real-world datasets that capture human tool-use behavior with sufficient scale, fidelity, and diversity. Existing benchmarks are often simulation-based, focus on simplified interactions, or lack detailed observations and annotations. We introduce ToolDex, a large-scale egocentric-exocentric (ego-exo) human demonstration dataset for creative physical tool use. ToolDex captures scenarios in which humans select, adapt, and repurpose available objects as tools. Using synchronized egocentric cameras and eight exocentric cameras, the dataset provides high-fidelity multi-view observations and rich annotations for hands, tools, target objects, and their deformable interactions. Beyond data collection, we establish a benchmark suite characterizing three core capabilities: physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D and 4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning. ToolDex provides a foundation for studying human tool-use behavior and developing embodied agents that can adaptively use tools in complex real-world environments. Dataset visualizations and benchmarking results are available at https://tooluse-dataset.github.io/.
authors: Mohamed Elmoghany, Kehan Li, Ruoqu Chen, Tarun Chiruvolu, Shutong Zhang, Ryan Wang, Stephen Tian, Yaru Niu, Michelle Guo, Ding Zhao, Weiyu Liu, Mengdi Xu, Li Fei-Fei, Jiajun Wu
bullets: Targets adaptive tool use when standard tools are unavailable, requiring reasoning about affordances, constraints, and manipulation.
Combines synchronized egocentric and eight exocentric cameras for high-fidelity observations.
Provides annotations for hands, tools, target objects, and deformable interactions.
Benchmarks physical tool-use reasoning, sparse-view 3D/4D reconstruction, and robot policy learning.
Supports research on embodied agents that adaptively repurpose objects in complex real-world settings.

papers.abstract: Human videos contain abundant object-manipulation demonstrations, but they do not directly provide motion cues that a robot can follow. We present HOC2R, a Hand-Object Contact trajectory extractor for Robot motion that combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand-object association and contact localization. HOC2R supports two modes: count-aware automation that detects, counts, and localizes visible contacts in untrimmed videos, and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers when contact frames are known. On a 30-task point-annotated benchmark, count-aware automation improves contact-count accuracy from 58.1% to 71.4% and reduces mean localization distance from 19.81 to 10.46 pixels relative to an adapted VRB2 baseline. On seven unseen RGB-D rollouts, a five-task fixed-two checkpoint reduces mean localization distance from 67.67 to 27.02 pixels. Across six robot evaluation sequences, the 30-task fixed-two checkpoint produces four feasible trajectories and succeeds on three tasks, compared with two feasible trajectories and one successful task for each adapted baseline. HOC2R is competitive in the evaluated single-hand scenes, robust to the hand-color shift, and strongest in the evaluated multi-hand scenes. These results support HOC2R as a practical pseudo-labeling method for extracting robot-usable contact trajectories from human demonstrations.
authors: Hongkun Yu, Francisco M. L\'opez, Francisco Cruz
bullets: Addresses the challenge of converting human object-manipulation videos into motion cues for robots.
Combines frozen DINOv3 and SAM 2.1 features with learned heads for hand–object association and contact localization.
Supports count-aware contact detection in untrimmed videos and fixed-two localization for two-finger grippers.
Improves contact-count accuracy and localization distance over an adapted VRB2 baseline on a 30-task benchmark, with further gains in RGB-D rollouts.
Produces more feasible trajectories and successful tasks than adapted baselines in six robot evaluation sequences; evaluation focuses on single-hand scenes and selected multi-hand scenes.

figures.caption: Figure 2: HOC2R inference architecture. Shared outputs comprise contact-region proposal boxes, per-box touch scores, an enclosing-region contact-count prediction, and a whole-image contact-likelihood heatmap. Count-aware automation reranks heatmap candidates using touch scores and emits the predicted number of points. Fixed-two localization filters candidates through proposal boxes, progressively examines more heatmap maxima until two eligible candidates are found, applies touch reranking, and returns two points for a known active contact segment. Their midpoint is lifted with aligned depth and camera calibration into a robot-base trajectory.

Figure 1: HOC2R training architecture. The proposal head uses frozen DINOv3 features and patch labels to predict candidate contact-region boxes. The proposalbox touch head uses each proposal’s SAM feature crop and box label to predict whether the box contains contact. The enclosing-region count head uses the SAM feature crop covering the top-ten proposal boxes and frame-level labels to predict contact presence and count. The whole-image heatmap head uses SAM features and Gaussian targets to predict pixel-wise contact likelihood.
Figure 6: In-domain contact-count confusion over 210 held-out frames. Rows show ground truth, and columns show predictions.

Figure 4: Comparison on seven external RGB-D rollouts. In (a), points show aggregate F1@10, and thin bars show task-level bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. In (b), points show mean localization distance, thin bars show its 95% confidence interval, and wide stems span the median-to-90th-percentile error. Shorter stems indicate more consistent localization.

Figure 5: External multi-hand diagnostics. VRB2 associates its prediction with the resting hand. EgoHOS responds to the resting hand and the clothing sleeve beside the manipulating arm, and its point adapter retains these unrelated boundaries. In contrast, HOC2R proposal boxes focus on the manipulating hand, and the fixed-two decoder localizes the pencil contact. The assignment errors are 156.11 px for VRB2, 126.00 px for EgoHOS-Point, and 17.81 px for HOC2R.

Figure 3: Robot evaluation workflow illustrated on the pen-motion demonstration. HOC2R extracts two image contacts (a), whose midpoint forms a 2D trajectory (b). Aligned depth and camera calibration map the trajectory into the robot base frame (c). Shared filtering and waypoint resampling are applied before inversekinematics execution (d).

Figure 9: Robot executions for HOC2R fixed-two (5 tasks). Four selected frames are shown for each executed trajectory. Both feasible trajectories succeed.

papers.abstract: Long-horizon ego/exo data contains rich procedural evidence, but are redundant, noisy, and costly to process or retain. We propose a compact framework that converts continuous multimodal workplace video into a structured Procedural State Memory, implemented as a Work Environment Model (WEM). Inspired by event segmentation theory, we detect boundaries using changes in visual context, location, motion, narration, gaze/object interaction, and optional exocentric workspace evidence, rather than fixed windows or visual novelty alone. Each segment is abstracted into an evidence-linked event card containing actor, interval, location, action, objects/tools, pre/post state, confidence, and provenance. These event cards incrementally update the WEM, enabling compact, auditable documentation and retrieval under on-premise privacy constraints. We instantiate the design with frozen DINOv2 and VJEPA-2 encoders and a local language model, and outline evaluation criteria for segmentation quality, memory compression, retrieval fidelity, and long-horizon QA.
bullets: Segments continuous multimodal video at meaningful procedural boundaries using context, location, motion, narration, gaze, object interaction, and optional workspace evidence.
Summarizes each segment as an evidence-linked event card covering actors, timing, location, actions, objects, state changes, confidence, and provenance.
Incrementally builds a compact Work Environment Model (WEM) rather than retaining all raw video.
Uses frozen DINOv2 and VJEPA-2 encoders with a local language model under on-premise privacy constraints.
Proposes evaluation of segmentation quality, memory compression, retrieval fidelity, and long-horizon question answering.

figures.caption: Fig. 1: Framework overview. Ego–exo recordings are processed offline with frozen encoders to extract visual, motion, gaze/object, narration, location, and exocentric cues. A multi-cue boundary score segments the stream into procedural events. Each event is converted into an evidence-linked event card and inserted into a Work Environment Model (WEM), which supports compact documentation, retrieval, and QA.

papers.title: A Framework for Egocentric and Exocentric Procedural Understanding via Temporal Segmentation and Semantic Abstraction
papers.tldr: A privacy-preserving framework compresses long-horizon egocentric and exocentric workplace video into an auditable procedural memory for retrieval and question answering.

papers.abstract: Modern video models possess strong visual priors, yet do not natively represent human action in metric 3D space. We present EgoGeneralist, which adapts pretrained video generators to unify action-conditioned video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation for egocentric manipulation. Our role-adaptive action renderer provides video-native representations for multidirectional action-video learning, making metric motion usable as both a spatial control signal and a recoverable generation target. Cross-stream action-video coupling establishes close correspondence between metric motion and visual dynamics through lightweight adaptation while preserving the pretrained visual prior. Together, these designs establish a generalist framework spanning six action-video tasks. With only narrow-domain data, EgoGeneralist generalizes to diverse unseen scenes and interactions with effective action control and visual quality, bridging pretrained visual knowledge and metric 3D human motion.
bullets: Addresses the lack of native metric-3D human-action representations in modern video models.
Supports action-conditioned video generation, pose estimation, and joint action-video generation for egocentric manipulation.
Uses a role-adaptive action renderer and cross-stream action-video coupling to align motion with visual dynamics.
Covers six action-video tasks and generalizes from narrow-domain data to unseen scenes and interactions.
Provides effective action control and visual quality while preserving pretrained visual knowledge.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of EgoGeneralist. Role-adaptive rendering (Sec. 3.2) tailors the visual representation of metric 3D action to its task role: an ego-view map with a fixed 3D anchor for conditioning, or a multiview Posegrid for generation and metric readout. A shared frozen video VAE encodes rendered action and video into two latent streams. Cross-stream coupling (Sec. 3.3) uses joint self-attention and attention LoRAs activated only for generation targets, retaining the backbone weights and per-stream input structure. The bottom panel illustrates condition–target assignments for the three prediction directions defined in Sec. 3.1.

Figure 5. World-action policy on HOT3D. Top: EgoGeneralist’s generated video and 3D action in ego and side views. Bottom: action predictions from all three methods in a shared top view. GT object meshes and scene points are used only for visualization. Additional examples are provided in supplementary Fig. S7.

Figure 3. Action-conditioned image-to-video generation. Comparisons on EgoDex (left) and Xperience-10M (right, out-of-distribution). Adapted only on EgoDex, EgoGeneralist generalizes to in-the-wild scenes. The generated videos follow the prescribed motion with physically coherent interactions, correctly removing the purple block (left) and tilting the bucket (right).

Figure 6. Text-only joint action–video generation. Each example shows jointly generated video and 3D action, with the action projected onto video frames. Insets show the generated 3D upper-body skeleton and camera pose. Best viewed in the supplementary video.

Figure 4. Action-conditioned text-to-video generation. EgoGeneralist generates videos that share the same prescribed 3D motion while varying scenes and object appearances according to different text prompts. Actions are drawn from EgoDex (top) and Xperience-10M (bottom).

Table 3. Hand, upper-limb, and camera reconstruction on EgoDex and Xperience-10M. EgoGeneralist remains competitive with specialist estimators while jointly recovering body, hand, and camera motion. HaMeR † and EgoForce † use HaWoR’s camera estimates with camera scores reported in the HaWoR row. ReViV keeps its native two-second input context and all methods are evaluated on 41 frames.

Table 4. World-action policy evaluation on HOT3D. Our method outperforms specialized policy baselines in target reaching on unseen HOT3D scenes while jointly generating video. All methods receive an initial observation and instruction. VITRA and EgoGeneralist also receive initial action states. †Being-H0 uses a single wrist-anchored rigid alignment to the GT initial hand.

Table 2. Action-conditioned text-to-video generation on 100 action–prompt instances per dataset. Since the varied prompts have no corresponding ground-truth videos, we evaluate motion control and video–text semantic alignment. Our method maintains competitive action adherence across text-specified visual contexts.

Table 1. Action-conditioned image-to-video generation on EgoDex and Xperience-10M. EgoGeneralist achieves strong visual fidelity and action control in both datasets. PCK, IoU, and Failure are in percentages; best and second-best are bold and underlined. EgoSimO/EgoSimQ use dataset-provided/Qwen-generated prompts.

Table 7. Pose estimation with and without an initial action state. GT first-frame conditioning lowers most reconstruction errors on both datasets. Metrics and units follow Tab. 3. All 41 frames are evaluated. Lower errors are bold.
Table 5. Hand, upper-limb, and camera readout on EgoDex. Multiview Posegrid gives lower reconstruction errors, indicating that its VAE latents better preserve metric action information for readout.

Table 6. Ablations of two design components for action-conditioned video generation. We evaluate how different action–video coupling strategies and action renderings affect video controllability under matched data and training budgets. The full configuration performs best on most metrics, supporting our cross-stream coupling and role-adaptive rendering design. Best and second-best scores are bold and underlined.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots are typically trained as solitary agents, leaving them unable to coordinate physically with human partners who naturally anticipate and adjust to one another. To bridge this gap, we present Social Humanoid, a hierarchical system that generates and executes socially responsive whole-body motion on a 29-DoF Unitree G1 conditioned on a human partner's motion. Its high-level policy performs flexible sequence modeling of human and humanoid motion through a shared tokenized representation, generating reactive humanoid motion and anticipating the partner's motion when they are occluded, while a low-level whole-body tracking controller executes the generated motion on the robot. To train the system, we introduce a two-phase adaptive retargeting procedure that retargets one interaction partner to the robot while morphing the other partner to preserve contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale. We apply this procedure across five motion-capture datasets to produce a new Human-Humanoid Interaction (HHI) benchmark of 260 hours of human-humanoid interactions. Our results demonstrate that Social Humanoid produces coordinated, human-aligned behavior across diverse interaction types in simulation and the real world. Project page: https://von31.github.io/social-humanoid/
bullets: Addresses the lack of physical coordination in humanoid robots trained as solitary agents.
Uses a hierarchical system with shared-token sequence modeling for reactive and anticipatory human–robot motion generation.
Combines high-level motion generation with a low-level whole-body tracking controller for robot execution.
Introduces adaptive retargeting that preserves contact dynamics, reachability, and relative body scale.
Builds a 260-hour Human-Humanoid Interaction benchmark from five motion-capture datasets and demonstrates coordinated behavior in simulation and the real world.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Social Humanoid Architecture. From RGB-D observations of a human partner (red), we reconstruct the human pose and localize the body in 3D using depth and estimated gravity. Relative human and humanoid states are encoded through the VQ-VAE encoders Eh and Er. The resulting latent motion tokens z∗, relative pose transforms T ∗, and canonical motion transforms ∆T ∗ are concatenated and processed by the DFoT policy, then decoded via Dh and Dr to future human behavior (blue) and socially coordinated humanoid motion (purple). SONIC executes the motion in sim or the real-world, and the robot state is updated for closed-loop interaction.

Figure 5: Retargeting Qualitative Results. Each panel shows a ground-truth human–human interaction (ego in orange, partner in dark blue) next to its retargeted counterpart. The ego is retargeted to the humanoid (tan), and the partner’s pose is morphed to preserve interaction (light blue). Across diverse interactions our Adaptive-HHI Retargeting method preserves the contacts and relative positioning between the two agents.

Figure 6: Real-world deployment. Frames run left to right in time. Top two rows: separate highfive and hand-wave trials. Bottom: a single continuous take in which the humanoid transitions directly from a handshake into a bend

Figure 7: Shadow teleoperation. The G1 shadows a human operator performing arm movements (top) and sitting down on a couch (bottom). The operator’s motion is encoded with Eh, quantized against the shared codebook C, and decoded with Dr into humanoid motion. Frames run left to right in time.

Figure 3: Shared-Codebook VQ-VAE. Human and humanoid motion sequences are independently encoded into latent features and mapped to a shared vector-quantized codebook that learns a common motion vocabulary across embodiments. Embodiment-specific decoders reconstruct the respective motions, enabling aligned, transferable motion representations between humans and humanoids.

Figure 4: Adaptive-HHI Retargeting. Our retargeting pipeline starts from two ground truth humans. In the first pass, we retarget the ego human (orange) to the humanoid using a contact-adaptive weight matrix to encourage body pose in regions close to the physical interaction to be preserved. In a second pass, we co-morph the partner’s pose towards more plausible interaction via a contactgated morphing strategy driven by the amount of physical contact present in the interaction.

Figure A.1: Cross-embodiment motion translation with a shared-codebook VQ-VAE. Human motion (red) is encoded into a discrete latent space shared between the human and humanoid embodiments, then decoded into humanoid motion (purple). Each example shows three frames of the input human motion alongside the translated humanoid motion in simulation (top row), and the same frames executed on the physical humanoid robot (bottom row).
Table 3: Retargeting comparison across three interaction datasets. Best per column in bold; ↑/↓ indicate higher/lower is better.

Table A.2: Comparison of retargeting methods. Adaptive-HHI extends OmniRetarget’s interaction-mesh SOCP base with partner co-morphing (joint optimization over the partner SMPLX) and distance-weighted, wrist-boosted adaptive Laplacian weighting for interaction and humanscale preservation.

Table A.6: Network configuration details. T is the raw sequence length and T ′ = T/ω the number of tokens after temporal compression (ω=4); P is the number of interacting agents; Din is the peragent pose dimension (Dh or Dr); Dc is the local conditioning dimension; de is the embedding dimension; and Dm = dvq + 4 × 9 × P is the unified motion token dimension tracking localized cross-agent transformations.
Table A.1: Summary statistics of our retargeted benchmark. Clip counts, frames, and durations are reported after retargeting each source dataset to the Unitree G1 with Adaptive-HHI.
Table A.4: Retargeting hyperparameters. Values are shared across all datasets without per-clip tuning.
Table A.3: Adaptive retargeting ablation on CHI3D. Mean ± std over clips. Best per column in bold.

Table A.5: Shared-codebook design ablation on HHI. H and R denote human and robot motion; H→R and R→H denote encoding in one embodiment and decoding in the other. FD is Fréchet distance. MPJPE is the root-relative mean per-joint position error of the decoded pose against ground truth (cm; 21 SMPL-X body joints for H, 29 actuated joints of the G1 for R, hands excluded). Code Agree. is the fraction of paired H/R frames assigned the same code. Best per column in bold.
