papers.abstract: VREgo trains manipulation policies from demonstrations recorded on consumer VR headsets; we instantiate it with EgoKit on one such headset, the PICO 4 Ultra. On-device head and hand tracking and stereo object localisation allow the operator to begin a demonstration at the table. We adapt HumanEgo's preprocessing to estimate grasp thresholds per recording, update object positions after release, and propagate segmentation masks between keyframes. We evaluate policies in simulation on two tabletop tasks recorded by one operator. For cube placement, we compare PICO and Project Aria recordings of the same 41 layouts. With 40 training demonstrations, the PICO policies placed the cube on the tray in 67, 74, and 60 of 100 evaluation layouts across three training seeds. The corresponding Aria results were 73, 78, and 0. For a two-stage stacking task recorded with the PICO alone, the baseline placed the block on the tray in 94 of 100 layouts and met the end-of-episode criterion for both placements in two. In one diagnostic episode, repeated replanning deferred release beyond the eight executed steps. Demonstration replays also showed that the open gripper could displace the cube before grasping it. After adapting the training trajectories and adding task-specific execution rules that use simulator object positions, the system met both placement criteria in 93.8% of episodes across four evaluation noise seeds. The same 100 layouts informed rule development and evaluation. VREgo is available at https://vrego.chuange.org/.
bullets: Uses a PICO 4 Ultra headset with on-device head/hand tracking and stereo object localisation for tabletop demonstrations.
Adapts preprocessing to estimate grasp thresholds, update object positions after release, and propagate segmentation masks between keyframes.
Evaluated two tabletop tasks in simulation using demonstrations from one operator; cube-placement performance varied across training seeds and headsets.
A baseline struggled with two-stage stacking due to replanning and gripper–object interactions observed in diagnostic replays.
After task-specific trajectory and execution adaptations, the stacking policy met both placement criteria in 93.8% of episodes across four noise seeds.

papers.selection_reason: Learns robot manipulation policies from egocentric VR demonstrations, fitting both robot learning and human-video learning.
papers.title: VREgo: Consumer VR Headsets for Learning Robot Manipulation from Egocentric Demonstrations
papers.tldr: VREgo uses consumer-VR egocentric demonstrations to train robot manipulation policies, achieving reliable cube placement and stacking after trajectory and execution-rule adaptations.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human video offers a scalable source of manipulation priors for robot learning, yet translating raw data scale into generalizable robot policies demands rigorous data curation and training recipes. We introduce Open-HumanScale, the first fully open recipe for scaling egocentric pretraining to 50,000 hours, anchored by Open-HumanScale-50K---a curated egocentric video corpus densely annotated with hand motion and natural language. Leveraging this corpus, we systematically investigate pure human pretraining via closed-loop simulation evaluations and uncover an empirical log-linear scaling law linking pretraining data hours to downstream robot success rates. Grounded in these findings, we develop HumanWAM-Vanilla, a world--action model pretrained exclusively on 50k hours of egocentric human video. Upon robot post-training, HumanWAM-Vanilla reaches 92.08% success on RoboTwin 2.0 Clean2Clean and 68.88% on Clean2Random, alongside a 14.17% mean success rate and a 19.00 mean progress score on RoboDojo. To push the capability frontier further, we explore joint human--robot pretraining with HumanWAM-Goal, a visual-goal-conditioned world--action model. Hybrid data scaling unlocks broad zero-shot generalization across both simulation and physical benchmarks, propelling post-trained RoboTwin 2.0 performance to new state-of-the-art levels: 92.70% on Clean2Clean and a substantial leap to 84.60% on Clean2Random. On physical robots, HumanWAM-Goal further exhibits emergent embodied in-context learning, dynamically adapting its manipulation behavior to unseen visual goals without parameter updates. To support reproducible scaling research in embodied AI, we open-source the Open-HumanScale-50K corpus, data curation and pretraining pipelines, alongside the pretrained and post-trained HumanWAM checkpoints, inference code, and simulation evaluation suites.
authors: Juncheng Ma, Jiaxin Li, Jiankai Tu, Bo Liang, Guodong Lv, Yufan Deng, Junzhe Tang, Liangzhu Yang, Chen Bian, Zicong Cao, Baohao Zhu, Jianxin Bi, Tengfei Yan, Yinyuan Zhang, Kewei Zhang, Xinglong Chen, Kaiqi Chen, Duomin Wang, Xiaotian Tang, Liang Tan, Li Li, Yuan Xu, Haosen Yang, Yuqi Wang, Jingfei Xia, Songyan Huang, Zhiyang Dou, Zhen Dong, Enze Xie, Tat-Seng Chua, Daquan Zhou
bullets: Curates egocentric human video with dense hand-motion and language annotations for scalable robot-learning pretraining.
Finds a log-linear relationship between human-video pretraining hours and downstream robot success in closed-loop simulation.
HumanWAM-Vanilla, pretrained only on human video, achieves strong RoboTwin 2.0 and RoboDojo performance after robot post-training.
Joint human–robot pretraining with goal conditioning improves zero-shot generalization, reaching 84.60% on RoboTwin Clean2Random.
Releases the corpus, curation and training pipelines, model checkpoints, inference code, and evaluation suites.

figures.caption: Figure 3 Model architecture of HumanWAM-Vanilla and experimental protocol. (a) Egocentric pretraining, robot post-training on clean demonstrations, and closed-loop evaluation under clean, scene-ood, and random conditions. (b) Conditioned on language and proprioception, the video and action experts interact through joint masked self-attention. The masks specify visibility among current-frame (C), future-video (F), and action (A) tokens under isolated attention (IA) and inverse-dynamics (IDM) attention.

Figure 1 Overview of Open-HumanScale. Using a curated 50,000-hour egocentric corpus, we show that scaling human data improves robot generalization after post-training, with greater task and scene diversity yielding steeper scaling curves. We then extend this pretraining approach to combine human and robot data, finding that hybrid scaling improves zero-shot success in simulation and across 20 real-world tasks.

Figure 16 HumanWAM-Goal architecture. (a) Conditioning. An explicit goal image augments language instructions, current and optional historical observations, and the 49-D robot state. (b) Joint rectified-flow sampling. With conditioning tokens held fixed, the shared video-action Generator iteratively predicts video and action velocities via UniPC updates.

Figure 15 Robot pretraining data overview. The top row reports the overall robot pretraining budget. Word clouds summarize selected (a) action and (b) object terms, while the adjacent bars show label-level percentages for the eight most frequent terms in each group. Percentages use all 751 normalized task-collection labels as the denominator.

papers.abstract: Dexterous robotic hands are increasingly coupled to large-scale human data and foundation models, yet progress in hardware, representation learning and evaluation is often assessed separately. This survey reviews work from January 2024 to early November 2026, with earlier studies included to establish technical lineages. We organize the literature into five interdependent layers: hardware; data collection and curation; cross-embodiment transfer; learning and foundation models; and evaluation and applications. Human hand-object understanding and tactile sensing provide two cross-cutting perspectives. A system-level architecture, comparative tables and five case analyses connect design choices across these layers. We distinguish within-study experimental comparisons from heterogeneous corpus statistics, vendor specifications and company-reported results. Three conclusions emerge. First, the value of human data depends on kinematic, visual and contact alignment, not recording volume alone. Second, shared action representations and foundation policies do not remove embodiment-specific constraints on force, latency and contact. Third, task completion is insufficient to establish physical correctness or deployment readiness. Evidence remains limited for zero-shot transfer of contact-rich skills between morphologically different hands, long-duration reliability, and cross-sensor tactile generalization. We identify eleven open problems and propose reporting interfaces and controlled comparisons that can make full-stack progress more measurable. The review is a structured narrative synthesis rather than a pooled performance ranking or an exhaustive systematic review.
bullets: Organizes recent research into five interdependent layers: hardware; data collection and curation; cross-embodiment transfer; learning and foundation models; and evaluation and applications.
Highlights human hand-object understanding and tactile sensing as cross-cutting perspectives, supported by a system-level architecture, comparative tables, and case analyses.

Finds that human-data value depends on kinematic, visual, and contact alignment—not recording volume alone—and that foundation policies cannot eliminate embodiment-specific force, latency, and contact constraints.
Argues that task completion alone does not demonstrate physical correctness or deployment readiness.

Identifies limited evidence for zero-shot transfer across morphologically different hands, long-duration reliability, and cross-sensor tactile generalization; proposes reporting interfaces and controlled comparisons.

papers.abstract: Humanoid soccer requires a robot to seamlessly combine agile locomotion, ball manipulation, and impact-rich contact dynamics across a continuous, dynamic behavioral spectrum. Yet existing approaches either cover only a limited set of skills, or forego motion priors entirely and produce unnatural behaviors, leaving the combination of a unified skill set and human-like motion quality unaddressed. We present soccerbot, a hierarchical reinforcement learning framework that resolves both limitations through a structured latent motion prior distilled from large-scale human soccer motion capture data. By constraining policy learning within this dynamically plausible motion manifold, a single skill-conditioned policy naturally learns to perform moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking in a unified formulation, while inherently producing human-like motion and fluid transitions during commanded skill switching. Augmented by robustness-oriented simulation design, soccerbot transfers zero-shot to the Unitree G1 humanoid robot, demonstrating agile, natural, and robust execution of the full soccer skill repertoire under real-world conditions.
authors: Haoyu Shao, Yunshen Wang, Jingze Zhang, Shaohang Zhu, Yong-Lu Li, Tianzhu Zhang, Baoxiong Jia, Siyuan Huang
bullets: Targets the challenge of combining locomotion, ball control, and contact-rich dynamics across continuously changing soccer behaviors.
Distills a latent motion prior from large-scale human soccer motion-capture data to constrain learning to dynamically plausible movements.
Trains one skill-conditioned policy for moving, dribbling, trapping, and kicking, including fluid transitions when switching skills.
Uses robustness-oriented simulation design to enable zero-shot transfer to the Unitree G1 humanoid.
Demonstrates agile, natural, and robust execution of the full skill repertoire in real-world conditions.

Real-world deployment uses an external motion capture system for ball state estimation.

papers.abstract: Manipulating diverse objects with multi-fingered dexterous hands is challenging due to the high dimensionality and complex dynamics. Human-Object Interaction (HOI) datasets provide rich knowledge about task information and embodied interactions. Instead of solely imitating the human demonstrations, our method learns to holistically predict future hand-object states by leveraging these datasets. The predicted future states of the object can serve as a general-purpose reward term for reinforcement learning, reducing reliance on task-specific reward engineering and enhancing generalization across tasks. We conduct extensive experiments on three manipulation tasks in simulation and the real world. Our approach outperforms existing SOTA methods in both success rate and generalizability on novel objects. Furthermore, we validate the cross-embodiment compatibility of our methods by successfully deploying the skills on different robot hands.
bullets: Addresses the high-dimensional, complex dynamics of multi-fingered manipulation of diverse objects.
Predicts future hand–object states holistically rather than directly imitating human demonstrations.
Uses predicted object futures as a task-agnostic reinforcement-learning reward, reducing task-specific reward engineering.
Evaluated across three simulation and real-world manipulation tasks, including novel objects.
Reports improved success rate and generalization over existing methods, with successful transfer across different robot hands.

Notably, since the learned priors are general to hand morphologies, our framework is adaptable to various dexterous hands.

papers.abstract: We study physics-based retargeting of human demonstrations for robot learning: finding robot controls that reproduce reference motions under contact dynamics. We propose GRASP (Gradient Recovery from Archived Samples for Proposals), which combines sampling-based exploration with gradient-guided refinement without requiring a differentiable simulator. GRASP-TO extends tempered sequential Monte Carlo by fitting local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts and using their gradients to guide Markov chain Monte Carlo rejuvenation. Metropolis-Hastings correction preserves the target distribution for each fixed proposal kernel, and a population analysis connects the recovered gradients to Gaussian smoothing. GRASP-MPC scales this optimizer to long demonstrations through warm-started receding-horizon planning. Experiments on dexterous hands and humanoids show accurate retargeting with a shared tracking objective and no task-specific contact rewards, including 92.8% success on 1352 bimanual OakInk2 demonstrations. The refined references improve PPO tracking in pen spinning and humanoid-object interaction. We also demonstrate dexterous manipulation and whole-body humanoid motion on real hardware.
authors: Yang Liu, Tong Wang, Yiming Bao, Heng Yang
bullets: Targets retargeting of human demonstrations under contact-rich robot dynamics.
GRASP-TO fits local quadratic cost models to archived rollouts and uses recovered gradients to guide MCMC proposals, with Metropolis-Hastings correction.
GRASP-MPC extends the approach to long demonstrations through warm-started receding-horizon planning.
Achieves 92.8% success on 1,352 bimanual OakInk2 demonstrations using a shared tracking objective without task-specific contact rewards.
Improves PPO tracking and transfers to dexterous and whole-body humanoid manipulation on real hardware.

papers.abstract: Robot imitation learning is limited by the scarcity of action-labeled data, while action-free demonstrations such as videos are abundant. Recent latent-action methods learn action-relevant representations from observation transitions, but they do not optimize latent actions for downstream control, leading to latent representations that are difficult for policies to model and difficult to accurately decode into continuous robot actions. This paper introduces ELA, an end-to-end framework for learning from video demonstrations via latent actions jointly optimized for policy learning and action decoding. ELA jointly trains a latent action model, latent action policy, and action decoder, enabling policies to leverage abundant video data with only a handful of action-labeled robot demonstrations. Experiments on simulated and real-world manipulation tasks show that ELA consistently outperforms prior latent action baselines. Moreover, it integrates seamlessly with existing imitation learning methods through lightweight 4M-parameter action decoders, requiring no changes to policy architectures or training objectives. Additional materials can be found on: https://end2end-latent-action.github.io/

papers.abstract: Robot foundation models have shown remarkable performance in robot control, yet adapting them to a new task still relies heavily on teleoperated demonstrations. Egocentric human videos offer a scalable substitute, but overlaying rendered robots on human videos or retargeting human poses into robot actions leaves significant visual or action gaps for high-DoF robot embodiments. To address this limitation, we propose RoboTryOn, which treats human-to-robot translation as virtual try-on: try-on keeps the person and swaps the garment, RoboTryOn keeps the demonstrated motion and swaps the human for the robot. Specifically, RoboTryOn converts a human video into a video of the target robot specified by a reference image, while preserving the original task, objects, and background. To maintain visual consistency, we translate selected keyframes autoregressively and use them to guide video synthesis with motion conditioned on the human hand skeleton. Additionally, we use an inverse dynamics model (IDM) that incorporates depth features to infer action labels from synthesized videos for policy learning. Our experiments across multiple humanoid embodiments show that policies trained with our synthetic data improve the average success rate on novel tasks, including challenging bimanual manipulation, from 2% to 60%, without any real robot demonstration of those tasks. Moreover, training with our synthetic data matches the performance of policies trained solely on teleoperated demonstrations at approximately a third of the collection cost, demonstrating the cost efficiency of our approach.
authors: Seungyong Lee, Suhyeok Jang, Minyoung Kim, Jinwoo Shin
bullets: Addresses the scalability and visual/action gaps of adapting human videos to high-DoF robot embodiments.
Uses autoregressive keyframe translation and motion-conditioned video synthesis guided by human hand skeletons.
Infers action labels from synthesized videos with a depth-aware inverse dynamics model.
Across multiple humanoid embodiments, synthetic-data policies improved novel-task success from 2% to 60%, including bimanual manipulation.
Matched teleoperation-trained policy performance at roughly one-third of the data-collection cost.

papers.abstract: Pretrained video generation models distill internet-scale motion priors into robot policies, but full video is a redundant signal for action prediction. We argue that dense 3D motion is the medium through which video pretraining best transfers to robot actions, and that predicting motion rather than video affords better sample-efficiency for action prediction. FloMo is a 5B video-generation model fine-tuned to predict 3D scene-flow and action tokens. Rendering scene flow as RGB and encoding it into the same latent space as video enables a pretrained video generation backbone to efficiently adapt to predict 3D scene flow. Co-trained on action-free human video and action-labeled robot teleoperation data, our model benefits from human-video pretraining and generalizes to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks. Replacing motion prediction with a video prediction objective degrades out-of-distribution generalization, while adding a video prediction target alongside motion lowers policy success rather than improving it. When motion, video, and action are predicted jointly, action tokens attend far more to motion than to video, suggesting that predicting video wastes model capacity. Together, these results indicate that motion effectively mediates the transfer from video pretraining to action. More information can be found at flomo-wam.github.io.
authors: Jeremy Collins, Namra Patel, Ayush Agarwal, Shitij Govil, Animesh Garg
bullets: Motivation: Full video is redundant for action prediction; dense 3D motion may transfer video-learned priors more effectively.
Method: A 5B video-generation model is fine-tuned to predict 3D scene flow and action tokens, using rendered flow encoded in the video model’s latent space.
Training: The model combines action-free human video with action-labeled robot teleoperation data.

Findings: Motion prediction supports generalization to unseen objects, motion primitives, and tasks; replacing or augmenting it with video prediction harms policy success and out-of-distribution generalization.
Interpretation: Action tokens attend substantially more to motion than video, indicating that video prediction can waste model capacity.

papers.abstract: A robot world model that serves as a simulator must do more than generate plausible videos: it must faithfully follow commanded actions, maintain consistency across camera views, and sustain coherent long-horizon rollouts. We present PrimeSim, an action-conditioned, multiview world model simulator that addresses these challenges through progressive midtraining and posttraining. Starting from a pretrained video generator, we midtrain on 30,110 hours of robot demonstrations spanning 22 platforms. To improve action following, we introduce a unified cross-embodiment action representation and frame-aligned dual-path conditioning to strengthen action-frame correspondence. To maintain multiview consistency, we develop view-aware interleaved attention with explicit camera identities, enabling cross-view information exchange while preserving view-specific representations. We further introduce a fast-video, slow-memory posttraining framework that transforms the bidirectional video generator into an efficient autoregressive simulator. By combining fast causal generation, self-rollout training, and hierarchical temporal memory, PrimeSim mitigates error accumulation from self-generated histories and supports coherent long-horizon simulation. PrimeSim runs at 10.1 FPS, remains stable over long-horizon rollouts on rigid and deformable manipulation tasks, and transfers to held-out platforms within 100 to 200 gradient steps where the pretrained backbone does not. Against five open-source action-conditioned world models it leads four of the five WorldSimProbe suites and posts the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration still trails the field; its rollouts are faithful enough to support GRPO-based policy optimization. We release the model weights, inference code, and training code.
authors: Travis Davies, Wentao Ma, Lihao Guo, Tengfei Ma, Xiaowen Chang, Jiafeng Xu, Shilong Wang, Yiqi Deng, Shaowen He, Xiaoqi Li, Qian Zhu, Ran Cheng, Hao Dong
bullets: Targets faithful action following, multiview consistency, and stable long-horizon rollouts beyond merely plausible video generation.
Midtrains a pretrained video generator on 30,110 hours of demonstrations across 22 robot platforms using unified actions and frame-aligned conditioning.
Uses view-aware interleaved attention plus camera identities to preserve consistency across views.
Converts the bidirectional generator into a 10.1-FPS autoregressive simulator with fast-video, slow-memory posttraining, self-rollouts, and hierarchical temporal memory.
Leads four of five WorldSimProbe suites and achieves the best overall EWMBench score, while fine-grained local calibration remains weaker; released with model weights and code.

Rows are cameras (head, left wrist, right wrist) and columns are seven frames sampled uniformly from a single rollout. (b) After 200 gradient steps the arm trajectories and the cloth deformation track the commanded actions much more closely and the three views stay mutually consistent, so most of the cost of the transfer is recovered.

Similar embodiments do occur in the corpus, and they are what make transfer possible at all, since a wholly alien platform would leave nothing to build on. They are still new embodiments, however, and adaptation between embodiments does not happen for free: each brings its own kinematics, camera mounting and data distribution, which have to be acquired rather than inherited. All initialisations are finetuned under an identical recipe with single-trajectory batches at a batch size of 1, and none receives an embodiment identifier or any embodiment-specific parameters. The midtrained model reaches an action-following rollout within 100 to 200 gradient steps on all three platforms. The pretrained backbone, which must initialise the action-conditioning and multiview modules from scratch, does not reach the same regime even at ten to twenty times that budget.

Static scene elements remain stable across the rollout while the commanded motion is carried out, indicating that the generated future is driven by the action rather than by visual plausibility alone.

papers.title: PrimeSim: A Generalist World Model Simulator from Large-Scale Cross-Embodiment Demonstrations

papers.abstract: Video games provide a practical setting for collecting vision-language-action (VLA) data, whose acquisition in physical environments is costly. Existing datasets, however, remain limited by restricted game coverage, sparse language supervision, or temporal hierarchies that do not necessarily reflect changes in task objectives. We introduce AceAction, a dataset of human gameplay across multiple 3D games for learning skill composition and subgoal transitions. AceAction organizes demonstrations around complete tasks, linking overall instructions, ordered subgoals, and local skill instructions to temporally aligned visual observations and keyboard-and-mouse actions. To construct these annotations, we develop a vision-language model pipeline that identifies subgoals from changes in objectives or interaction targets, anchors navigation goals to visually recognizable waypoints, and composes adjacent subgoals into task instructions. The resulting demonstrations cover navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery, with explicit stage boundaries that connect task progression to fine-grained control. We assess annotation quality through model-based verification and human inspection. An audit of 500 trajectories yields a 95.8% pass rate across independent reviewer assessments. AceAction provides a data foundation for studying how agents execute, combine, and switch skills to follow complex instructions in dynamic game environments.
authors: Kailing Li, Ruoxuan Zhang, Zheyuan Zhou, Boyang Chu, Yingshan Lei, Hongxia Xie, Liang Du, Zixun Sun
bullets: Covers diverse 3D-game tasks including navigation, reconnaissance, combat, interaction, and recovery.
Organizes demonstrations into complete tasks with overall instructions, ordered subgoals, local skill instructions, visual observations, and keyboard-mouse actions.
Uses a vision-language pipeline to detect objective or interaction-target changes, ground navigation goals in visual waypoints, and compose task instructions.
Explicit stage boundaries connect task progression with low-level control and skill transitions.
Annotation quality was evaluated through model verification and human inspection; an audit of 500 trajectories achieved a 95.8% pass rate.

figures.caption: Figure 2. Overview of the AceAction data construction pipeline. Gameplay from direct collection and public datasets is annotated with skill- and waypoint-based subgoals. Adjacent subgoals within each trajectory are composed into task-level instructions, followed by annotation and alignment validation. Two models then verify visual grounding and action consistency, retaining only samples approved by both at every annotation level. A sampled human audit further assesses data quality.

papers.title: AceAction-5M: Hierarchical Goals for Generalist Action Learning Across 3D Game Worlds
papers.tldr: AceAction-5M is a multi-game human gameplay dataset that links high-level goals, temporally aligned subgoals, and fine-grained actions for hierarchical VLA learning.

papers.abstract: AIRoA-0 (A-0) is a bimanual manipulation system learned from 16,151 hours of handheld demonstrations, with no robot data collected at any stage. The demonstrations are recorded with YUBI, our open-source handheld gripper, which lets people record manipulation data anywhere with no robot present. From a single instruction, A-0 sorts more than a dozen small parts into their numbered cells and changes the mop pads and brush of a robot vacuum; among other tasks, it unzips a pencil case and folds a towel. It performs these tasks using only a camera on each wrist, with no head or scene camera, at a site where none of its training data was recorded. Across the ten tasks of our evaluation, it averages a success rate of 78%, against 27% for the strongest of four other vision-language-action models post-trained on the same task demonstrations. We collect no teleoperation data and use no reinforcement learning or on-robot corrections, and the robot appears only at test time. The system learns which regions of each wrist view matter for the task, predicts the stage the task has reached, and decodes actions as a continuous stream. A-0 is embodiment-agnostic: it runs on robots that mount the YUBI gripper, such as a bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm and UR. We are releasing the dataset, to our knowledge the largest open dataset of handheld-gripper demonstrations with task and subtask instructions, together with the pre-trained weights and the post-training recipe. Videos of A-0 on every task are on the project page, https://a-0.airoa.io. Anyone can build the gripper, record a task of their own and post-train the model on it in under four hours on a single node of eight H200 GPUs.
authors: Yueh-Hua Wu, Kei Ota, Hanlong Li, Hayata Yuasa, Jason Wang, Kengo Ikeuchi, Kensuke Chiyoma, Makoto Sugiura, Masafumi Takahashi, Masatoshi Tateno, Naoaki Kanazawa, Nicola Scianca, Petr Khrapchenkov, Satoshi Otsubo, Takehiko Ohkawa, Takuya Okubo, Tatsuya Matsushima, Yuki Noguchi, Yuma Shin, Zixuan Zhong

Performs tasks including sorting parts, servicing a robot vacuum, unzipping a pencil case, and folding a towel from a single instruction.
Relies only on wrist-mounted cameras and predicts relevant visual regions, task stage, and continuous actions.
Transfers across multiple robots that mount the YUBI gripper, including bimanual Franka, TX-G2, OpenArm, and UR platforms.
Releases the demonstration dataset, pretrained weights, and post-training recipe; evaluation averages 78% success versus 27% for the strongest comparison model.

papers.abstract: We present SpatialDex, a framework that learns 3D-grounded bimanual dexterity from RGB-only human videos through reconstruction-augmented visuomotor pre-training. The central idea is to learn human behavior together with its spatial context. From each video, we reconstruct the scene geometry and estimate the hand motion, align them at a shared video-level scale using the hand-size prior of 3D hand estimates. We retain the reconstructed geometry as both a policy input and a prediction target. The policy grounds the token grid of a pre-trained vision-language model in this geometry through gated residual fusion, is trained to predict future scene geometry alongside wrist and finger actions, and generates finger motion conditioned on the predicted trajectories of both wrists. Pre-trained on 1M human-video clips and fine-tuned with a small number of robot demonstrations, SpatialDex outperforms the state-of-the-art methods by 16.5 points on nine simulated dexterous tasks across two embodiments and by 38.3 points on six real-world bimanual dexterous tasks. Under a matched comparison, pre-training with reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over pre-training on hand motion alone.
bullets: Learns behavior together with spatial context by reconstructing scene geometry and estimating hand motion from each video.
Aligns geometry and hand motion at a shared scale using a 3D hand-size prior.
Uses gated residual fusion to ground a pre-trained vision-language model in geometry, while predicting future geometry and wrist/finger actions.
Generates finger motion conditioned on predicted trajectories of both wrists.
Pre-training on reconstructed geometry improves success by 14.2 points over hand-motion-only pre-training; the method also reports gains on simulated and real-world bimanual tasks.

figures.caption: Fig. 5: Real-world rollouts. SpatialDex on Spray Plant, Unzip Bag, and Sweep Trash with Wuji hands and Tianji arms, which involve tool actuation, a deformable object, and coordinated two-hand sweeping. Each row runs from the initial frame on the left to task completion on the right.

Fig. 1: SpatialDex reconstructs scene geometry and estimates hand motion from RGB-only human videos and aligns them at a shared video-level scale to jointly supervise policy pre-training. The policy maps RGB-D observations to bimanual dexterous actions and is adapted to specific tasks through fine-tuning on robot demonstrations. The lower panel shows the six bimanual dexterous manipulation tasks for real-world evaluation.

Fig. 3: 3D-grounded visuomotor policy. Reconstructed geometry enters the policy in two roles. As an input, depth samples from each image patch are encoded jointly in 3D and pooled back to their patches, so that the geometry grid g arrives on the same token grid as the visual features x and is fused into f through two gates and a residual whose weight warms up from zero, leaving the priors of the pre-trained VLM intact. As a target, a training-only predictor estimates future scene geometry from the shared context, which requires the representation to retain spatial structure that the action losses alone do not demand. From the same context, a wrist expert predicts both wrist trajectories and a finger expert predicts finger actions conditioned on them.

Fig. 2: Aligned scene and hand reconstruction. From an RGB-only video, SpatialDex recovers hand meshes and wrist trajectories, point clouds and camera poses up to an unknown scale. Aligning the reconstructed hand points with the estimated hand meshes across frames yields one scale shared by the whole video and a rigid transformation per frame, which places the scene geometry and the hand motion in a common frame for pre-training. The aligned reconstruction supplies the depth observations, the wrist and finger action targets, and the future geometry targets for policy pre-training.
Fig. 4: Wuji–Tianji simulation tasks. Three Wuji–Tianji tasks are used in addition to the six DexJoCo [43] tasks for evaluation in simulation.

papers.abstract: General-purpose mobile manipulation requires a combination of capable robot hardware, scalable demonstration collection, expressive whole-body control, and effective policy learning. Yet these components are often developed independently, creating mismatches that limit the capabilities of the complete system. We present Pixel, a co-designed full-stack system for learning general-purpose mobile manipulation. Pixel combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers, multiple teleoperation and robot-free human data-collection interfaces, a unified whole-body controller, and a common policy learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations. A hierarchical learning stack further enables language-conditioned visuomotor control and long-horizon task execution. We evaluate the system across hardware, data collection, and policy learning, and demonstrate mobile-manipulation behaviors requiring dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination. We hope that Pixel provides an integrated and extensible foundation for studying how robot hardware, data, control, and learning can be designed together for robot learning. More results at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel
bullets: Combines a low-cost wheeled humanoid with human-aligned kinematics and compliant grippers.
Supports multiple teleoperation and robot-free interfaces for scalable human demonstration collection.
Uses a unified whole-body controller and shared policy-learning pipeline across human and robot demonstrations.
Adds hierarchical, language-conditioned visuomotor control for long-horizon tasks.
Demonstrates behaviors involving dexterity, active perception, navigation, and whole-body coordination.

papers.abstract: Sensorized human demonstrations offer scalable data for mobile manipulation, but embodiment differences complicate policy learning. We present Pixel-UMI, a pipeline for learning environment-aware whole-body policies from human data. We first introduce Environment-Aware Retargeting (EAR), which combines reconstructed scene geometry with demonstrated head and gripper trajectories to determine robot posture and generate collision-aware joint and base targets. Delay-calibrated action assignment converts these trajectories into actions. However, kinematic differences can leave residual pose errors, creating viewpoint mismatches between human demonstrations and robot observations. We therefore introduce Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking (REAM), which uses these errors during training to reduce reliance on mismatched views at deployment. Finally, because estimated actions cannot fully capture contact-rich interactions, we collect on-policy human corrections through DAgger to improve performance. We evaluate Pixel-UMI on five challenging tasks spanning articulated-object manipulation, deformable-object handling, constrained-space reaching, whole-body collision avoidance, and contact-rich bimanual coordination, achieving 87.0% average task progress. Video results are available at https://pixel-robot.com/pixel-umi
bullets: Addresses embodiment differences between human demonstrations and mobile manipulation robots.
Uses Environment-Aware Retargeting to convert scene geometry and human head/gripper trajectories into collision-aware robot joint and base targets.
Applies Retargeting-Error-Aware Masking to reduce reliance on observation views mismatched by residual retargeting errors.
Uses delay-calibrated action assignment and on-policy human corrections via DAgger to handle imperfect, contact-rich actions.
Evaluated across five challenging manipulation tasks, achieving 87.0% average task progress.

papers.abstract: Learning from human data offers a scalable path toward embodied intelligence, yet it requires models to accurately understand fine-grained human actions from egocentric observations. However, existing benchmarks remain limited in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association. We introduce EgoActionBench, a benchmark that represents continuous human manipulation as temporally localized atomic actions associated with the left hand, right hand, or both hands. EgoActionBench contains 1,407 episodes with 41,132 human-refined action annotations. To evaluate such dense predictions, we propose an evaluation protocol that retrieves temporally eligible candidates, selects a prediction by content agreement, and scores semantic fidelity and temporal overlap alongside action precision and recall, jointly capturing what happens, when it happens, and which hand performs it. We benchmark 20 baseline models and systems on EgoActionBench and further adapt two backbones, Qwen3-VL-4B and LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B, through supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning on automatically annotated training episodes. EgoAction improves EgoActionScore by 15.9 and 23.2 points on the two backbones, and both adapted models outperform all open-source baselines. Our experiments reveal substantial limitations of current models in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association, highlighting the gap between general video understanding and the action understanding required for embodied intelligence.
bullets: Introduces 1,407 episodes with 41,132 human-refined annotations of temporally localized atomic actions linked to the left hand, right hand, or both.
Proposes an evaluation protocol measuring semantic fidelity, temporal overlap, action precision, and recall.
Benchmarks 20 models and systems, including adapted Qwen3-VL-4B and LLaVA-OneVision-2-8B backbones.
Supervised fine-tuning followed by reinforcement learning improves EgoActionScore by 15.9 and 23.2 points on the two adapted backbones.
Finds persistent limitations in action atomicity, temporal precision, and hand-action association.

papers.title: EgoActionBench: Benchmarking Dense Action Captioning for Egocentric Human Videos
papers.tldr: EgoActionBench evaluates fine-grained, temporally precise, hand-aware action captioning in egocentric human videos and shows that adapted vision-language models substantially improve performance while revealing major remaining gaps.

papers.abstract: Contact transitions allow humanoid robots to redistribute object support across the whole body, enabling manipulation beyond hand-only grasps. Human videos provide a scalable source of such transitions for robots to learn from. However, body occlusion disrupts object pose tracking and corrupts retargeted motion. Moreover, accurately reproducing the object trajectory does not ensure that the robot applies stabilizing forces at the intended contacts, risking slips or drops in later phases. To address these challenges, we propose ReContact, which reconstructs and retargets human-object interactions through an object-centric contact plan. The plan specifies contact phases, contact pairs, anchors, pressing directions, and sticking or sliding modes. Contact priors stabilize object pose reconstruction through occlusion. A residual policy over a frozen whole-body tracker is rewarded for making contact at planned anchors with forces aligned to the specified directions. In simulation, on a thigh-supported regrasp task, ReContact achieves the planned two-palm bottom hold in 83.5 of episodes over three training seeds, versus 0.16% for the best adapted baseline. One policy trained on 247 references re-solved for new placements raises in-workspace tube-transfer success from 20.4% (source reference only) to 97.8%. On a real Unitree G1, policies execute seven contact-rich manipulation and two loco-manipulation tasks.
bullets: Addresses occlusion-corrupted object tracking and the gap between matching object motion and applying stabilizing contact forces.
Uses an object-centric contact plan with phases, contact pairs, anchors, pressing directions, and sticking/sliding modes.
Stabilizes pose reconstruction with contact priors and adds a residual policy over a frozen whole-body tracker to achieve planned contacts and force directions.
In simulation, the method achieves the planned two-palm bottom hold in 83.5% of episodes versus 0.16% for the best adapted baseline.
A policy trained on 247 references generalizes to new placements, increasing tube-transfer success from 20.4% to 97.8%; real-robot tests cover seven manipulation and two loco-manipulation tasks.

papers.abstract: World-action models (WAMs) predict scene changes to guide robot actions, yet their RGB futures entangle state changes with appearance and lack 3D geometry. Recent WAMs add geometry as a training signal or a control interface, or build native 3D models, but decide what geometry to model rather than how the action should read it. Intuitively, control-relevant cues lie at embodiment--object interactions and their transitions, yet probing existing WAMs reveals that their action attention underweights these interactions in favor of the rest of the embodiment. To focus the action on these interactions, we present Gnomon4D, a WAM that jointly generates future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D geometric motion field recording the image-plane displacement and depth change of embodiment and object points. With the embodiment and objects in one field, their relative motion, which marks an interaction, can be read off. Guided by this motion and the task, Interaction-Salient Attention (InSAttn) selects where the action reads, and Transition-Anchored Aggregation (TransAgg) selects when, around grasp and release. As GeoDelta encodes surface motion rather than embodiment-specific controls, it serves as a human--robot quasi-action that links action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H, which we curate, to robot mid-training on Robot-30H. Gnomon4D leads on RoboTwin~2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms real-robot baselines, especially under visual shifts. Project page: https://droliven.github.io/Gnomon4D.
bullets: Addresses the problem that RGB-based world-action models entangle appearance and state changes, while action attention often overlooks control-relevant interactions.
Jointly predicts future video, robot actions, and GeoDelta, a video-aligned 4D field of image-plane displacement and depth changes for embodiment and object points.
Uses Interaction-Salient Attention to select where to attend and Transition-Anchored Aggregation to focus around grasp and release transitions.
GeoDelta enables action-free pretraining on EgoManip-5000H and robot mid-training on Robot-30H by acting as a human–robot quasi-action.
Leads on RoboTwin 2.0, VLABench, and RoboDojo, and outperforms real-robot baselines, particularly under visual shifts.

papers.abstract: Understanding holistic 3D human motion and the surrounding environment from egocentric video is fundamental for applications in AR/VR and robotics. Although these tasks are inherently coupled, existing methods treat them separately. In particular, egocentric motion reconstruction methods typically assume access to metric, gravity-aligned camera trajectories from specialized inertial sensors. Recovering such trajectories from monocular egocentric video remains a significant challenge due to rapid head movements and motion blur. We present EgoMo3R, a joint optimization framework that simultaneously reconstructs 3D human motion and scene geometry from casual egocentric video. It leverages the robustness of low-level visuo-geometric primitives, including monocular depth, optical flow, and point tracks, integrated with a diffusion-based human motion prior via first-order optimization. We propose an alternating optimization scheme that establishes a synergistic feedback loop: scene reconstruction provides physical grounding and trajectory conditioning for the motion prior, while the motion prior regularizes the camera trajectory and anchors the scene in a metric, gravity-aligned world frame. We evaluate EgoMo3R on the highly dynamic sequences of the EgoExo4D and Nymeria datasets and show that it outperforms specialized baselines in both 3D scene reconstruction and egocentric motion estimation.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of estimating metric, gravity-aligned camera trajectories under rapid head motion and blur.
Combines monocular depth, optical flow, and point tracks with a diffusion-based human motion prior.
Uses alternating optimization so scene geometry guides motion and trajectory estimation, while motion regularizes and anchors the scene.
Evaluated on dynamic EgoExo4D and Nymeria sequences.
Outperforms specialized baselines in both 3D scene reconstruction and egocentric motion estimation.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Given an input video I , we leverage a monocular depth estimator to obtain relative depth Dr as a geometric base, optimizing only the per-frame scales S to derive metric depth D. Our framework jointly optimizes for camera poses C, which transform metric depth into a global worldframe pointmaps PW , and 3D human motion M . We employ an alternating optimization strategy: (1) Scene Refinement updates C and S using optical flow, point tracks, and a scene-alignment loss to anchor the reconstruction in a canonical frame provided by motion; (2) Motion Alignment refines M by leveraging a diffusion motion prior conditioned on C. This synergistic loop prevents optimization collapse and ensures physically grounded joint 3D scene and motion reconstruction.

papers.abstract: Humans continuously acquire knowledge from carefully crafted materials such as books and tutorial videos, carrying that understanding into future tasks. Millions of such instructional videos are uploaded online every day, yet LLM agents remain unable to exploit this ever-expanding wealth of human teaching. Their capabilities are frozen after training, while parameter updates at scale remain prohibitively expensive. This raises the central question: can LLM agents learn from this vast instructional resource without parameter updates? We introduce Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL), a nonparametric continual-learning paradigm that consolidates tutorial videos into a persistent, structured tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that harvests hard, video-grounded questions and uses them to refine the memory. At inference time, TAL retrieves through a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, tying retrieval directly to the model's reasoning rather than to embedding similarity. To study this setting, we introduce VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark built from 72 chess tutorial videos spanning 12 openings. On VidLearn, TAL outperforms all evaluated baselines and improves monotonically as more videos are consumed, achieving up to 113% and 91% relative gains over the corresponding vanilla MLLMs on the training and test splits, respectively. In actual gameplay, TAL reaches a stronger opening-phase position than its vanilla counterpart in 69% of head-to-head games. Evaluation in a second domain further demonstrates the generality of TAL. Together, these results highlight instructional videos as a scalable resource for parameter-update-free agent continual learning.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of exploiting instructional videos when model parameters are frozen and large-scale updates are costly.
Builds a tutorialbook memory through a two-stage adversarial process that generates hard, video-grounded questions to refine stored knowledge.
Uses a Table-of-Contents tree for reasoning-guided retrieval instead of embedding similarity alone.
Evaluated on VidLearn, a multimodal QA benchmark from 72 chess tutorials across 12 openings, with performance improving as more videos are consumed.
Also improves opening-phase gameplay and shows generality in a second domain.

figures.caption: Figure 2: Overview of Tutorial Agentic Learning (TAL). In Stage I, TAL performs video-grounded agent– model adversarial consolidation, where a video agent harvests hard question–answer pairs from instructional videos that are supported by tutorial evidence yet unsolved by the frozen model, forming a question bank. In Stage II, TAL performs question–memory adversarial consolidation, using this question bank to iteratively refine tutorial memory through a read–write loop. At inference time, TAL retrieves relevant tutorial units via a Table-of-Contents (TOC) tree, enabling the frozen model to access structured tutorial knowledge for downstream reasoning without parameter updates.

papers.abstract: Processing every video frame through Vision-Language Models (VLMs) adds significant inference cost and limits their ability to comprehend real-time video. Existing approaches either sub-sample frames uniformly, ignoring content and missing important events, or prune visual tokens inside the VLM to cut per-call cost while still invoking the model on every sampled frame. We introduce FOCUS, a training-free three-layer framework that reduces the number of invocations and steers each one towards what matters. Temporal gating measures inter-frame dissimilarity in the patch-embedding space of a smaller VLM from the same family, triggering burst captures only when the scene changes in a semantically meaningful way. Patch-level dissimilarity is then accumulated across the burst and fused with a top-down attention prior into a spatial focus map that encodes where motion and semantic relevance coincide. That map calibrates the VLM's value cache during generation, progressively amplifying vision tokens in task-relevant regions and attenuating off-target ones, without removing any token from the context. The loop closes after each response: text-to-vision cross-attention is extracted from the decoder and fed back as the prior for the next burst, letting the system converge on semantically important regions over successive observations. We evaluate FOCUS on the 500-video EgoSchema subset in streaming mode, with a single Qwen3-VL-8B backbone shared by every method. It reaches 74.8% accuracy using 25.4 VLM calls per clip, against 74.6% with 55 calls for uniform sampling and 74.2% with 55 calls for BOLT. On egocentric video captioning across four domains, it matches the best baseline's quality while issuing 57% fewer VLM invocations than uniform sampling.
bullets: Detects meaningful scene changes with patch-embedding dissimilarity and triggers burst captures selectively.
Combines motion-based patch changes with top-down attention to focus on task-relevant regions.
Reweights, rather than removes, visual tokens during generation using a calibrated value cache.
Feeds decoder text-to-vision attention back into the next observation cycle for iterative refinement.
On a 500-video EgoSchema subset, achieves 74.8% accuracy with 25.4 calls per clip; captioning matches the best baseline with 57% fewer calls than uniform sampling.

papers.abstract: Garment flattening and folding require robots to identify garment structure during manipulation and adapt their actions as the cloth deforms. We present ClothDojo, a simulation platform that generates adaptive manipulation trajectories at scale across diverse garments and initial states and evaluates policies in closed loop. ClothDojo encodes each garment's canonical mesh coordinates as an NOCS texture, providing canonical surface-position cues through the visual interface of a pretrained vision-language-action model. We fine-tune the model on human demonstrations and corrections to obtain a data-generation policy. The policy autonomously generates simulated manipulation trajectories, and we retain rollouts that satisfy task-specific success criteria. Each retained trajectory is re-rendered under a randomly sampled appearance to provide RGB observations for downstream policies that do not receive NOCS. Across both tasks, the policy produces nearly 8,000 successful trajectories over hundreds of garments. RGB policies trained on these generated trajectories outperform those trained directly on the original human demonstrations and corrections across all evaluated garment splits and appearance settings. Evaluations across multiple policy models show that overall performance and appearance robustness vary across models and tasks, while generalization to unseen garments remains a common challenge.
bullets: Addresses the challenge of adapting manipulation to changing garment geometry and appearance.
Uses NOCS-textured garment meshes to provide canonical surface cues to a pretrained vision-language-action model.
Fine-tunes the model on human demonstrations and corrections, then filters autonomously generated rollouts by task success.
Re-renders successful trajectories with randomized appearances for training policies that use only RGB observations.
Generated data improves RGB-policy performance over original human data across evaluated garment splits and appearances, though unseen-garment generalization remains difficult.

papers.abstract: Scaling humanoid motion foundation models is constrained by the scarcity of diverse, robot-executable data and by the difficulty of jointly learning from heterogeneous multimodal inputs while supporting real-time closed-loop control. We present Movens-5M, constructed from raw Internet videos through clip generation, quality filtering, semantic annotation, motion recovery, and physical refinement with humanoid retargeting and execution verification. It contains 15 million human-motion sequences and 5 million physically executable humanoid-motion sequences spanning over 10,000 hours, aligned with text, RGB video, speech, and music. Building on this data, we introduce Movens-Zero, a scalable understanding-generation-execution architecture that supports joint learning across modalities and real-time closed-loop execution. Task-mixed flow-matching training jointly optimizes a single action expert across seven generation tasks, enabling direct motion generation from text, speech, music, and video. Multimodal Real-Time Chunking connects overlapping chunks under continuously updated instructions and robot states for continuous closed-loop execution. We further introduce Movens-Intent, a four-track benchmark with 8,192 expert-verified condition-motion pairs across text, speech, music, and video. Experiments show consistent gains across all four modalities when scaling execution-verified data from 1% to 100% and action-expert capacity from 64M to 911M parameters, while demonstrating that data quality and cross-modal supervision improve generation and execution.

papers.abstract: Learning dexterous manipulation from human videos remains an open challenge, particularly in the context of transferring a single demonstration into a spatially generalizable robotic skill and maintaining physically plausible human-like interactions. Unlike prior works that emphasize hand-motion imitation, we introduce an object-centric framework for acquiring dexterous skills from egocentric human RGB-D videos. Within our framework, we formulate the reinforcement learning (RL) objective in terms of object motion to decouple the underlying skill from the specific hand trajectory and impose constraints on hand-object interaction states to promote more anatomically natural hand configurations. Extensive experiments in simulation and on real robots demonstrate that our method enables efficient learning from human videos and generalizable skill transfer across novel spatial configurations.

papers.abstract: Computer vision models learn hand action only from its visual consequences, without access to the underlying embodied motor signals. We address this absence with MotorSense, the first large-scale paired egocentric video and surface electromyography (EMG) dataset. MotorSense pairs bimanual EMG bands with egocentric video and yields synchronized video, bimanual EMG and IMU, and audio across 100 hours of unscripted manipulation. EMG offers a powerful scalable alternative to manual annotation: it captures finger movement, hand configuration, and the forces exerted between hand and environment as a dense signal free of occlusion and labeler bias, whereas manual annotation is costly, subjective, and unreliable under occlusion. We use MotorSense to learn sensorimotor alignment, producing an organization of action that is shared across the visual and motoric spaces, through cross-modal pre-training between video and EMG. The resultant vision models are then transferred to downstream tasks that benefit from sensorimotor alignment: in this case, action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction. We further demonstrate a generative application in which EMG motor signals are used to condition a video diffusion model, yielding videos of fine-grained hand manipulation. Across four action-centric computer vision tasks and eight popular video datasets, we demonstrate that sensorimotor alignment provides a stronger foundation for visual representation learning than conventional self-supervised learning methods over video, outperforming every baseline across all tasks and datasets evaluated.
authors: Eadom Dessalene, Michael Maynord, Amir-Hossein Shahidzadeh, Botao He, Yasamin Tabatabaee, Ruoshi Liu, Ruohan Gao, Paul Pu Liang, Yiannis Aloimonos

Transfers the learned representations to action recognition, 3D hand reconstruction, and 3D contact reconstruction.
Also conditions video diffusion on EMG to generate fine-grained hand-manipulation videos; the approach outperforms evaluated video self-supervised baselines across four tasks and eight datasets.

papers.abstract: Robot-free human demonstrations offer a promising route to scaling dexterous manipulation data. The key challenge is to preserve the demonstrator's natural dexterity while producing contact-grounded observations and actions that transfer to robot hands. We present Contact Imitation Interface (CIMI), a framework with contact-grounded demonstration and learning interfaces. The demonstration interface combines shared contact geometry and fingertip RGB views with contact-alignment-first retargeting and reprojection of wider scene views. The learning interface introduces a hierarchical policy in which a contact-surface planner predicts relative contact-surface trajectories and a controller coordinates wrist and finger commands to improve contact alignment. CIMI combines contact-grounded observations, retargeting, and action representations, improving mean final-stage success by at least 50 percentage points over baseline policies across six hand-task pairs on LEAP and Wuji. Hardware designs and software are publicly available.

Hardware and software designs are publicly available.

papers.abstract: Egocentric videos offer an abundant source of hand-scene interactions for embodied learning, which requires recovering hands, camera, and scene consistently in a shared 3D world. Existing methods focus on either camera-frame hands or world-space hand trajectories, without jointly recovering the scene pointmaps or interaction information. Building a complete reconstruction from such specialized predictions therefore typically requires per-sequence optimization. We propose EgoHSI3R, a unified feed-forward framework for online 4D hand-scene interaction reconstruction from egocentric monocular video. To jointly recover these components, it maintains a recurrent scene representation that accumulates geometric evidence over time and provides a shared world space and scale. We introduce hand-centric prompts that fuse pretrained hand priors and local scene context, while MANO vertex queries attend to scene features to predict dense per-vertex contact. These designs enable a single network to jointly estimate camera motion, dense scene geometry, world-space bilateral MANO hands, and per-vertex hand contact. Despite operating causally, EgoHSI3R achieves the lowest world-space hand joint error on ARCTIC among the evaluated methods, while offering faster inference than existing world-space hand reconstruction pipelines and competitive camera and scene reconstruction accuracy.
authors: Mingzhi Pei, Zhangchen Ye, Ruoqu Chen, Liu Cao, Mengdi Xu
bullets: Addresses the lack of unified hand, camera, scene, and interaction reconstruction in existing methods.
Maintains a recurrent scene representation to accumulate geometry and establish shared world space and scale.
Uses hand-centric prompts combining pretrained hand priors with local scene context.
Predicts dense per-vertex contact through MANO vertex queries attending to scene features.
Reports the lowest evaluated world-space hand joint error on ARCTIC, with faster inference and competitive camera/scene accuracy.

figures.caption: Figure 4: Qualitative comparison of camera-space hand reconstruction. The predicted hand meshes are overlaid on the input egocentric frames. Our method produces accurate articulated hand poses and consistent alignment with the observed images.

Figure 3: Overview of EgoHSI3R. Each incoming egocentric frame is encoded by the scene encoder Es into image tokens, and each detected hand is processed by the pretrained hand encoder Eh. The Hand Prompt Builder fuses the hand prior with local scene context obtained via RoIAlign, producing scene-conditioned hand prompts. The decoder jointly processes scene tokens and hand prompts while reading from and updating a persistent scene state. The Scene Head predicts camera pose and world-space pointmaps, and the MANO Head reconstructs bilateral MANO parameters. The interaction-aware Contact Builder combines decoded hand tokens with local scene features, which are then used by the Contact Head to predict per-vertex contact and refine hand reconstruction. All outputs are produced online in a shared world space without test-time optimization.

papers.abstract: Learning humanoid skills from videos typically requires a successful human demonstration, which often demands custom data collection. Although failures have traditionally been treated only as negative examples in robot learning, they can still reveal a usable trajectory prefix before the task fails, as well as the intended outcome. To leverage this information from a failed-attempt video, we propose TRACC, a pipeline that imitates the useful portion of the motion trajectory and then completes the task based on the inferred task outcome. The usable motion prefix serves as prior knowledge until the failure occurs, after which the task-completion reward guides the policy to learn the intended task goal without requiring a successful task trajectory. We evaluate our method on six in-the-wild failed human tasks from the Oops! dataset. Our experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed approach for learning from failed attempts when no successful demonstration is available. Thus, these findings establish failed human videos as a viable source of supervision for humanoid skill learning.
bullets: Failed demonstrations provide both a usable trajectory prefix and clues about the intended outcome.

The method targets settings without any successful task demonstration.

Results support failed human videos as a viable supervision source for humanoid skill learning.

papers.abstract: Extending Vision-Language-Action models (VLAs) to humanoid robots requires coordinated whole-body control and diverse demonstrations that are costly to collect in real-world scenarios. Although egocentric human demonstrations provide a complementary source of task experience, differences in visual embodiment and missing robot proprioception complicate transfer to humanoid policies. To address these challenges, we introduce HuGe, a family of Humanoid Generalist VLAs pre-trained on over 2,000 hours of egocentric human and robot data. Specifically, HuGe employs three existing representative VLA architectures to predict latent motion tokens for a pretrained whole-body controller, together with hand-control signals. Based on this, we introduce a three-stage training pipeline that combines egocentric pre-training, humanoid adaptation, and downstream fine-tuning. To facilitate transfer across embodiments, we construct pseudo-proprioceptive states through simulation playback during pre-training and modify arm appearance in egocentric observations through re-rendering during downstream fine-tuning. With this pipeline, HuGe achieves the state-of-the-art on simulation benchmark HumanoidArena. Furthermore, real-world experiments on the Unitree G1 indicate that augmenting robot demonstrations with visually adapted egocentric demonstrations significantly increases success on a pick-and-drop task.

papers.abstract: As robots and intelligent systems increasingly interact with humans, they must anticipate long sequences of future actions from only brief observations. While purely neural models typically require extensive observations to predict future actions and remain difficult to interpret and adjust, symbolic priors offer a structured alternative. To this end, we introduce SymAnt, a novel neuro-symbolic approach that unifies the expressiveness of neural networks with the structured reasoning of scene and knowledge graphs. Given a short video, SymAnt performs a joint-search over both graphs to construct a symbolic context, enabling unified reasoning over spatial relationships, object attributes, affordances, and associated actions. This symbolic context serves as a prior for an iterative refinement process that progressively generates and improves the sequence of future actions. By grounding predictions in symbolic context, SymAnt anticipates long-horizon actions from short observation windows in a parameter-efficient manner, while enabling users to directly edit the underlying knowledge to adjust predictions without further training. Through our experiments, we demonstrate the effectiveness of SymAnt, particularly when only short observation contexts are available, across five diverse datasets: Breakfast, 50 Salads, EPIC-KITCHENS, EGTEA Gaze+, and Assembly101.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations offer an efficient and scalable source of data for dexterous robot manipulation, but differences in sensing and hand morphology complicate the transfer of contact-rich interactions. We present TouchBridge, a hardware--software co-designed framework for human-to-robot data transformation. A wearable human demonstration interface and a corresponding robot interface establish cross-embodiment correspondence in visual and fingertip tactile sensing. We introduce Tac-Retarget, a tactile-conditioned retargeting method that uses measured contact to align fingertip contact patches and preserve their spatial relations within and across hands. Unlike object-aware or simulation-based transfer pipelines, Tac-Retarget requires no object mesh, object-pose estimate, or physics simulation for retargeting, enabling direct and scalable conversion of human demonstrations into robot-domain training data. Combined with visual synthesis and camera-anchored action conversion, TouchBridge produces robot-domain demonstrations for fine-tuning a pretrained vision-language-action (VLA) model. Across four real-world contact-rich tasks, policies fine-tuned solely on TouchBridge-converted human demonstrations achieve a 72.5% average success rate, compared with 77.5% using an equal number of teleoperated robot demonstrations, while human demonstration collection is 7.0x faster. Under the same policy and training setup, Tac-Retarget outperforms DexPilot and UniDex by 25.0 and 42.5 percentage points, respectively.

papers.abstract: Bimanual dexterous manipulation requires continuous coordination of wrist motion, finger contact, and object motion. Human videos provide rich manipulation experience. Using this experience for robot control requires aligning human poses with robot commands and accounting for embodiment-specific kinematics and contact dynamics. We present AcrossDEX 1.0, a learning system that connects human motion pretraining, simulation-based expert learning, robot demonstration collection, and visual closed-loop execution. Pretraining on HOT3D Aria predicts one second of bimanual motion from five images and thirty annotated hand states over the preceding second. Robot adaptation preserves the visual encoder, temporal backbone, and wrist parameters. Shared wrist representations, separate finger fields, and validity masks support both six-channel Inspire hands and sixteen-joint Allegro hands. The robot policy predicts sixty control targets from frontal images, command history, and task conditions. It executes a prefix and replans from updated observations. We compare direct regression, diffusion, and flow matching on lid opening and return and closed-lid object reorientation. Direct regression achieves success rates of 40.6\% for opening and return, 100.0\% for Inspire reorientation, and 93.3\% for Allegro reorientation. Flow matching achieves 90.0\% on Allegro reorientation. Paired comparisons further show that constraining replanning with the previous plan improves the continuous execution of generative policies. These results demonstrate a common adaptation pipeline for two hand embodiments and highlight the roles of contact coordination and action-chunk continuity.

papers.abstract: Understanding how humans interact with the world requires a representation of physical interactions at the hand surface. Tactile sensing captures these interactions, but collecting tactile data at scale requires specialized hardware. We introduce TactoHand, a model that predicts three dense hand-surface interaction fields---contact, proximity, and 3D force---from monocular video. We derive geometry-based contact and proximity labels and motion-derived force labels from eligible training data within a curated collection spanning approximately 50 million source frames. TactoHand uses a temporal transformer to aggregate visual evidence across frames, while three learned queries decode the corresponding hand-surface fields. A differentiable physics layer further constrains force predictions using observed object motion. Across in-domain and out-of-domain benchmarks, TactoHand improves contact and proximity estimation over prior methods. In addition, physics supervision reduces position and rotation errors in motion rollouts, and the predicted contact and proximity fields improve downstream hand-object reconstruction. Together, these results show a scalable, low-cost path to learning hand-surface interaction fields without collecting tactile measurements. Code will be released at https://github.com/zhenqis123/Tactohand.

papers.abstract: Universal Manipulation Interface (UMI) devices allow human experts to demonstrate tasks for robot learning without teleoperating physical robots. Using these demonstrations as training data still requires a consistent hardware setup, calibration, and data processing. We present UMI-Live, a full-stack open-source bimanual UMI system for in-the-wild data collection. We design our custom UMI-Live hardware to integrate camera and LiDAR--inertial sensing, onboard compute, and power, without external tracking equipment or calibration within the collection environment. We implement a simple user interface for recording data while an asynchronous pipeline performs parallel SLAM reconstruction and publishes training-ready datasets. We also release software that supports dual-YAM teleoperation and VLA policy training and inference. We validate UMI-Live data quality by fine-tuning $\pi_{0.5}$ and MolmoAct2, achieving success rates of 10/10 and 8/10, respectively on a bimanual pick-and-place task. Furthermore, we release 40 hours of UMI-Live data across three tasks, and complete hardware designs, software, and reproduction guides at our $\href{https://umi-live.github.io/}{\text{project website}}$.

papers.abstract: Egocentric video has emerged as one of the most scalable sources of data for learning generalizable manipulation priors. Yet, despite its growing use in pretraining robotic policies, it has been underutilized as a validation tool for physical intelligence, a key component of which is understanding where to make contact with an object to achieve an intended interaction. We present EgoContact, a large-scale egocentric dataset for evaluating the generalizability and precision of learned manipulation priors through future contact-point prediction. EgoContact contains 22.5K manually verified interaction events, each with a pre-contact observation, semantic intent, and pixel-precise contact locations. We find that current methods often struggle to predict precise interaction contacts and sometimes fail to localize the target object in diverse, in-the-wild scenes, even when allowed multiple predictions. Furthermore, we demonstrate the usefulness of EgoContact's annotated interactions for robotic manipulation: simply using EgoContact as the memory bank of an existing affordance-transfer policy improves grasp success from 14.2% to 31.2% in simulation and from 16% to 58% on a real robot.

papers.abstract: Collecting naturalistic human manipulation demonstrations with accurate contact force and hand pose is essential for robot dexterous manipulation policy and foundational world model learning - yet no existing wearable platform provides both calibrated fingertip force sensing and occlusion-resilient hand tracking in a form factor that preserves natural manipulation behavior. We present Tactus, a textile-integrated sensing glove that co-optimizes three design pillars: (1) a thin, conformal 3D-knit form factor (1.5 mm fingertip stackup) designed to minimize interference with natural manipulation, (2) strategically placed capacitive tactile sensors at manipulation-relevant regions informed by empirical contact studies, and (3) IMU-fused pose tracking that maintains accuracy through the hand-object occlusions where manipulation data is most valuable. Tactus includes a documented calibration pipeline for cross-glove consistency and per-session calibration for subject-dependent correction. To enable objective comparison, we introduce standardized benchmarking protocols for tactile force regression and hand pose estimation, and apply them to Tactus and two commercially available tactile gloves - to our knowledge the first quantitative cross-platform evaluation of this kind. Tactus resolves a minimum detectable force of 0.59 N at 95% confidence, 1.6 - 2.7x lower than the commercial baselines, and with 0.87 cross-participant consistency, while our pose tracking sustains 11.0 mm fingertip keypoint relative error during manipulation, when occlusion is heaviest. We show that these combined signals support object property estimation, slip detection, and representative recording of hand-object interaction - yielding demonstration data with the fidelity required for contact-aware manipulation policies and world models.
