On a held-out session, the classifier agrees with manual annotations on 92.4% of frames. Across four household skills, DexStitch achieves 80.0% single-skill success and 77.5% sequence success.
authors: Byeonggyeol Choi, Seongmin Jung, Unghui Nam, Youngbo Song, Sunhong Min, MinHyung Lee, Byonghyo Shim, Yongseok Lee
bullets: Addresses the costly collection of robot demonstrations for both manipulation skills and their transitions.
Segments human videos into skills and transitions, then converts them into aligned robot observation–action–skill data.
Uses per-finger contact-aware retargeting and robotic inpainting to preserve contact geometry and occlusion ordering.
Pretrains a shared skill-conditioned policy on synthetic data and lightly finetunes it with single-skill teleoperation data.
Reports 92.4% frame-level agreement with manual skill annotations, 80.0% single-skill success, and 77.5% sequence success across four household skills.
papers.selection_reason: Learns and composes dexterous manipulation skills from human videos with contact-aware retargeting and skill-conditioned policies.
papers.title: DexStitch: Learning and Composing Dexterous Skills from Human Videos via Contact-Aware Robotic Inpainting
papers.tldr: DexStitch transfers human-video demonstrations to robots by preserving finger–object contacts and composing the resulting dexterous skills into long-horizon sequences.

papers.abstract: While expert demonstrations on real robots are difficult to collect, human ego-centric videos are easy to collect and abundant on the internet. However, learning dexterous manipulation policies from human videos remains challenging---one of the most important challenges being the difficulty of reconstructing physically grounded robot trajectories due to the large embodiment gap. In this paper, we propose EgoCPT, a novel paradigm for learning high-quality retargeted dexterous hand trajectories directly from an ego-centric video, which can then be deployed directly on real robots. The only inputs to our method are an ego-centric RGB video and a reference hand pose trajectory, which can be easily obtained through off-the-shelf software or specialized cameras during recording. Our method is particularly robust to noisy hand poses attributed to our novel contact-aware optimization framework, which iteratively optimizes the contact points between the robot hands and objects. Across five manipulation tasks, our method achieves overall success rates of 67.3% on noisy EgoDex hand-pose reconstructions and 92.0% on high-quality TACO reconstructions collected using motion-capture hardware, outperforming multiple baselines on both benchmarks.
authors: Zhixin Sun, Kairui Shi, Tianao Ren, Ming Yang, Mark Cutkosky, James Jingxi Xu
bullets: Addresses the embodiment gap between human videos and physically feasible robot hand motions.
Uses iterative contact-aware optimization to refine robot–object contact points and handle noisy hand-pose reconstructions.
Requires only an ego-centric RGB video and a reference hand-pose trajectory.
Evaluated on five manipulation tasks, achieving 67.3% success with noisy EgoDex poses and 92.0% with high-quality TACO poses.
Outperforms multiple baselines on both benchmarks.
papers.selection_reason: EgoCPT learns dexterous manipulation policies from human ego-centric videos by retargeting trajectories and using contact-aware optimization.
papers.title: EgoCPT: Learning Dexterous Manipulation from a Single Ego-Centric Video with Contact-Aware Optimization
papers.tldr: EgoCPT turns a single human ego-centric video and reference hand poses into contact-aware, robot-deployable dexterous manipulation trajectories.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations can capture task-relevant manipulation without using the target robot, but the recorded hand motions cannot directly serve as robot action supervision. Hand reconstruction and motion retargeting provide a direct route to such supervision, yet recovering hand motion alone does not ensure physically consistent hand-object interactions. To address this issue, we introduce Hand2Robot, an object-centric 4D hand reconstruction framework for robot policy post-training. Given videos of humans performing the target task, Hand2Robot extracts interaction clips, reconstructs object geometry, and generates robot action supervision through hand-object interaction optimization and motion retargeting. For object tracking, we combine observation confidence with temporal motion constraints to select a globally consistent object pose trajectory from per-frame pose candidates. For hand refinement, we use object geometry and motion as a reference and combine staged 2D alignment with object-local contact constraints to refine hand trajectories and finger joint configurations. Experiments on DexYCB and HO3D-v3 show improved object pose accuracy and hand-object interaction quality. Experiments on three real-robot dexterous manipulation tasks further show that reconstructed and retargeted human demonstrations can effectively supplement limited robot data for target-task policy post-training.
authors: Zetao Du, Weiqing Wang, Hanbing Zhang, Yimiao Zhou, Ye Shi, Liang Wang, Jingya Wang
bullets: Addresses the gap between human hand demonstrations and usable robot action supervision, especially for physically consistent hand-object contact.
Extracts task-relevant clips, reconstructs object geometry, tracks globally consistent object poses, and refines hand motion and finger configurations.
Combines staged 2D alignment with object-local contact constraints, followed by motion retargeting to the robot.
Improves object pose accuracy and hand-object interaction quality on DexYCB and HO3D-v3.
Real-robot experiments across three dexterous manipulation tasks show the demonstrations can supplement limited robot data for policy post-training.
papers.selection_reason: Uses human demonstration videos to reconstruct hand-object interactions and retarget them into robot policy supervision, fitting learning from human video and manipulation.
papers.title: Hand2Robot: Object-Centric 4D Hand Reconstruction from Human Demonstrations for Robotics
papers.tldr: Hand2Robot reconstructs physically consistent 4D hand-object interactions from human videos and retargets them into robot supervision for dexterous policy post-training.

papers.abstract: Recent advances in 3D hand-object interaction (HOI) perception have opened new opportunities for learning dexterous robotic skills from human videos. However, existing dexterous imitation learning methods often rely on costly and manually teleoperated robot demonstrations, requiring substantial human effort. Therefore, we build DEXCAST, a framework that learns dexterous robotic hand control directly from monocular RGB-D videos by leveraging joint HOI reconstructions, without requiring any teleoperation. Furthermore, how to model high-dimensional robotic hand motion and extract temporal context to inform future action generation remains a key challenge. To this end, we propose a DexHand Motion Perception Module (DMPM) to capture inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies in compact latent representations that condition our diffusion policy. Extensive real-world experiments demonstrate that DEXCAST achieves exceptional performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.
authors: Zihan Gao, Yuhong Zhang, Mengzhe Wang, Kaisheng Liu, Shengpeng Li, Siyao Xiao, Runqing Cheng, Xiao Lin, Zhifang Liu, Haoqian Wang
bullets: Addresses the need for expensive, manually teleoperated demonstrations in dexterous imitation learning.
Uses joint 3D hand-object interaction reconstructions from monocular RGB-D videos as learning input.
Introduces the DexHand Motion Perception Module to encode inter-joint coordination and temporal dependencies.
Conditions a diffusion policy on these compact motion representations to generate future robot actions.
Real-world experiments show strong performance across diverse dexterous manipulation tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Learns dexterous robot control from human videos, fitting robot learning and human video learning.
papers.title: DexCast: Learning Real-World Dexterous Control from Human Videos
papers.tldr: DexCast learns dexterous robot control directly from monocular RGB-D human videos, avoiding costly teleoperation through joint HOI reconstruction and diffusion-based action generation.

papers.abstract: Most existing approaches rely on video or motion-capture data for reinforcement learning (RL) training; however, all of these methods require an upper-level module to generate reference trajectories in real time. In object carrying tasks, the humanoid can only lift objects from designated locations along the reference trajectory, resulting in poor spatial generalization. Moreover, existing policies can only be evaluated inside a motion-capture studio. To address these limitations, we propose \textbf{MOVER}, a multi-stage, Teacher-Assistant-Student, RL training framework for humanoid object carrying. We first collect data from videos and employ GENMO and GMR to retarget the video data, combining this with data augmentation techniques to generalize the data across objects of varying shapes and sizes. In the \textbf{first stage}, building upon the DeepMimic \cite{peng2018deepmimic} motion-training framework, we train the humanoid to transport objects from specified locations along designated trajectories. In the \textbf{second stage}, we relax the tracking of the reference motion and adjust the reward so that the humanoid learns to transport objects from different positions. In the \textbf{third stage}, we apply a Dagger-PPO distillation method to distill away the proprioceptive position observations and reference joint position of the humanoid. This allows the deployed policy to operate without relying on global position information from a motion-capture system; instead, the humanoid can directly perceive the object's pose from its onboard RGB-D camera to complete the carrying task. We design a series of simulation experiments to compare the success rates across stages (Stages 1 vs. 2) and before versus after distillation. We further transfer the policy to a real humanoid, successfully transporting objects at varying positions in a motion-capture-free setting.
bullets: Addresses poor spatial generalization and reliance on real-time reference trajectories and motion-capture systems in humanoid carrying.
Uses a three-stage Teacher-Assistant-Student RL framework based on retargeted human video, augmentation across object shapes and sizes, and progressive task relaxation.
Applies DAgger-PPO distillation to remove global position and reference-joint observations from the deployed policy.
Simulation experiments compare training stages and pre-/post-distillation performance.
Transfers successfully to a real humanoid that carries objects from varying positions without motion capture.
papers.selection_reason: Multi-stage RL from human video with distillation for generalizable humanoid carrying without motion capture.
papers.title: From Video to Vision: Learning Generalizable Humanoid Carrying from Human Motion
papers.tldr: MOVER trains humanoids to carry objects from varied locations using video-derived motion data and onboard RGB-D perception, without motion-capture deployment.

papers.abstract: Retargeting human demonstrations into dynamically feasible dexterous hand trajectories requires resolving complex contact physics, yet current methods either omit physical constraints or rely on computationally expensive sampling-based optimization in simulation. Reinforcement learning has previously been used to achieve planning and control through contact dynamics; however, standard policies require object-specific training and fail to generalize across arbitrary geometries. This work reframes physics-based retargeting as a residual learning problem, where we demonstrate that zero-shot generalization across objects relies on structured state representations. Specifically, formulating the observation space to include a localized contact-error signal guiding each robot link to its target coordinate on the object surface enables a single, unified residual policy to successfully grasp novel, unseen object geometries. Rolling out this policy in simulation on a kinematic reference trajectory yields a physics-based retargeter, OATH. Operating at 0.4 seconds of compute per second of reference, OATH achieves 2.4x faster-than-real-time performance and a 60-350x reduction in computational cost compared to sampling-based methods. The system recovers 58% of held-out and 54% of unseen-object DexYCB trajectories while maintaining a sub-2 cm tracking error.
authors: Solvin Sigurdson, Prasanna Sriganesh, Juan Borbon, Joel Burdick, Dingqi Zhang, Jiuguang Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of producing dynamically feasible hand trajectories under complex contact physics without costly sampling-based optimization.
Uses a unified residual reinforcement-learning policy with structured observations that encode each robot link’s contact error relative to the object surface.
Generalizes zero-shot to novel object geometries, including held-out and unseen objects.
Runs at 0.4 seconds of compute per second of reference, achieving 2.4× faster-than-real-time performance and 60–350× lower computational cost than sampling-based methods.
Recovers 58% of held-out and 54% of unseen-object DexYCB trajectories with sub-2 cm tracking error.
papers.selection_reason: Residual policy for physics-based dexterous hand retargeting from human demonstrations, generalizing to unseen objects.
papers.title: OATH: Object-Agnostic Tracking for Dexterous Hands, Enabling Rapid Physics-based Retargeting
papers.tldr: OATH enables fast, object-agnostic physics-based retargeting of dexterous hand demonstrations using a residual policy guided by localized contact errors.

papers.abstract: World-action models inherit broad visual and physical priors from video pre-training. However, standard within-video next-frame prediction allows them to rely on appearance shared between the context and future, rather than learning interactions that transfer across scenes and embodiments. We introduce WATCH, a cross-video pre-training that learns from task-paired human demonstrations collected across diverse environments. Conditioned on the video and actions of one demonstration, the model jointly predicts another demonstration's actions and future frames from its current observation. Predicting one demonstration from another encourages the model to learn task-relevant interactions that transfer across scenes and demonstrators. Our pre-training shows that these capabilities can be learned from readily scalable human-human pairs alone, without requiring matched human-robot demonstrations. Analyses before robot post-training show improved motion alignment across embodiments and better action and video prediction on unseen robots, with representations closer to those learned from robot pairs. After robot post-training, WATCH improves MimicDroid in-context success from 40.9% to 68.3% with Cosmos Policy and from 59.8% to 77.7% with Cosmos3, with the largest gains on the unseen levels. Gains persist under context-free post-training across robot embodiments. WATCH outperforms within-video pre-training and co-training baselines, supporting cross-video prediction as a scalable approach to learning transferable world-action representations.
authors: Jeongeun Park, Taekyung Kim, Dongyoon Han, Sangdoo Yun
bullets: Addresses the limitation of within-video prediction, which can rely on appearance overlap rather than transferable task interactions.
Uses cross-video pre-training on task-paired human-human demonstrations across diverse environments, without requiring human-robot pairs.
Jointly predicts the paired demonstration’s actions and future frames conditioned on the source video, actions, and target observation.
Improves motion alignment and action/video prediction on unseen robots before robot post-training.
Raises MimicDroid in-context success from 40.9% to 68.3% with Cosmos Policy and from 59.8% to 77.7% with Cosmos3; gains are largest on unseen levels and persist across embodiments.
papers.selection_reason: Cross-video human-demonstration pretraining for transferable world-action models directly fits learning from human video and video world models.
papers.title: Learning Transferable World-Action Models from Task-Paired Human Videos
papers.tldr: WATCH learns transferable world-action representations by predicting one human demonstration’s actions and future frames from another, improving robot imitation across unseen environments and embodiments.

papers.abstract: Embodied and assistive agents must do more than recognize objects: they must reason about where an object belongs given the layout of an environment and the habits of the people who live in it. Progress on this problem has been limited, in part because no dedicated benchmark or dataset exists to define and evaluate it. Existing RGB-D scan datasets reconstruct static rooms without human activity, while human-object-interaction datasets capture motion without a navigable, fully reconstructed scene or a ground-truth notion of an object's natural destination. We introduce contextual object placement as a benchmark task: predicting an object's destination during an observed object-carrying episode. To support this task, we present Embodied Camera observations of Human Object carrying (ECHO), a large-scale synthetic dataset that pairs dense RGB-D scans of indoor scenes with recordings of an embodied human carrying everyday objects to context-appropriate destinations. ECHO is the first publicly available dataset to combine reconstructed scenes, human activity, natural language, and contextual-placement annotations. It comprises 3,805 human-annotated episodes across 159 floors of 115 HM3D scenes, involving 198 distinct objects. Each floor includes a complete RGB-D scan with human-annotated room labels and a surface list. Each episode provides synchronized RGB-D encounter clips; 6-DoF camera, human, and object trajectories; start and destination surfaces; an action caption; and a human-written context: a single sentence describing the inhabitant's routine that implies the destination without naming it. We evaluate contextual object placement using input-masked probes and an end-to-end baseline. Results show that no single input modality is sufficient, highlighting the need to jointly reason over scene structure, human activity, and contextual knowledge.
bullets: Defines contextual object placement: predicting an object’s destination during an observed carrying episode.
Provides 3,805 annotated episodes across 159 floors, 115 HM3D scenes, and 198 everyday objects.
Combines dense RGB-D scene scans, human/object/camera trajectories, destination surfaces, action captions, and routine-based context descriptions.
Evaluations with masked-input probes and an end-to-end baseline show that no single modality is sufficient.
Supports joint reasoning over scene structure, human activity, and contextual knowledge.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces a benchmark for contextual object placement using embodied camera observations of human carrying, directly fitting learning from human video for embodied agents.
papers.title: ECHO: Embodied Camera Observations of Human Object Carrying
papers.tldr: ECHO introduces a benchmark and synthetic dataset for predicting where people naturally place carried objects by combining reconstructed indoor scenes, human activity, and contextual routines.

papers.abstract: Scaling generalist robotic policies is limited by the high cost of collecting embodied interaction data. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer a rich alternative, but they lack robot action labels, and existing action annotation methods are often noisy under real-world visual complexity and diverse manipulation dynamics. We introduce LAPT-Scale, a scalable latent action pre-training paradigm with two components: LAPT-Scale-LAM learns continuous latent actions by explaining frame-to-frame visual transitions in human videos and uses them as human-derived supervision, while LAPT-Scale-Policy trains a VLA policy through human-video latent-action pre-training, target-robot embodiment alignment, and task-specific post-training. Unlike prior vector-quantized LAMs, LAPT-Scale-LAM uses a continuous latent space to preserve fine-grained motion and interaction dynamics. We further combine perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals to improve transition-level supervision beyond pixel reconstruction. Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, LAPT-Scale-LAM provides implicit action supervision for policy pre-training, yielding consistent scaling gains and improving real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% as annotated human video scales from 1K to 5K hours. The learned policy also generalizes to unseen visual conditions.
authors: Zhiyuan Xiang, Peidong Liu, Mingyang Li, Jiawei Li, Wenhow Li, Wenbo Ding, Xiang Deng
bullets: Addresses the high cost of collecting robot interaction data and the lack of action labels in human videos.
Learns continuous latent actions from frame transitions using perceptual, semantic, and optical-flow alignment signals.
Pre-trains a vision-language-action policy, aligns it to the target robot embodiment, and applies task-specific post-training.
Trained on 23.3K hours of egocentric video, it improves real-robot success from 63.3% to 85.0% when annotated human video increases from 1K to 5K hours.
The resulting policy generalizes to unseen visual conditions.
papers.selection_reason: Scales latent-action pre-training from human egocentric videos to robot VLA policies, directly fitting embodied learning from human video and action models.
papers.title: LAPT-Scale: Scaling Embodied Policies with Latent Action Pre-Training on Human Videos
papers.tldr: LAPT-Scale uses continuous latent actions learned from large-scale human videos to pre-train generalist robot policies, substantially improving real-robot performance as video data scales.

papers.abstract: Humanoid tennis requires reactive whole-body coordination under rapidly changing ball dynamics, yet collecting task-specific motion-capture demonstrations that cover diverse approach states, contact locations, and timing conditions is costly. Inspired by how humans acquire new skills by combining reusable motor experience with task-specific demonstrations, we present ATHLETE, a framework for learning reactive humanoid tennis from generic locomotion data and ordinary tennis videos. ATHLETE combines LAFAN1 locomotion with video-derived striking motions and uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching (TGMM) to construct diverse task-conditioned whole-body references. These references are transformed into a reactive policy through physics-based teacher--student learning with online DAgger distillation, followed by PPO fine-tuning for the tennis task. The resulting policy responds directly to robot and ball observations without requiring reference-motion inputs at deployment. On a real humanoid robot, ATHLETE achieves forehand and backhand hit rates of $90.00\%$ and $86.67\%$, respectively, and enables multi-shot rallies with human players. These results demonstrate that ATHLETE can learn dynamic humanoid tennis skills from reusable locomotion data and video demonstrations. Result videos and code can be found at https://anonymous.4open.science/w/ATHLETE2027/.
authors: Zhihao Tian, Zifan Wang, Enzheng Zhu, Xun Yang, Jialong Qin, Mengbo Wang, Junwei Liang
bullets: Addresses the costly need for extensive task-specific motion-capture data covering diverse tennis states.
Uses Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching to build task-conditioned whole-body references from locomotion data and ordinary tennis videos.
Distills these references into a reactive physics-based policy with online DAgger, then fine-tunes it with PPO.
The deployed policy uses only robot and ball observations, without reference-motion inputs.
On a real humanoid, it achieves 90.00% forehand and 86.67% backhand hit rates and supports multi-shot rallies.
papers.selection_reason: Learning reactive humanoid tennis from locomotion data and video demonstrations.
papers.title: ATHLETE: Learning Reactive Humanoid Tennis via Trajectory-Guided Motion Matching
papers.tldr: ATHLETE enables a humanoid robot to play reactive tennis by combining generic locomotion data with video-derived striking motions and trajectory-guided motion matching.

papers.abstract: Action-conditioned world models offer a promising foundation for generalist robotic intelligence by predicting the consequences of actions. However, existing robotic datasets provide limited coverage of the diverse interaction dynamics required for generalizable world modeling. Large-scale egocentric human videos offer complementary interaction experience, yet the embodiment gap between human hands and robotic manipulators hinders effective cross-embodiment learning. Meanwhile, the predominance of successful demonstrations leaves failure dynamics substantially underrepresented, limiting the ability of world models to anticipate unsuccessful executions. To address these limitations, we introduce HF-WM, an action-conditioned world model that combines Human interaction learning with Failure-aware post-training. To bridge the embodiment gap, we develop a dual-branch framework that couples video generation with auxiliary pointflow prediction, using stabilized pointflow as a unified motion representation across human and robot interactions while suppressing egocentric camera motion. To improve failure modeling, we further perform Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) post-training on perturbed actions derived from successful demonstrations, guided by action alignment and physical plausibility rewards, enabling the model to learn plausible failure dynamics without paired ground-truth videos. Extensive experiments demonstrate that HF-WM achieves state-of-the-art performance in action-conditioned video generation and exhibits strong utility for policy evaluation in downstream robotic tasks.
authors: Peiyan Tu, Cong Wang, Hanxin Zhu, Xin Jin, Zhibo Chen
bullets: Addresses limited interaction diversity, the human–robot embodiment gap, and the underrepresentation of failures in robot datasets.
Uses a dual-branch model combining action-conditioned video generation with auxiliary pointflow prediction.
Employs stabilized pointflow to represent motion across human and robot interactions while reducing egocentric camera-motion effects.
Applies GRPO post-training to perturbed actions, guided by action-alignment and physical-plausibility rewards, without paired failure videos.
Experiments report state-of-the-art action-conditioned video generation and strong utility for downstream robotic policy evaluation.
papers.selection_reason: Action-conditioned world model learning from human videos and modeling failure dynamics.
papers.title: Beyond Successful Robot Demonstrations: Learning from Human Interactions and Modeling Failure Dynamics
papers.tldr: HF-WM improves robotic world modeling by learning from human interactions and synthesizing failure dynamics from perturbed successful demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Collecting dexterous manipulation demonstrations for each robot hand requires repeated task-specific data acquisition. We ask whether one shared corpus of natural human demonstrations can instead serve as a reusable data interface for different dexterous hands, without collecting task demonstrations on each target robot. We present Human2Dex, a wrist-centric human demonstration interface that separates shared human observation and motion semantics from embodiment-specific execution. It aligns observations through local hand-appearance adaptation and a shared 21-point hand representation with consistent structural semantics across human and robot observations. It constructs executable supervision by retargeting fused human hand motion to each target hand, and introduces the Grasp-Pocket Interaction Representation (GPIR) to express tracked objects relative to a hand-centered Functional Grasp Pocket. The corpus is converted into separate training sets for Linker O6 and Wuji, while action labels, normalization, training, and diffusion-policy checkpoints remain hand-specific. Across six real-world tasks, Human2Dex achieves 109/120 (90.8%) successes on Linker O6 and 97/120 (80.8%) on Wuji. Across both hands, Human-Raw achieves 63/240 (26.3%) successes, whereas the complete Human2Dex configuration achieves 206/240 (85.8%). These results support the use of wrist-centric human demonstrations as a reusable interface across calibrated dexterous hands while retaining embodiment-specific policy learning. The project website is publicly available at https://human2dex.pages.dev/.
authors: Jiachen Zhang, Yuanyuan Li, Shaqi Luo
bullets: Addresses the need to repeatedly collect task demonstrations for each robot hand.
Uses local hand-appearance adaptation and a shared 21-point hand representation to align human and robot observations.
Retargets human motion to each hand and introduces GPIR for hand-centered object representation.
Evaluated on six real-world tasks: 90.8% success on Linker O6 and 80.8% on Wuji.
The complete configuration reaches 85.8% success across both hands, versus 26.3% with raw human demonstrations.
papers.selection_reason: Uses wrist-centric human demonstrations for dexterous manipulation, directly relevant to learning from human videos and robot manipulation.
papers.title: Human2Dex: Dexterous Robot Learning from Wrist-Centric Human Demonstrations
papers.tldr: Human2Dex reuses wrist-centric human demonstrations to train policies for different dexterous robot hands, achieving high real-world task success without robot-specific data collection.

papers.abstract: Third-person human videos offer a scalable alternative to task-specific reward engineering, teleoperation, and manually scripted demonstrations for humanoid loco-manipulation. Recent video-to-humanoid systems have shown that noisy human motion, object trajectories, and contacts can be extracted from unstructured videos and refined into deployable skills. However, a key gap remains for contact-rich imitation: the task is often defined by world-frame contacts whose poses, timing, and speed must survive embodiment mismatch and runtime scene changes. Towards this, we present VICAR (Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting), a pipeline for learning humanoid interactive skills from third-person human videos. The system first recovers human motion, reconstructs task-relevant obstacles from monocular video, and then retargets the motion to a humanoid while preserving global contact poses, motion speed, and collision clearance. Unlike retargeting methods that only remove penetration or preserve local interaction geometry, our formulation represents user-specified contact poses and collision clearance as high-priority Lagrangian penalty terms and optimizes the full motion to remain smooth through contact-rich transitions. The resulting motions are used to train a contact-conditioned motion generator whose inputs include movable contact points enabling runtime adaptation to new contact positions. We demonstrate the framework on ten diverse third-person video skills, including six table-tennis serves, three object-pickup tasks, and ladder climbing, and deploy the learned skills on hardware. These results suggest that contact-preserving retargeting is a practical step toward humanoids that learn useful interactive behavior by watching humans.
authors: Dvij Kalaria, Bike Zhang, S. Shankar Sastry
bullets: Addresses contact-rich imitation under embodiment mismatch and changing runtime scenes.
Recovers human motion and task-relevant obstacles from monocular video, then performs contact-aware humanoid retargeting.
Uses high-priority Lagrangian penalties for user-specified contact poses and collision clearance while optimizing smooth motion.
Trains a contact-conditioned motion generator with movable contact points for adapting to new contact positions.
Demonstrated on ten skills—including table-tennis serves, object pickup, and ladder climbing—with hardware deployment.
papers.selection_reason: Presents VICAR for learning humanoid interactive skills from third-person human videos using contact-aware retargeting, effectively bridging video imitation and robot manipulation.
papers.title: VICAR: Video Imitation with Contact-Aware Retargeting for Humanoid Interactive Skills
papers.tldr: VICAR learns deployable humanoid interactive skills from third-person videos by retargeting human motion while preserving contacts, speed, and collision clearance.

papers.abstract: Learning from Demonstrations (LfD) enables robots to learn object manipulation directly from human demonstrations. In contrast to resource-intensive and labor-intensive teleoperation, egocentric demonstrations are easy to collect, enabling scalable data collection. Manipulated objects are often partially occluded in everyday environments, yet prior egocentric demonstration-based methods that require no robots or specialized teaching devices do not explicitly address occlusions. To fill this gap, we propose EgoReveal, a framework that learns viewpoint-repositioning together with manipulation actions from egocentric human demonstrations to reposition the viewpoint and obtain target visibility under partial occlusions. EgoReveal instantiates this as two imitation policies: one predicts the future camera-arm pose sequence from the current view and camera-arm pose, and the other predicts the future control commands from object keypoints and a history of control commands. EgoReveal switches between the two based on target visibility. In experiments where the manipulated object is partially occluded initially, EgoReveal repositions the camera to obtain visibility and completes the task more reliably than fixed-camera baselines.
authors: Hiromu Kurihara, Kazutoshi Tanaka, Masashi Hatano, Tadashi Kozuno, Hideo Saito, Mariko Isogawa
bullets: Addresses partial object occlusions, which prior robot-free egocentric demonstration methods do not explicitly handle.
Uses two imitation policies: one predicts camera-arm repositioning, and the other predicts manipulation controls.
Switches between viewpoint repositioning and manipulation based on target visibility.
Experiments show more reliable task completion than fixed-camera baselines when objects are initially occluded.
papers.selection_reason: Learns active vision and manipulation from egocentric demonstrations to handle partial occlusions, combining imitation learning with viewpoint repositioning.
papers.title: EgoReveal: Learning Active Vision and Object Manipulation under Partial Occlusions from Egocentric Demonstrations
papers.tldr: EgoReveal learns when to reposition a robot’s viewpoint and how to manipulate partially occluded objects from egocentric human demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Humanoid robots have many degrees of freedom and contact surfaces, yet most loco-manipulation research restricts manipulation to the hands and avoids other body contacts with the environment. To extend manipulation beyond the hands, we present PanTact, a system that learns humanoid whole-body dexterity, the capability to manipulate with any suitable body surface, directly from robot-free human demonstrations. Our key idea is to use contact as manipulation-centric information that transfers across embodiments. Contact locations and timing specify the interactions needed to accomplish a task, while the robot chooses how to coordinate its body to realize them within its own physical constraints. Specifically, PanTact captures, learns, and executes whole-body contact via: 1) a wearable, robot-free data collection interface that augments egocentric vision and bimanual UMI grippers with whole-body modular contact patches to record body contact locations and states; 2) a visuomotor policy that mitigates the egocentric observation gap and predicts whole-body contact goals; and 3) contact-aware whole-body control formulations that realize active contact goals using suitable robot surfaces. We deploy PanTact on a Unitree G1 humanoid without additional body contact sensors, demonstrating whole-body dexterity involving body support, pushing, sweeping, and load-sharing. Website: https://pantact.github.io
authors: Xiaomeng Xu, Han Zhang, Zhian Ruan, Xiaofeng Guo, Jinkun Cao, Ruihan Yang, Carmelo Sferrazza, Shuran Song, Guanya Shi
bullets: Addresses the limitation of hand-only loco-manipulation by enabling manipulation through diverse body surfaces.
Uses a wearable interface combining egocentric vision, bimanual grippers, and modular whole-body contact patches to capture demonstrations.
A visuomotor policy predicts whole-body contact goals while accounting for the egocentric observation gap.
Contact-aware whole-body control realizes these goals within the robot’s physical constraints.
Demonstrated on a Unitree G1 for support, pushing, sweeping, and load-sharing without additional body contact sensors.
papers.selection_reason: Fits whole-body robot manipulation learning from human demonstrations with contact and egocentric vision.
papers.title: PanTact: Teaching Whole-Body Dexterity with a Wearable Contact Interface
papers.tldr: PanTact teaches humanoid robots whole-body dexterity from robot-free human demonstrations by transferring contact locations and timing across embodiments.

papers.abstract: While learning dexterous manipulation from a single human video offers a promising alternative to costly robot demonstrations, many recent methods predominantly imitate demonstrated motions. Such strict motion matching often limits generalization to initial object poses, goal poses, and grasps not shown in the video. Alternatively, discovering a policy via reinforcement learning (RL) allows for broad generalization, but without prior guidance, it struggles with high-dimensional exploration in complex, multi-stage tasks. To address these coupled generalization and exploration challenges, we present Dex-One2Many, a real-to-sim-to-real framework that learns a generalizable dexterous manipulation policy from a single human video. Our key insight is to abstract the video into sequential scene graphs that guide RL, enabling efficient exploration while preserving broad generalizability. The graphs serve as generative constraints for sampling diverse reset states and provide dense rewards for each stage. Because the graphs constrain relations rather than exact poses, these reset states cover object poses and grasps beyond the video, while initializing each stage from them with dense rewards keeps exploration short and guided. Trained entirely in simulation, Dex-One2Many transfers zero-shot to a real multi-fingered hand. Across five tool-use and manipulation tasks, Dex-One2Many exceeds baselines by 6.5% in seen configurations, while its robust generalization widens this gap to 71% in unseen scenarios.
authors: Jusuk Lee, Sungha Kim, Yeonsoo Park, Jonguk Cheon, Yoonkyo Jung, Yongjun You, H. Jin Kim, Jia-Bin Huang, Furong Huang, Youngseok Jang, Seungjae Lee
bullets: Addresses the limited generalization of motion imitation and the difficult exploration of unguided RL in dexterous manipulation.
Abstracts the video into sequential scene graphs that guide multi-stage RL.
Uses scene graphs to generate diverse reset states and provide dense, stage-specific rewards.
Trains entirely in simulation and transfers zero-shot to a real multi-fingered hand.
Across five tasks, improves over baselines by 6.5% in seen configurations and 71% in unseen scenarios.
papers.selection_reason: Learns a generalizable dexterous manipulation policy from a single human video by abstracting the video into scene graphs to guide reinforcement learning, enabling broad generalization to unseen configurations.
papers.title: Dex-One2Many: Learning Dexterous Manipulation from a Single Human Demonstration
papers.tldr: Dex-One2Many turns one human demonstration into scene-graph-guided reinforcement learning, enabling a dexterous robot hand to generalize beyond the demonstrated poses and grasps.

papers.abstract: World models offer a promising alternative to physics-based simulators, yet remain far from practical deployment. We ask how far scaling ego-centric human video takes them, using a dataset of 30,000 hours spanning over 1,000 scene types and 14,000 contributors. Rather than relying on opaque downstream metrics, we directly evaluate agent and object-interaction fidelity on a challenging out-of-distribution benchmark. Increasing training data by 100x improves both, but unevenly: the agent is modeled well, while object fidelity remains far lower and improves slowly. We show that the agent gains need not come from data, and a careful visual conditioning design saturates fidelity with a fraction of it, which lets us measure object fidelity on its own and discover its saturation point. We then introduce a supervision scheme that shifts capacity from scene appearance toward object dynamics, improving object fidelity though a substantial gap remains. Finally, our conclusions transfer to downstream humanoid modeling. Overall, our results suggest that scaling ego-centric data brings agent modeling close to its limit while leaving its effects on the world far behind, and that closing this gap will depend on how models are trained, not only on how much data they see.
authors: Jiahua Dong, Anurag Bagchi, Yash Jangir, Muhammad Zubair Irshad, Sergey Zakharov, Martial Hebert, Homanga Bharadhwaj, Yu-Xiong Wang, Vitor Campagnolo Guizilini, Pavel Tokmakov
bullets: Evaluates agent and object-interaction fidelity directly on a challenging out-of-distribution benchmark.
A 100× increase in training data improves both capabilities unevenly: agent modeling is strong, while object fidelity improves slowly and remains low.
Visual conditioning can reach agent-fidelity saturation with much less data, enabling isolated measurement of object fidelity and its saturation point.
A supervision scheme reallocating capacity from scene appearance to object dynamics improves object fidelity, but a substantial gap remains.
Findings also transfer to downstream humanoid modeling, suggesting training design is more important than data scale for closing the gap.
papers.selection_reason: Scaling study of ego-centric video for world models, evaluating agent/object fidelity; relevant to world models and human video learning.
papers.title: What 30,000 Hours of Ego-centric Video Does Not Teach
papers.tldr: Scaling 30,000 hours of ego-centric video models human agents well, but object interactions remain substantially less faithful and require better training—not just more data.

papers.abstract: Human demonstrations are a scalable data source for learning dexterous manipulation, but the embodiment gap prevents human motion from being executed directly on robots. Inverse kinematics (IK) retargets human motion to robots efficiently but ignores dynamics, often producing infeasible motions. Reinforcement learning (RL) and sampling-based model predictive control (MPC) are commonly employed to yield dynamically feasible motions, but both are sample-inefficient and sensitive to hyperparameters. RL suffers from costly and unstable training and tedious reward engineering; MPC avoids policy optimization, yet retargets each trajectory in isolation, and solving one does not make the next easier. Sampling cost grows rapidly with dataset size and task difficulty. We hypothesize that dynamically feasible trajectories concentrate near a low-dimensional manifold shared across demonstrations, so that retargeting can be reduced to sampling from that manifold, conditioned on human motion, rather than solving a fresh optimization problem for every demonstration. We propose \textbf{Generative Neural Retargeting} (GNR), which uses a flow matching model to sample feasible trajectories. GNR outperforms MPC with only $8.5\%$ of the samples required by MPC, achieving a success rate of $56.20\%$ compared to $27.20\%$ for MPC. GNR can be used for scalable and efficient retargeting of large-scale, long-horizon, and millimeter precision human demonstrations: by applying GNR within a real-to-sim data engine, we produce a dexterous manipulation dataset with dense contact-force labels, spanning $223$k demonstrations and $3.3$k object geometries.
authors: Dechen Gao, Yue Yang, Ben Abbatematteo, Nathan Godwin, Pengcheng Wang, Roger Boldu, Steven Man, Zhiyang Dou, Chuan Qin, Sho Nakagome, Eric Whitmire
bullets: Human-to-robot retargeting faces an embodiment gap: IK is efficient but neglects dynamics, while RL and MPC are costly and sample-inefficient.
GNR models dynamically feasible trajectories as a low-dimensional manifold shared across demonstrations and samples from it conditioned on human motion.
It achieves a 56.20% success rate versus 27.20% for MPC while using only 8.5% as many samples.
Applied in a real-to-sim data engine, GNR generates a dataset of 223k demonstrations across 3.3k object geometries with dense contact-force labels.
papers.selection_reason: Generative retargeting of human demonstrations to dexterous robot manipulation via flow matching.
papers.title: Generative Neural Retargeting for Human-to-Robot Dexterous Manipulation
papers.tldr: Generative Neural Retargeting uses flow matching to efficiently convert human demonstrations into dynamically feasible robot trajectories.

papers.abstract: Teaching a humanoid to follow instructions with its whole body runs into two obstacles. Its action space is large and tightly coupled: legs, arms, and fingers must move together while the robot keeps its balance, which makes joint-level actions hard to learn. And humanoid demonstrations are scarce, so current humanoid generalist policies do not follow new instructions out of the box and are fine-tuned on teleoperated demonstrations of each task before deployment. Human demonstrations exist in far larger numbers, but a person's motion is not a robot command. We remove both obstacles by changing what the generalist policy predicts. We introduce VioLA, a generalist humanoid policy that predicts body and hand motion latents instead of joint commands. A pretrained body- and hand-controller execute these latents on the robot. Their corresponding motion encoders map human and robot motion into the same latent spaces. A human recording is therefore labeled in the policy's action space, and the training demonstration pool contains 140.6 million frames, 93.2% of them human. As a result, VioLA follows locomotion instructions on the real robot zero-shot, without task-specific fine-tuning, reaching 100% success where GR00T N1.7 and $\Psi_0$ reach 16.7% and 0%, respectively. It also reaches 88.6% manipulation success without task-specific fine-tuning. The same approach works across two VLA and one world-action model backbones. A generalist policy trained on human demonstrations alone performs locomotion tasks on the real robot zero-shot. Code and checkpoints will be released.
authors: Mert Albaba, Jens Bei{\ss}wenger, Anna Manasyan, Daniel Marta, Michael J. Black, Wieland Brendel, Andreas Krause, Georg Martius, Martin Riedmiller
bullets: Humanoid control is difficult because whole-body actions are high-dimensional, tightly coupled, and require balance; robot demonstrations are also scarce.
VioLA predicts body and hand motion latents, which pretrained controllers convert into robot actions.
Shared motion encoders align human and robot movements, allowing human recordings to directly supervise the policy.
Training uses 140.6 million frames, 93.2% from humans, and supports multiple policy backbones.
On a real robot, VioLA achieves 100% zero-shot locomotion success and 88.6% manipulation success without task-specific fine-tuning.
papers.selection_reason: Introduces VioLA, a generalist humanoid policy that predicts body and hand motion latents instead of joint commands, enabling zero-shot locomotion and manipulation from human demonstrations. This directly addresses the large action space and data scarcity challenges in embodied AI.
papers.title: VioLA: Learning Generalist Humanoid Control Policies from Human Data
papers.tldr: VioLA enables zero-shot humanoid control by predicting body and hand motion latents learned from large-scale human and robot motion data instead of joint commands.

papers.abstract: Generating realistic human-object interactions (HOI) in complex 3D scenes requires two complementary capabilities: reasoning about interaction feasibility in the environment and synthesizing realistic human-object motion. However, supervision for these capabilities is rarely available jointly at scale. Human-scene datasets provide rich information about environment-aware motion, while human-object datasets capture detailed interaction dynamics, yet paired human-object-scene data remain scarce. We present MAMHOI, an affordance-mediated factorization for scene-aware human-object interaction generation. MAMHOI factorizes scene-aware HOI generation through an explicit motion-affordance interface between scene understanding and motion synthesis: a scene-conditioned model first predicts where and how an interaction can be feasibly executed, and an affordance-conditioned HOI model then generates the corresponding human-object motion. This factorization allows scene understanding and interaction dynamics to be learned from complementary sources of supervision without requiring paired human-object-scene data. Experiments in complex indoor environments show that MAMHOI reduces object--scene penetration while better preserving human--object interaction quality, yielding more realistic and physically feasible scene-aware interactions. Project page: https://leimingyuan.github.io/MAMHOI-project-page/
authors: Mingyuan Lei, Yoonchang Sung, Tat-Jen Cham
bullets: Addresses the scarcity of paired human–object–scene training data.
Uses a scene-conditioned model to predict where and how an interaction can feasibly occur.
Feeds these motion affordances into a separate human–object interaction model to synthesize motion.
Experiments in complex indoor scenes show reduced object–scene penetration while preserving interaction quality.
Scope: relies on affordances as the interface between complementary scene and interaction supervision.
papers.selection_reason: Affordance-based scene-aware human-object interaction generation is plausibly transferable to embodied manipulation and human video learning.
papers.title: MAMHOI: Factorizing Scene-Aware Human-Object Interaction through Affordances
papers.tldr: MAMHOI generates realistic, physically feasible human–object interactions in complex 3D scenes by mediating scene reasoning and motion synthesis through predicted affordances.

papers.abstract: Egocentric world models predict first-person observations conditioned on an agent's actions, but most focus on a single agent. Real embodied settings often involve multiple agents that act and interact within a shared environment. Existing multi-agent world models rely on coarse actions like locomotion, camera control, or discrete commands, leaving fine-grained embodied interactions underexplored. We formulate multi-agent egocentric world modeling as synchronized ego-stream generation for multiple agents interacting through fine-grained actions in a shared world. This requires cross-view action consistency, shared-environment consistency, and consistent propagation of interaction-induced state updates. We propose Multi-agent Egocentric World Model (ME-World), which jointly denoises multiple ego streams in a shared token sequence, conditions each stream on all agents' target-view poses, and grounds generation with shared environment memory. We train and evaluate on real and synthetic multi-agent data and introduce shared-world consistency metrics for environment, update, and identity consistency. Experiments show ME-World improves shared-world consistency, action control, identity preservation, and video quality over existing methods.
authors: Dahyun Chung, Siyoon Jin, Hyunwook Choi, Honggyu An, Junyoung Seo, Hyunsung Kim, Seung Wook Kim, Seungryong Kim
bullets: Addresses the limited modeling of multi-agent embodied interactions beyond coarse movement and camera actions.
Jointly denoises multiple ego streams while conditioning on all agents’ target poses.
Uses shared environment memory to maintain cross-view, shared-world, and interaction-update consistency.
Introduces metrics for environment, update, and identity consistency.
Experiments on real and synthetic multi-agent data show improvements in consistency, action control, identity preservation, and video quality.
papers.selection_reason: Proposes a multi-agent egocentric world model for fine-grained embodied interaction, directly relevant to Embodied AI and World Models.
papers.title: Multi-Agent Egocentric World Model with Fine-Grained Embodied Interaction
papers.tldr: ME-World generates synchronized first-person videos for multiple agents performing fine-grained interactions in a shared environment.

papers.abstract: A robot that assists people must often act on what a person has shown rather than said: which of several identical cartons was pointed at, or which box was handled. The plan is executed from the final scene, whereas the evidence occurs earlier, possibly on objects that have since moved. We propose instance-anchored interaction evidence (IAE), which registers every object of the final scene to its public identifier, keeps each identity through the video by backward mask propagation, and describes every frame by the geometry between hands, forearms and these instances. An evidence network trained only from task outcomes scores the instances. For pointing tasks, a grammar-constrained dynamic program trained with a structured loss decodes object-destination programs; symbolic programs handle reference disambiguation and, without learning, episodic tasks. On 1,255 WatchAct benchmark requests, scored by symbolic execution, IAE reaches 64.2% plan success on implicit-intent tasks against 27.5% for a 32B vision-language model (strict success 49.7% against 15.4%), and 46.4% against 27.0% on restoration, reversal and imitation without task-specific training. Controls with the same perception overlays, the same 32 frames, forward tracking, or a relation model trained on the same labels do not explain the gain. Given IAE's evidence as text with its meaning explained, the same language model reaches 57.4%: most of the gain comes from the instance-anchored evidence, and the explicit programs add 6.8 points at a fraction of the cost. Pointing remains the hardest case, with 16.9% strict success. The code is available at https://github.com/WeiZhou96/iae-watchact.
authors: Xinliang Xiao, Bowen Yang, Wenjing Zhang, Li Yang, Wei Zhou
bullets: Addresses the challenge of linking earlier pointing or handling actions to objects that may later move or look identical.
Tracks final-scene object identities backward through video and represents hand–forearm–object geometry as interaction evidence.
Uses an outcome-trained evidence network, grammar-constrained program decoding for pointing, and symbolic programs for reference resolution and episodic tasks.

On 1,255 WatchAct requests, IAE achieved 64.2% plan success on implicit-intent tasks versus 27.5% for a 32B vision-language model, and improved restoration, reversal, and imitation tasks without task-specific training.
Pointing remains difficult, with 16.9% strict success; language-model reasoning over textual IAE evidence captured most of the gain, while explicit programs added 6.8 percentage points.
papers.selection_reason: Grounds robot plans in human pointing and handling from video; fits learning from human video and embodied interaction.
papers.title: Instance-anchored interaction evidence: Grounding robot plans in human pointing and handling
papers.tldr: Instance-anchored interaction evidence helps robots infer which objects people indicated or handled, substantially improving plan execution from visual interaction history.

papers.abstract: Physically grounded manipulation of articulated objects requires understanding both the maximum forces encountered during contact and the work performed as their parts move. Peak contact force and mechanical work quantify these complementary aspects, but estimating them from egocentric video is challenging because physical interaction cues are local and indirect. Moreover, peak force is associated with brief contact events, whereas mechanical work depends on force-motion coupling throughout the contact duration. To address these challenges, we propose EgoPhys, an RGB-only framework comprising Contact-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CASA) and Target-Specific Multi-Expert Temporal Routing (TMTR). CASA integrates appearance and geometry features to emphasize interaction-relevant cues, while TMTR models semantic, event, and motion cues with specialized temporal experts and routes them separately for force and work prediction. On the test split from Hoi! dataset, EgoPhys substantially improves predictions of peak force and mechanical work, achieving MAEs of \(5.205 \pm 0.584\) $N$ and $0.894 \pm 0.081$ $J$, respectively.
authors: Zhuo Dong, Jianhua Yang, Haohao Li, Yumeng Zhao, Keji He, Yan Huang, Liang Wang
bullets: Addresses the challenge of inferring local, indirect physical interaction cues from egocentric manipulation video.
Uses Contact-Aware Spatial Aggregation (CASA) to emphasize appearance and geometry around interactions.
Uses Target-Specific Multi-Expert Temporal Routing (TMTR) to separately model cues for force and work prediction.
On the Hoi! test split, reports MAEs of 5.205 ± 0.584 N for peak force and 0.894 ± 0.081 J for mechanical work.
papers.selection_reason: Estimates physical interaction quantities from egocentric manipulation video, yielding embodied knowledge transferable to robot learning.
papers.title: EgoPhys: Estimating Peak Contact Force and Mechanical Work from Egocentric Manipulation Video
papers.tldr: EgoPhys estimates peak contact force and mechanical work from egocentric RGB video by combining contact-aware spatial features with task-specific temporal modeling.

papers.abstract: Humanoid loco-manipulation requires coordinated locomotion and manipulation informed by future scene evolution and whole-body motion, yet learning these capabilities is constrained by scarce robot demonstrations. Human video and motion datasets offer scalable supervision, but many contain only video or motion rather than paired video-motion data. Moreover, human motion does not directly specify executable robot actions. We present Being-M0.7, a latent world-action model that transfers visual-motion priors learned from mixed-modality human data to humanoid control through pre-training, robot mid-training, and action post-training. We curate a corpus from more than 10,000 hours of raw human-centric data, integrating video-only, motion-only, and paired video-motion streams to learn complementary visual dynamics and whole-body kinematic structure. Joint prediction of future latent visual states and motion encourages visual representations to encode future kinematics. Robot mid-training adapts this coarse-grained prior to robot viewpoints and body dynamics. During action post-training, an action expert combines visual predictive representations from the frozen, adapted prior with current images and proprioception through gated cross-attention, grounding predictive context in executable whole-body commands. Being-M0.7 achieves the highest aggregate success rate among the compared baselines on SIMPLE and matches the strongest baseline on real-world Unitree G1 loco-manipulation tasks.
authors: Junpeng Yue, Boyuan Li, Yuxuan Wang, Zepeng Wang, Yuhui Fu, Feiyang Xie, Yu Zhang, Jing Zhang, Xianqi Zhang, Weibo Li, Xiaofei Zheng, Yuming Fang, Jiangxing Wang, Zongqing Lu
bullets: Addresses the need for coordinated locomotion and manipulation that anticipates future scene changes and whole-body motion.
Pre-trains on mixed video-only, motion-only, and paired video-motion data, using joint future visual-state and motion prediction.
Adapts the learned prior to robot viewpoints and dynamics through robot mid-training.
An action expert combines frozen predictive representations with images and proprioception via gated cross-attention.
Achieves the highest aggregate success among compared baselines on SIMPLE and matches the strongest baseline on real-world Unitree G1 tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Latent world-action model for humanoid robots from human video/motion; fits embodied AI and world models.
papers.title: Being-M0.7: A Latent World-Action Model for Humanoid Robots
papers.tldr: Being-M0.7 transfers large-scale human video and motion priors into executable humanoid loco-manipulation actions despite scarce robot demonstrations.

papers.abstract: Monocular videos of human manipulation provide abundant dexterous demonstrations, yet reconstructing hand-object interaction from a single view and transferring it to robot hands remain difficult, limiting their direct use for robot execution. Prior methods either require task-specific RL training, limiting scalability, or assume clean motion-capture trajectories and thus cannot operate directly on video. We present OmniHOI, a pipeline that turns an RGB video of hand-object interaction into an interaction-faithful trajectory on dexterous hands. The key idea is to enforce physical consistency using the evidence available at each stage: image evidence during reconstruction, contact geometry during retargeting, and dynamics during physics-in-the-loop refinement. Each stage optimizes the corresponding representation directly, correcting errors before they propagate downstream or must be absorbed by a learned policy. Across 150 motion-capture trajectories transferred to each of five dexterous hands with 6 to 22 DoF, we achieve 39-89% success, compared with at most 31% for prior transfer methods. On 60 monocular video clips, we achieve 53% success, compared with 28% for the best prior video-to-robot pipeline. Its trajectories also execute on a real bimanual robot across diverse tasks.
authors: Ting Mao, Yanming Shao, Ziheng Wang, Haoyu Liu, Yiqun Wang, Xuanye Wu, Yao Mu
bullets: Addresses the challenge of transferring single-view human hand-object interactions to robot hands without task-specific RL or clean motion-capture input.
Uses image evidence for reconstruction, contact geometry for retargeting, and physics-in-the-loop dynamics refinement.
Evaluated across five dexterous hands, 150 motion-capture trajectories, and 60 monocular video clips.
Reports 39–89% success on motion-capture transfer and 53% on video-to-robot transfer, outperforming prior methods described in the abstract.
Demonstrates execution on a real bimanual robot across diverse tasks.
papers.selection_reason: Reconstructs dexterous hand-object interaction from monocular human video and transfers it to robot hands, directly fitting robot manipulation and learning from human video.
papers.title: OmniHOI: Dexterous Hand-Object Interaction from Monocular Human Video
papers.tldr: OmniHOI converts monocular human manipulation videos into physically consistent, executable dexterous-hand trajectories through staged reconstruction, contact-aware retargeting, and dynamics refinement.

papers.abstract: As we move through the world and carry out everyday tasks, we encounter objects that may become relevant only later. We are capable of recalling where we left something or what was inside a container, even without knowing we would need it later. Here, we study how an embodied assistant can build a similar memory from egocentric videos, by observing a person's day-to-day activities. We present Ledger, a persistent 3D object memory that combines object locations, their histories, and contextual descriptions. It associates observations across the recording and retains objects after they leave the view, including those the person never touches. It clusters each object's observations by resting locations and records a move only after repeated evidence, reducing the effect of localization noise. Short descriptions preserve details such as an object's contents or supporting surface. It saves these records to later answer spatial questions without having to access the original images or video. Our memory raises HD-EPIC accuracy from 29.7% to 42.6%, UCS-Bench accuracy from 33.8% to 38.5% and localizes Ego4D objects with a 0.99 m median error on returned predictions. Our analyses identify complementary roles for temporal persistence, contextual descriptions, and retrieval. Our study on 100 stitched streams of multiple scenes each further exposes failures in both retrieval and construction. Per-scene construction partially recovers the performance lost across scene changes compared to that of single scene streams.
bullets: Ledger combines object locations, histories, and contextual descriptions from egocentric video.
It clusters observations by resting locations and records moves only after repeated evidence, reducing localization noise.
It retains objects after they leave view, including objects the person never touches.
On HD-EPIC, accuracy improves from 29.7% to 42.6%; on UCS-Bench, from 33.8% to 38.5%.
Ego4D objects are localized with 0.99 m median error on returned predictions.
papers.selection_reason: Builds persistent 3D object memory for an embodied assistant from egocentric human video, directly matching embodied memory and human-video learning.
papers.title: Never Look Back: Understanding Persistence in 3D Object Memory from Egocentric Videos
papers.tldr: Ledger builds a persistent 3D object memory from egocentric video, improving spatial question answering and object localization by retaining object histories and contextual descriptions without re-accessing original video.

papers.abstract: Large-scale egocentric human interaction data is becoming an important source of physical supervision for embodied learning, yet video alone leaves the contact and pressure that characterize physical interaction unrecorded. Recent visual-tactile datasets provide this missing supervision, but their synchronized tactile data remain far smaller in volume than human video. Moreover, the largest resources often merge recordings from different sensors or annotation procedures, which makes the effect of data scale difficult to isolate. We therefore introduce TouchScale, a 500-hour dataset of contact-rich human interaction recorded with a single unified wearable setup. Its approximately 2K predefined task descriptions span everyday activities and structured manipulation, and each recording temporally aligns egocentric RGB-D video with wrist RGB video and dense full-hand bimanual tactile measurements. Compared with prior tactile data, training on the full TouchScale raises zero-shot contact IoU on data from an unseen tactile sensor from 0.134 to 0.383. Pretraining a visual encoder on TouchScale also yields the highest action recognition accuracy on three benchmarks among the compared visual-tactile datasets. Used for visual-tactile mid-training of a robot policy, TouchScale improves the average real-world success rate across four contact-rich manipulation tasks from 22.5% to 57.5%. With the sensor and collection protocol held fixed, both zero-shot tactile prediction and robot success show an overall upward trend as more TouchScale data is used. These results suggest that human visual-tactile data collected at scale with consistent sensing benefits both perception and robot manipulation. We will publicly release TouchScale, including all synchronized visual-tactile recordings and reconstructed object models, to support future research on scalable visual-tactile learning.
bullets: Addresses the limited scale and inconsistent sensing protocols of existing visual-tactile datasets.
Contains approximately 2K task descriptions covering everyday activities and structured manipulation.
Synchronizes egocentric RGB-D, wrist RGB, and dense full-hand bimanual tactile measurements from one wearable setup.
Improves zero-shot contact IoU from 0.134 to 0.383 and raises average robot success from 22.5% to 57.5% across four tasks.
Performance generally increases with more data; the dataset and reconstructed object models will be publicly released.
papers.selection_reason: Unified egocentric visual-tactile dataset directly supports embodied skill learning and robot manipulation.
papers.title: TouchScale: 500 Hours of Human Vision and Touch for Visual-Tactile Learning
papers.tldr: TouchScale is a unified 500-hour visual-tactile dataset showing that scaling consistent human interaction data improves tactile prediction, action recognition, and robot manipulation.

papers.abstract: Recently, approaches that leverage human video datasets for robot policy training have become increasingly prevalent. However, most existing hand trackers regress pose from cropped frames with limited priors on hand motion and object interaction, resulting in inaccurate and physically inconsistent estimates. Moreover, the lack of physical cues, e.g., contact and force, limits the use of human videos for robot policy training. To this end, we propose RLHND, a video foundation model-based hand tracking model that jointly estimates hand pose and realistic tactile information from monocular egocentric videos. RLHND turns the pre-trained Cosmos 3 video diffusion backbone into a deterministic clip-level feature extractor via clean-latent conditioning, carrying its learned priors on hand motion and hand-object interaction into tracking. For pose estimation, RLHND (i) predicts hand poses with anatomically plausible joint angles and (ii) enables optional conditioning on the shape parameter to maintain consistent hand shape within the same video and even across videos recorded by the same actor. For tactile estimation, a separate tactile expert stream, trained with the pose stream frozen, predicts dense contact and force over the hand surface. We further adopt LBS-based feature spreading to enable vertex-wise feature extraction without costly per-vertex attention. RLHND achieves state-of-the-art performance across various benchmark datasets for pose estimation, while also achieving state-of-the-art performance in contact and force estimation. Moreover, we demonstrate the utility of RLHND for robot learning through retargeting results and real-world robot experiments. The code will be publicly available at https://seungjun-moon.github.io/rlhnd/.
bullets: Addresses inaccurate, physically inconsistent hand tracking and the lack of contact/force cues in human-video-based robot training.
Uses a pretrained Cosmos 3 video diffusion backbone as a deterministic clip-level feature extractor with learned motion and hand–object interaction priors.
Predicts anatomically plausible poses, supports hand-shape conditioning, and uses a separate tactile stream for dense contact and force estimation.
Applies LBS-based feature spreading for efficient vertex-wise hand features.
Reports state-of-the-art pose, contact, and force estimation across benchmarks, with retargeting and real-world robot demonstrations.
papers.selection_reason: Hand tracking and tactile estimation from egocentric human video for robot learning and retargeting.
papers.title: RLHND: Video Foundation Models as Physically Grounded Hand Trackers for Robot Learning
papers.tldr: RLHND adapts a video foundation model to jointly track physically plausible hand poses and estimate tactile contact and force from monocular egocentric video for robot learning.

papers.abstract: Human videos provide rich motion targets for humanoid learning, yet visually plausible references can still produce persistent failures under physics-based execution. These failures reveal where training supervision should change. We present MimicX, a policy-in-the-loop framework that uses execution feedback to refine video-driven humanoid motion tracking. Starting from reconstructed and retargeted motion, MimicX localizes difficult transitions and affected body regions, then jointly adapts tracking objectives and the reset curriculum for policy continuation. Repeated rollout verification selects execution-priority improvements subject to tracking guards. Across four core video tasks, MimicX consistently improves tracking accuracy and Robust Execution Horizon relative to the Fixed Reference baseline. Task-averaged results show a 25.7% reduction in body-tracking error and a 255.6% increase in execution horizon. Additional video, motion-reference, and collision-scene studies evaluate the method beyond the core tasks, while MimicX-HLoop accelerates feedback through heterogeneous execution. Overall, MimicX turns policy failure into actionable supervision for deciding what to refine and which refinement to retain.
bullets: Addresses persistent physics-execution failures despite visually plausible video-derived motion targets.
Localizes difficult transitions and affected body regions, then jointly adapts tracking objectives and reset curricula.
Uses repeated rollout verification with tracking guards to retain execution-priority refinements.
Across four core video tasks, reduces body-tracking error by 25.7% and increases Robust Execution Horizon by 255.6% versus a fixed-reference baseline.
Additional studies examine video, motion-reference, collision-scene, and heterogeneous-feedback settings.
papers.selection_reason: Directly addresses video-driven humanoid motion tracking and policy learning from human videos, fitting embodied AI and robot learning.
papers.title: MimicX: Policy-in-the-Loop Supervision Refinement for Video-Driven Humanoid Motion Tracking
papers.tldr: MimicX uses policy execution feedback to refine motion-tracking objectives and reset curricula, improving humanoid tracking and robustness from video references.

papers.abstract: Video-based policy learning is particularly promising, as it illustrates target behaviors without requiring action annotations or embodiment-matched demonstrations. A central challenge is deciding what information should be transferred from the video to the robot. Existing approaches commonly convert visual observations into scalar similarity or value signals, or ask foundation models to directly generate reward code. These approaches can make the temporal structure of a task difficult to inspect, ground, and reuse. We present Video2STL, a framework that converts observation-only videos into parametric Signal Temporal Logic (STL) specifications and uses the resulting formal representation for robot learning. A vision-language model extracts an embodiment-independent semantic event trace and constructs a bank of symbolic temporal specifications. The model determines the task structure, while numerical predicate thresholds and temporal bounds are grounded from successful robot trajectories. For policy learning, we separate short- and long-timescale temporal information: short-horizon specifications provide dense rewards through rolling-window quantitative robustness, while a causal monitor over a retained long-horizon specification provides one-time progress rewards for valid temporal prefixes. The same representation supports cross-embodiment transfer from human or animal videos to robot control. Across four manipulation tasks, Video2STL achieves $85.8\%$ average success-once and $67.0\%$ success-at-end, compared with $81.5\%/59.5\%$ for native dense PPO and $65.0\%/42.3\%$ for Text2Reward; in quadruped locomotion, Qwen-3.8 and GPT-5.6-based Video2STL policies achieve $100\%$ success across velocities from $0.3$ to $2.1\,\mathrm{m/s}$ while remaining competitive in high-speed energy efficiency. Project webpage: \href{https://video2stl.github.io/}{video2stl}.
bullets: A vision-language model extracts embodiment-independent semantic event traces and proposes symbolic temporal specifications.
Robot trajectories ground predicate thresholds and temporal bounds, making the specifications executable and reusable.
Short-horizon STL rules provide dense rewards, while causal monitoring of long-horizon rules supplies progress rewards for valid temporal prefixes.
The framework supports transferring behaviors from human or animal videos across robot embodiments.
Across four manipulation tasks, it reports 85.8% success-once and 67.0% success-at-end; quadruped policies achieve 100% success across 0.3–2.1 m/s velocities.
papers.selection_reason: Converting human and animal videos into temporal specifications for robot learning directly fits learning from human videos and robot learning.
papers.title: Video2STL: Grounding VLM-Generated Temporal Specifications for Robot Learning
papers.tldr: Video2STL turns observation-only videos into interpretable Signal Temporal Logic specifications that provide grounded temporal rewards for robot policy learning.

papers.abstract: Egocentric human data offer a path to scaling robot learning beyond costly robot demonstrations, yet the embodiment gap makes raw human trajectories a poor supervisory target for control. Our key insight is that, although low-level actions are embodiment-specific, their underlying motion intent can capture task-relevant structure that transfers across humans and robots. We introduce EgoLAP, a VLA pre-training framework that jointly learns from human and robot trajectories through a shared language-based action chain-of-thought. EgoLAP expresses motion intent as structured, temporally abstracted language actions and pairs them with motion-level reasoning grounded in scene geometry, physics, and object affordances. Across extensive real-world and simulated experiments, EgoLAP transfers human experience to robot control more effectively than alternative action representations and reaches 80.1% mean real-world task progress, a 2.3x performance gain over alternative action representations. Motion-level reasoning also outperforms a composite reasoning format that combines subtask, object-box, and visual-trace reasoning.
bullets: Addresses the embodiment gap between human trajectories and robot control.
Jointly pre-trains on human and robot trajectories using a shared language-based action chain-of-thought.
Structures motion intent with reasoning grounded in scene geometry, physics, and object affordances.
Achieves 80.1% mean real-world task progress and a 2.3× gain over alternative action representations.
Motion-level reasoning outperforms a composite format combining subtask, object-box, and visual-trace reasoning.
papers.selection_reason: VLA pretraining from egocentric human videos with language-based action chain-of-thought; directly fits embodied AI, VLA, learning from human video, and robot learning.
papers.title: EgoLAP: Learning from Egocentric Human Data through Language-Action Reasoning
papers.tldr: EgoLAP transfers egocentric human experience to robot control by representing motion intent as language-based, temporally abstracted action reasoning.

papers.abstract: Modern action recognition models rely on video transformers pretrained on massive collections of web-crawled videos, such as Kinetics-700. However, the use of such data raises ethical concerns, as subjects' consent is typically not obtained. Recent high-quality synthetic video datasets generated from motion-capture data, such as BEDLAM2.0, offer a promising ethical alternative. In this work, we investigate self-supervised pretraining of video transformers on synthetic human-motion datasets.
